subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 KEMANO II PROJECT
speechtext: I have received one application pursuant to Standing Order 52. I will hear the hon. member for Skeena.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 KEMANO II PROJECT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 52 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the finding by the committee for the scrutiny of regulations of this House that the 1990 decision by the federal cabinet to exempt Alcan's Kemano II project from environmental assessment was both illegal and unconstitutional.
This matter must be debated here today because all other avenues have been exhausted, including an application to take this matter to the Supreme Court of Canada.
This is not a matter suitable to Question Period, statements or other parliamentary or legal venues. Five hundred million dollars has been illegally spent on the project and before any further consideration or evaluation of the project is made this House has a duty to debate the matter pursuant to Standing Order 52. Illegal and unconstitutional behaviour by the cabinet or Alcan is not to be condoned.
The scrutiny committee, which is composed of members of both this House and the other place, was created 15 years ago with the parliamentary responsibility to review government regulations. It operates under one of the most basic principles of parliamentary democracy, which is that the executive cannot make exemptions to the law unless Parliament gives it the power to do so.
I am sure you are aware, Madam Speaker, that the 1984 cabinet guidelines order under which Alcan was exempted from environmental assessment and review has no provision whatsoever in it to allow the cabinet or any minister of the Crown to exempt any project, let alone one of this size, from environmental assessment and review.
The project will remove 86 per cent of the natural flow from the Nechako River, one of the largest tributaries of the Fraser River which is one of the largest rivers in the western part of North America.
It may well be that members of the cabinet could, should and must be charged and perhaps fined or jailed for this illegal and unconstitutional activity, not the least of whom is the present Minister of the Environment.
I therefore urge you, Madam Speaker, to give active consideration over the next couple of hours to allowing an emergency debate under Standing Order 52 to proceed so that members of this House can perform our duties as all members must. This is the only forum in which this can be heard. Applications have been made to take the case to the Supreme Court of Canada and they have been turned down.
The Federal Court under the pen of Mr. Justice Walsh ordered that an environmental assessment and review be conducted and that was subsequently quashed by the Federal Court of Appeal.
There is no other opportunity for those Canadians who are affected to be heard in the legal system within Canada. There is no committee in this House now charged with this matter in that the Standing Joint Committee on Scrutiny of Regulations has performed its non-partisan duty in finding that this exemption is both illegal and unconstitutional. It bears directly upon members of the cabinet, including both members who are now running to replace the Prime Minister.
I think it is incumbent upon this Chamber to adjourn itself so that at eight o'clock we can hear from all sides of the House about one of the most serious constitutional and legal rulings ever made by a committee of this House. I would hope you would give it active consideration, Madam Speaker.
May 25, 1993

Routine Proceedings

Madam Speaker, I understand the interest that the hon. member has in this. As a member of the Standing Joint Committee on Scrutiny of Regulations I am wondering if he is not bringing this up a little prematurely.
He is referring to a report that is only a draft report at this time. It has not even been discussed at committee. It has not yet been presented to this House.
Madam Speaker, for your deliberation I would like to refer you to Beauchesne's sixth edition, page 241, citation 877 on premature disclosure of a report. It says:
(1) No act done at any committee should be divulged before it has been reported to the House. Upon this principle the House of Commons of the United Kingdom, on April 21,1937, resolved "That the evidence taken by any select committee of this House and the documents presented to such committee and which have not been reported to the House, ought not to be published by any member of such committee or by any other person".
This is a topic which is before another committee and I would suggest that in your deliberations, Madam Speaker, you should reserve judgment. This should not be a topic for further debate in this House before such time as the committee has had a chance to complete its deliberations and report to the House.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 52 KEMANO II PROJECT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am fully cognizant of the remarks just made by the member for Red Deer. I am sure you are aware this issue was printed on the front page of the business section of yesterday's The Globe and Mail. It was also referred to on the front page of The Globe and Mail and is being covered extensively by the media in this country.
The issue has been bogged down in the Standing Joint Committee on Scrutiny of Regulations for almost a year now. The actual legal finding that it was an illegal and unconstitutional decision of the cabinet was made almost a year ago. It may be reported to this House but it may not.
I think the time clock of this House is being intentionally observed to try to keep this extremely controversial issue out of the public domain and out of public debate. The member says that it may be reported and it may be voted on. There are a whole lot of "mays".
What we do know is that the legal counsel for this House and all members of that committee have now agreed that it was illegal and unconstitutional.
I think we would be entirely remiss in our duties if we did not at least debate this issue on behalf of all Canadians. If the cabinet is allowed to commit illegal and unconstitutional acts that affect my constituents and take 86 per cent of the flow out of rivers then they had better at least be debated here or we may as well shut this place down and keep it shut down.

Mr. Speaker, today I am speaking on an issue of critical concern to all Canadians.
The bill to implement the North American free trade agreement is before us today. It is my belief and the belief of my party that the bill threatens to dimmish the labour standards and the economic security of every Canadian.
As it stands now Bill C-115 does not have the teeth necessary to provide the economic security that Canadian workers need. It does not safeguard against environmental degradation. It does not safeguard against possible abuses and labour practices. It does not protect and provide for Canadians displaced because of the government's own economic mismanagement.
As we all know, in 1988 the government rammed through the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. At that time it promised it would create jobs and increase the standard of living for all Canadians. To date neither
of these promises has been realized. In fact the results of the free trade agreement have been dismal.
The official unemployment rate has risen from 7.5 per cent in 1989, to 10.3 per cent in 1991, to 11.4 per cent in April 1993. These figures are even more distressing when they are adjusted to include the underemployed, those Canadians wanting to work full time who are unable to find anything other than part-time work.
Almost 25 per cent of Canadians fall into this category. That is one out of every four Canadians. This, I would add, is a serious indictment of the government's economic mismanagement. At last count over 400,000 Canadian workers lost their jobs since the signing of the free trade agreement. Most of those jobs were lost as a result of permanent changes or closures of companies with plants in Mexico.
Furthermore, over-all production in the manufacturing sector in Canada has decreased by 14 per cent since 1988. Added to this poor economic performance has been the government's poor record in labour relations. The government has consistently demonstrated its disrespect for workers and has not consulted. It has repeatedly circumvented the collective bargaining process. It has consistently demonstrated its inability to prepare Canadian workers for changes in the global economy by failing to provide adequate worker adjustment programs.
As a result of both Canada's poor economic performance under the free trade agreement and the government's poor record on labour relations, millions of Canadian workers fear for their economic future. They justifiably feel the government has abandoned them to global forces.
My amendment is designed to provide the government with an opportunity to mend its ways in the area of labour relations by stating its resolve to respect the role which public and private sector unions have in representing the interests of workers; to honour the rights of all working people to organize, to bargain collectively and to strike; to encourage an open dialogue between management and labour, especially for decisions affecting the future of the work force as a result of this agreement; and to implement retraining and adjustment programs for workers displaced as a result of the agreement, including support for those wishing to become self-employed.
May 25, 1993

By accepting this amendment the government will be sending a very positive message to the Canadian people. It will be saying: "We are willing to protect the rights and standards of Canadian workers. We are committed to the meaningful negotiation of side accords with the U.S. and Mexico which will guarantee enforceable labour standards in all three countries". As a party we are not willing to pass a bill dramatically altering the economic future of Canada without adequately preparing the Canadian work force for those changes.
Before my short time concludes I want to talk a bit about the problems with this particular agreement. The reason we have an amendment such as this one in the preamble is that there has been no discussion as there has been in other countries of the importance of the work force or the importance of the protection of the standards of the people we as members of Parliament are here to serve.
It is our understanding that closure will be used at any minute in this place. We will be asked to pass NAFTA in a short three-day debate, whereas in the European Community it took 13 years. In those 13 years there has not been a fully integrated system for countries very similar to Mexico, those being Spain, Portugal and Greece. That is the concern that members on this side have about the government's attitude toward debates on fundamental change as it relates to the standards of the working people whom we are here to represent.
Let us look at what is wrong with the agreement. It is obviously a good deal for the multinationals, companies that are not interested in sovereignty, that are not interested in borders, but will flow back and forth anywhere in the world wherever they can get the best bang for their buck, wherever they can make the most money for their corporate friends and for the individuals they represent. What is bad about this deal is that it does not protect small business and it does not protect workers. It does not protect the sovereignty of Canada.
What members on this side of the House have tried to relate to their constituents and all Canadians is that we as a House of Commons, as parliamentarians who represent the people, should not be so quick to ram this agreement through the House.
Government Orders
What is missing in this agreement that is causing us such great concern? The Leader of the Opposition has said on many occasions that one of the big issues causing us a large amount of concern is that there is no subsidy code. Because there is no subsidy code we will in essence continue to get the kinds of harassment that we are getting from the American companies which feel threatened by our ability to be very productive and very competitive on the open market.
In conclusion I want to urge the government to give my amendment very serious consideration. It allows the government the opportunity to learn from its mistakes under the free trade agreement.
It is time for this government to do the right thing by the workers of this country and not to just look after the multinationals and their corporate friends. It should look after the bottom line which is the ability of workers to pay their taxes. If workers do not have jobs, which is what is happening under this corporate driven agenda, then we are going to be in desperate shape with regard to being able to pay our own way as a country.
We are going to have to turn around and redo this whole agreement once we are in office so I suggest to the government that it reconsider this whole issue.

Mr. Speaker, I too support the motion to which my hon. colleague was just speaking.
I sat in on the committee and I am very disappointed in not having the minister here today in order to get the answers we have been seeking at committee. I was in committee and I was assured that he would be here.
We are dealing with a bill of such importance that it can affect every part, every element of Canada for centuries to come. The consequences of this bill are huge. The thing that concerns us is this: Why are we rushing it through?
We said previously to Madam Speaker that we felt it was important, because we have five or six other bills today, that we deal with those bills first in order to get them through and, with the consent of the House, to debate them. I see other ministers here who are concerned about those bills. We could have in a serene, competent, efficient manner dealt with those other bills

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
and allowed the government to put up the competent people that it has, including the minister, to deal with Bill C-115 dealing with the application of the North American free trade agreement.
That is not what is happening. What is happening, as my colleague said earlier, is a type of treaty, a type of agreement that the European Economic Community took 13 years of compromise and discussion to negotiate. We are rolling up those 13 years into three days. That is a mockery of Parliament. That is a mockery of the parliamentary system. We were elected to represent our constituents.
I do not want to polarize the debate. I see that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has already said it is only the unions that are against Bill C-115. In my riding of Chambly I have heard very little from the unions against this bill. I have heard a lot from average nonunionized Canadians. In Quebec the workers in the cultural industries, particularly the composers, the authors and those who are writing computer programs are very concerned about what this bill does to the rights they have already acquired.
I see some of my friends on the other side. When we mention acquired rights in Quebec, we really touch a number of nerves. One of the nerves we touch is cultural rights because in Quebec authors or song writers will have less protection. After going through this bill in the next three days with this marathon legislation, if we pass it, artists will actually have less protection than they had from the 1971 Berne convention. That gave them and their estates protection so they could continue to sell their books, their songs and their screenplays.
If this bill becomes law in this marathon three day event, we are actually taking away acquired rights from Quebecers, from Ontarians, from artists all over this country. It is going to hit the artistic community right between the eyes. I think that is unpardonable.
It is not a union idea. It is not a union problem. It is a problem of basic common sense. When we talk about basic common sense and this government, it is an oxymoron. I am not calling this government a moron. I am saying essentially that when it comes to common sense and anything involving trade with the United States we seem to throw common sense out the window.
All the New Democratic Party is asking is that we behave as parliamentarians. Let us go through Bill C-115 with the minister present, with a serene debate on the issues so that we can know what is happening with this moving target with which we are dealing.
From day one the United States has had problems with the NAFTA. Right now it is teetering on the edge because it is seriously held up by the whole question of the side agreements that have to be passed. The Americans are saying that before they touch the NAFTA they want side agreements on the environment and on worker protection.
We in Canada are not saying that. We are saying: "We cover our eyes, Mr. Clinton. Give it to us and we will sign anything". That is not parliamentary. That is not even common sense. We should be dealing with this with our eyes open, with the minister here to help us, because it is a moving target. The whole question of sanctions has opened up a Pandora's box of definitions.
Speaking of definitions, we still do not know what is a subsidy. We have been hit hard by the question of subsidies. In Quebec our industries are concerned about what Americans call subsidies because we have a proud history of working hand in hand with our industries to help them out and to help our people out in order to create jobs. However, subsidies are not touched. Let us touch them. Let us define them.
Let us move ahead. Let us not just move sideways. Let us not start each side calling the other side a purveyor of actions which are only used to slow down the process. We are not doing that. We want the process to be meaningful. We want to be meaningful parliamentarians on this bill. As you yourself noted, Mr. Speaker, this bill has 27 individual motions, amendments, changes. On each one of those we have something to say but we need feedback from the other side. We do not want to talk in a vacuum. We want members on the other side who have studied this to tell us where we are wrong and also to have the presence of mind and the honesty to tell us where we are right. I will be darned if all 27 motions are wrong.
However, if we are going to do our job right and if the artists in Quebec, the artists in Kamloops, the artists in Ontario and the artists throughout the country are going to be protected then we need that free flow of informa-
May 25, 1993

tion. We need what we in the House of Commons call debate. I know that the idea may seem foreign to my friends on the other side, particularly when we do not have the minister with us to debate, but doggone it, it is not fair to come here prepared to argue a case as parliamentarians and then find we do not have anyone to argue with.
This is not some academic exercise. This is not where we simply make a show for our friends at home. They are vitally interested in both sides of the question. I will be darned if I will accept the minister of fisheries saying it is a union question. It is a Canadian question. It has nothing to do with unionism per se. It has to do with our sovereignty. It has to do with how we are going to live in the future. I am sorry to say again to my friends on the other side who have not understood it in the past that it has to do with jobs.
We are suffering right now a recovery which is called a jobless recovery. Why is it a jobless recovery? Where did those jobs go? Well, Mr. Speaker, I can only tell you a little bit of a modification on Horace Greely: "Go south, young man". That is where the jobs are going. The problem is that when we have an opportunity which we have not had in the past, to really go through the different motions on each side and debate in a free and open encounter, we cannot do so. I think that stinks.
I think both sides of the House should get down to business, look at each one of these motions and have the members on the other side give us the latest information that they have because, as I said, we are shooting at a moving target. The Americans are not going to give in. We are talking about parallel agreements which are substantial and the Americans are not going to sign a thing until they get those substantial side agreements. We should not touch or sign anything until we get the same.

Mr. Speaker, I am thankful to have the opportunity, even though it is only for 10 minutes, to speak in support of the motion of my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River.
My colleague in his former life was the vice-general chairman for the United Transportation Union. Because of that experience he brings to our Liberal caucus a very special understanding of the awareness and needs of
Government Orders
labour. I think in lieu of everything that has happened to labour in this country, especially in the last two and a half years, this motion is very appropriate.
I sometimes wonder where this government is coming from when it cannot support a motion like this. I read the words:
encourage an open dialogue between management and labour on all decisions affecting the future of the workforce as a result of this Agreement,
implement retraining and adjustment programs for workers displaced as a result of the Agreement, including support for those wishing to become self-employed;
This to me and to my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River is just basic dignity. One has to understand my experiences living in Toronto.
Our experience in the last little while in terms of plant closures in the manufacturing sector has everyone in our community scared out of their minds.
Just three weeks ago we had the funeral for the first complete assembly plant to be closed in Canadian history. It was the Scarborough van plant. It contributed over $2.5 billion to the balance sheet of General Motors Canada for 10 years. All of a sudden this plant is closed and in 18 months General Motors goes from employing 6,000 to 60,000 people in Mexico. The government wonders why we on this side of the House are objecting to this debate going on here today when we really have not had adequate discussion or the opportunity to look into every aspect of this. It is totally irresponsible.
This experience in terms of the trading relationship with Mexico has the confidence factor of every sector of the economy on its knees right now. The failure of the government to openly discuss this debate is wrong. Who is driving this debate? Who is pushing the government to move this forward in less than 12 parliamentary hours in the House of Commons? This is a bill that the Prime Minister himself said is going to change the entire the economic framework of our country.
There are members over there who stand by and say that 12 hours to 15 hours of debate is enough. It is wrong. It is wrong not just because of the time factor but because even the other principal partner in this agreement, the Americans, are not moving ahead.

Government Orders
President Clinton of the United States said that he would not send NAPTA to Congress without side deals. Here they are discussing the side deals, whether they are with labour or whether they are with environment, and yet we are sitting here ramming it through. There is absolutely no logic to that.
Canadians cannot understand why in this House of Commons this is going on. They wonder if there is not some way in the parliamentary process that the opposition can take the time to force debate. Try to explain closure to them where the government with its majority can just come in and put the hammer down and push this bill through.
I think my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River has put forward a motion here today that is very clear and very understandable. It is actually something that is not very much different from what President Clinton is saying. He wants to understand the same way my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River does. What are the implications in terms of labour and every aspect of it? What are the implications in terms of the environment?
All the children in Canada are learning in school right now that Mexican environmental standards are not the same as the standards we have in this country. There are no teeth in terms of an enforcement mechanism here to make sure that the Mexicans live up to a standard related to the environment that we have here.
Yet as we tiy to discuss these aspects or these flaws in the North American free trade agreement the government says: "We will give you a few minutes but then we are bringing in closure and that is the end of it because we are just going to hammer this North American free trade agreement through".
It is absolutely wrong. With only 12 to 15 weeks left of this government's tenure, which is in its fifth year, the very least it could do is to show courage and decency to all Canadians and have a proper debate.
This is a constructive motion put forward by my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River. The concerns of labour in this country should be dealt with in a meaningful and constructive way and in a way whereby we can
start getting some confidence going in this country again. However, the government walks away from it.
Once again the government shows its indifference and lack of sensitivity. This one really baffles me because the President of the United States has the common sense to say that there is no way they will have this NAFTA deal go to Congress unless they know specifically what the side deals are in relation to labour and the environment.
I do not even want to mention the Minister for International Trade today, but here we are with this momentous piece of legislation in this country and we are not even allowed as parliamentarians the privilege of debating it in full.
I think it is wrong and I think the people of Canada will let this government and this Conservative Party know it in the next 12 to 15 weeks.

Mr. Speaker, I hope this is not detracting from my 10 minutes. Ten minutes is what I have and 10 minutes is what members of this House are allowed to have on these very important amendments.
We can differ with the government on policies. We can argue extensively that the policies of this government have been devastating to the economy of this country. That is legitimate, fair and a difference of opinion.
However we cannot argue successfully against the arrogance of a government that would demand that this Chamber deal with these important amendments and this important legislation without the minister being present and then ram the legislation through again on closure.
There is a great deal of cynicism in this country about politicians per se. It is the behaviour of this government today that blackens the name of every single elected official in this Chamber. The cynicism that abounds in this land allows people to throw up their hands and say: "To hell with the whole system. We do not want to participate".
The same apathy that is out there is attacked by one of the contenders for the leadership of that party by saying that they are sons of bitches for being apathetic.

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
No, she did not.
May 25, 1993

That is exactly what she said. I want to say that the reason cynicism abounds in this country is because of the hypocrisy and stupidity of this government in the way it is handling this legislation. This is aside from the principle of disagreement which is the nature of the British parliamentary system. Crass cynicism is the method by which this is being rammed through the House.
My colleague, one of the members from Ontario who just spoke said how disappointed people were. They are not disappointed. They are disgusted. They are fed up and sick and tired of politics per se. We are all smeared because of this government.
The Prime Minister is not here. I accept that. However the Minister for International Trade is not here today for this debate. That is totally unacceptable and inexplicable in terms of how important this bill is and its impact on every single Canadian.
I have seven amendments all grouped into one envelope and I have 10 minutes to speak. My good friend, the member for Chambly, touched on an important issue that impacts on the survival of this country and that is the rights won in Quebec for the maintenance of a francophone culture.
There are ministers in this House who have argued that they believe in Canadian Confederation. They joined that government to maintain that strength and are now seeing sections of this bill striking at the very heart of the opportunity of intellectual property being maintained so that the regions of this country can survive under Confederation.
Quebec will be the first victim and that is a fact. One cannot deny it because these amendments and the debate on these amendments point out that the very fabric of what keeps this nation together is under assault by this bill.
I will not get a chance to go through all the detailed amendments that I put on. I will select one for a couple of minutes. Motion No. 27 asks simply and humbly for this government to assure some minimum standard of protection for people in this country such as the elderly, women and particularly children by adopting some of the aspects of the social charter of the European Community's economic union.
Government Orders
The European Community's economic union is being given by this government as the reason why we must expand these trading blocs. If that is indeed so and the government believes that, then for goodness' sake why do we not have the same safety standards and human rights standards as the European Community has put in writing?
I want to refer to one section, section 10, which concerns the protection of children and adolescents as it is written in the European Community social charter. It says that the minimum employment age must not be lower than the minimum school leaving age and in any case not lower than 15 years.
Why do I pick on this one narrow amendment? I will say why. We are going to join a low wage partner in Mexico that has no value of human rights or no health and safety standards. As a matter of fact that partner is still in the Dark Ages when it comes to the exploitation of young children on the job.
This government and that of the United States are embarked on a plan to throw employment standards back to the Dark Ages with a Dickensian threat that we had better accept this or we will have worse. Employers in this country have already threatened their workers by saying that if they do not accept changes in their contractual obligations then they will move to Mexico. The move will also imperil the kind of standards we have set in this country because there is not even a guarantee of minimum age for employment.
I challenge this government. It lied to me about going to Matamoros, Mexico and to Washington, D.C. I challenge this government to point out what protection there is from stopping the exploitation of children who are 12, 13 and 14 years of age in the Maquiladora zone. It never answered the challenge. There is no guarantee in this legislation that that kind of workshop mentality at 80 cents an hour will cease if we sign this agreement. As a matter of fact this bill is so evil that it will force us down to those standards rather than forcing them up to decent standards in Mexico.
It is the subject of a specific pastoral letter by the Mexican Council of Catholic Churches and it is one of their major concerns along with the Canadian Council of Catholic Bishops on economic statements who have looked at NAFTA and who are concerned about this.

Is that government to be condemned not only for signing this agreement and for permitting this to happen, but for prohibiting the kind of rational and thoughtful nation-wide debate there should be on this issue? It is to be condemned for that.
I am ashamed to be a member of this Chamber because after 25 years of public service we come down to a debate that is affecting the outcome of the country I love where there is a 10-minute speech allowed to each member of the opposition. I am ashamed of and disgusted by this government. Only a government that has cynically sold out any sense of nationhood or survival of this country could possibly parent this kind of legislation and the method of dealing with it.
There will not be a major broadcast of what I have to say. It will not be in headlines across this county. I have picked one small item: the exploitation of children.
It is there. It will happen. It will be condoned by this government and its successors in leadership. Let no Canadian citizen go by without marking today as the day a deliberate decision was made by the Conservative Party of this country to abandon a sense of decency and honour to ordinary people, particularly to children. Let it be marked with sadness. By God, I cannot wait for an election to get rid of this rotten, absolutely scandalous government.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak to the amendment I have moved this morning, Motion No. 33, in connection with Bill C-115, an act to implement the North American free trade agreement.

Again, may I thank the House for giving consent to allow the introduction of my motion.
The effect of the motion I have placed before the House would be to provide that this particular act not be proclaimed into law until we have achieved a position of full employment in this country, that is 4 per cent unemployment.
This amendment flows from a letter I wrote to the Prime Minister on November 3, 1992. Copies were sent to all the Progressive Conservative members of Parliament and all Progressive Conservative senators. That letter has received wide circulation and publicity in the media. I believe it is well known to all members of the House and to many members of the Canadian public.
The concern I have and the reason I moved this particular motion is not with the principles nor with the terms of NAFTA. It is with the timing of the NAFTA legislation going into effect. My concern with respect to this is that if it were implemented at the beginning of next year as is contemplated and if at that time we still have 11 per cent unemployment or anything of that nature, this would have a very negative impact on our country.
There is no question in my mind that the NAFTA is going to create some jobs. It is certainly going to create jobs in the long run. My concern is that it will not be creating jobs in the short run. My opinion is based upon statements made by people as learned as Gordon Ritchie who was our deputy free trade negotiator in 1988. He has said that Canada may benefit from NAFTA in the long run, but clearly Mexico will benefit most in the short run.
My feelings are also reinforced by a study which was done by the Toronto office of our own Department of Employment and Immigration. It said that NAFTA will accelerate trends to close Canadian branch plants and to move labour-intensive manufacturing firms to low-cost developing countries.
That does not mean to me that NAFTA is all bad. In fact, I believe that NAFTA is going to create some jobs but I have some real concerns about what the impact of NAFTA will be in the short run. This is at a time when our economy is being impacted by a great number of economic factors. Some of these factors are the global recession, adjustments due to technological change, the declining manufacturing base that is common to all industrialized countries, the globalization of production, the globalization of markets. There is the movement of
May 25, 1993

many head offices such as the Canadian head office of IBM in my own riding which has recently moved to the United States as have the head offices of many other companies. There is also the restructuring that has taken place inevitably due to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
All of those things are impacting on our economy. It is inevitable if we implement NAFTA in such an economic climate that some restructuring will take place and we are going to exacerbate a disturbing situation we presently have with respect to employment in this country.
Faced with all of those different factors going on in the economy, it is no wonder that many Canadians have enormous concerns about the future and their jobs. Many of them have lost their jobs already and are still unemployed; others fear they may very well lose their jobs. They are all concerned. Granted I believe the vast majority of Canadians realize the inevitability and that the benefits down the road from NAFTA are going to be substantial. Even with all of that however, it is understandable why it is so difficult for them to support implementing NAFTA at a time when unemployment is in excess of 11 per cent.
It seems to me if there were some alternative jobs to go to there would not be this problem. Flowever at this time we cannot offer hope of substantial change in the unemployment situation in the short run. If we could, I would be prepared to support implementation of this bill and the agreement immediately. Before it is implemented however, it seems to me that one way or another we are going to have to deal with the employment situation that has been brought on by the global recession, by the adjustments as a result of technology, by our declining manufacturing base, by the globalization of production and markets, by the movement of head offices elsewhere and by restructuring due to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement.
The only way we can do that is to refrain from adding another circumstance, another economic factor that is going to cause some problems until we have full employment in the traditional sense of a 4 per cent unemployment rate.
Government Orders
Many people have told me it is impossible to ever achieve a 4 per cent unemployment rate. As you know, Mr. Speaker, following the Second World War for some 25 years between 1946 and 1970 this country in effect had full employment. We had an unemployment rate that was less than 4 per cent. At the same time we had an inflation rate that was averaging some 3 per cent and we had interest rates lower than they are now, even though they are very low at the present time.
With that in mind, while I do support the principles of NAFTA and I do support the terms of the agreement, I cannot support the implementation of the NAFTA agreement at this time. I cannot support it until we have reached full employment in this country, an unemployment rate of 4 per cent or less. I hope the House is prepared to support my motion to ensure that although NAFTA is passed that it will not be implemented until we have full employment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to these amendments. Indeed, I cannot help but comment on some of the remarks that have been made. I remind my hon. friend from Don Valley that this is enabling legislation. Implementation of the NAFTA will not take place until some time later, after it is prepared for implementation as well in the other two countries involved. What we are dealing with here is the putting into place of the equipment that will allow the Government of Canada to put into effect the NAFTA when the other two partners have done the same.
I want to give my hon. friends opposite a little lesson in parliamentary procedure. There seems to have been a lot of huffing and puffing on the lack of opportunity to substantively debate the issues here. They have chosen to debate whether or not it is appropriate that the minister be in the House right now. I remind them that the process of legislation in this place has been for some time that it is the responsibility of the parliamentary secretary to the minister to shepherd legislation through the House. That is why I am here and will be here while this debate is proceeding.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
The minister has a variety of responsibilities, one of which is encouraging trade for Canada. That is what he is doing right now. He will be here to speak in these debates. I hope that my hon. friends, unlike when the minister spoke at second reading, will avail themselves of the opportunity to listen to what he has to say when he speaks in this debate as he will.
I cannot help but notice that my hon. friends from the New Democratic Party do not seem to want to debate NAFTA. They want to debate the procedure for debating NAFTA. Every time there is an opportunity to deal with the substance of the issues that are before this House, they prefer to discuss parliamentary procedure and whether we should be debating five minutes here or ten minutes there or twelve hours here or twenty-four hours there.
If the bottom line is that the New Democratic Party cannot stand in this place and debate the issues then my question is why have the-
