speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems that every time somebody on this side gets on a roll the members of the New Democratic Party feel they have to interrupt because somebody out there just might be listening.
In my usual rational and calm way, I would like to address myself to the amendments before the House right now. I would like to comment on each of them. In doing so I advise the House that there are no amendments in this particular cluster which the government can support and I would like to briefly say why.
Motion No. 1 tries to make the preamble specific. In fact the function and purpose of the preamble is to underline the general objectives of the government in implementing the agreement. That is why it is as it is.
The amendment proposed by my hon. friend in seeking to be more specific with respect to how it impacts on particular sectors or groups is not really appropriate in our judgment and therefore is unacceptable.
Motion No. 7 is unnecessary. The rules of NAFTA being based on article XI of GATT permit duties, taxes or other charges in appropriate circumstances and therefore the motion is unnecessary under the legislation.
Motions Nos. 27, 30, 31, 32 and indeed Motion No. 33, the one in the name of my hon. friend from Don Valley East, if accepted would take NAFTA far beyond where it is supposed to go. This is a trade agreement. I must say I have some difficulty listening to my hon. friends from time to time raise issues for example of sovereignty and concern themselves on whether or not other countries are going to be able to impact on what our standards and so on are here in Canada. This is simply a trade agreement.
If my hon. friends are concerned about the notion of a trade agreement with the United States and Mexico, I cannot imagine them wanting to give the right to the Mexicans and the Americans to legislate for us in a great variety of ways in the areas of social rights, the environment, human rights, and so on and so forth. I would remind my hon. friends that when we introduced this legislation it was to implement the NAFTA which is a trade agreement and a trade agreement only. That is what the legislation is before the House.
There is some suggestion that Motion No. 30 makes reference to labour and Motion No. 31 makes a reference to labour and the environment. I would remind all members that as we are dealing with this legislation, discussions are going on among Canada, the United States and Mexico to negotiate further agreements relating to topics including the environment and labour. As my hon. friends know they will be appropriate agreements if those parties can reach agreements with respect to those subjects.
I am sure if legislation is required by any of the agreements it will be brought in at a future date. This is a trade agreement and the government has made a commitment that this legislation will deal only with implementing that trade agreement. That is what it does and that is why those proposals are unacceptable. The same
May 25, 1993

thing would apply to the proposal relating to human rights in Motion No. 32.
Some of my hon. friends speak eloquently about the quality of life that is enjoyed or suffered by some people living in undesirable circumstances or conditions in Mexico. The best way to deal with those kinds of problems is to provide the economic development opportunities for the Mexican people to allow their economy to grow. Then they will see the kind of growth and development take place in their country as we have seen for example in Spain since it joined the common market. There has been tremendous growth and opportunity for increase in quality of lifestyle in that country. I think we have to look upon this as an opportunity for the Mexicans and to suggest that we should try to condemn the Mexicans to live in unacceptable circumstances forever is simply a proposition this government cannot accept.
We hear talk about the employment conditions in the Maquiladora region. If my hon. friends opposite will carefully read the NAFTA they will come to realize that the Maquiladora will cease to exist once the NAFTA is implemented because the reason for its existence will be removed.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a small miracle that we stand in the House today to support this motion which was proposed by my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River because of the extremely short duration of debate imposed upon us by the government regarding this legislation.
My colleague from Kenora-Rainy River has proposed an amendment which really would compel future governments to make retraining and adjustment programs for workers who are displaced as a result of the NAFTA readily available and accessible.
This is perhaps one of the most important and relevant motions in regard to this legislation for it directly affects the tens of thousands of Canadians who have lost their jobs since the free trade agreement was initiated. It will also allow those Canadians who will be displaced from their current employment by the NAFTA, if implemented, to receive some retraining and other forms of adjustment from the federally funded programs.
Retraining and adjustment programs have been the focal point of much discussion not only during this
Government Orders
debate on NAFTA but also during the free trade debate in 1988. Prior to the federal election the Prime Minister repeatedly asserted that his government would provide more than adequate adjustment and retraining programs for all displaced Canadian workers.
I quote from Hansard of December 13, 1988 when the Prime Minister said: "A responsible government must therefore provide the affected workers with the most generous programs possible". That is what we have done and will continue to do.
Either the government is very irresponsible or the Prime Minister was once again saying one thing while obviously meaning another: no new programs, no adjustment policies and no retraining for workers who have been inflicted with the pain of being unemployed as a direct result of the economic policies of the present government.
We recognize that in the global economy there will be job losses. However we also recognize the need for the federal government to assist those Canadians who are adversely affected. The federal government must play a leading role in initiating programs which will not act as a social safety net but as a trampoline for workers to launch themselves in a more positive direction.
The Advisory Council on Adjustment which was chaired by Jean de Grandpre presented its report to the House. In it were precise recommendations for the government to adopt in order to provide adjustment and retraining programs for Canadians.
Canadians from coast to coast are fed up with commissions whose results seem to be meaningless to the present government. Canadians who have been adversely affected by the FTA and will also be affected by the NAFTA want and deserve to know what the federal government will do to assist them in finding meaningful employment in the future.
In my riding of Nipissing and indeed throughout northern Ontario, as my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River has said, workers have lost their jobs and are now unable to find meaningful, well-paying jobs which would allow them to provide for their families and be productive members of Canadian society.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
In northern Ontario many communities depend solely on a single resource for their very survival. Many of the men and women who work in the mills and the mines as well as the secondary businesses in these communities have very little training in other fields. These people do not want to become wards of the state, dependent on welfare and social assistance. They want to work and they want to feel proud.
I have had people come into my office in North Bay and tell me how they have lost their jobs and can get no training or assistance to find a new job. I see their frustration and that is why today I am addressing members opposite and telling them directly that they have done absolutely nothing to create new programs for people to acquire new training. They have done absolutely nothing to provide displaced Canadians with the means to acquire further education so they can find jobs. They have cut employment and training programs by over 30 per cent during their tenure in office. Most recently, funding for programs such as FEDNOR which is crucial for economic development in northern Ontario has been cut and will continue to see a decrease in government funding over the next five years.
It is very clear to members on this side of the House that the government has done the complete opposite of what all its multimillion dollar commissions have recommended. Rather than expand programs it seems to have cut them. The Conservative government has literally inhibited Canadians from dealing with the new global trading realities and has shown no sign of changing its course.
It is interesting to note that as we talk about the need for a complete change in the retraining and adjustment programs in this country one of the Conservative leadership candidates has repeatedly stated that she supports all that free trade stands for in strengthening the different regions. The minister of defence has gone on the record as saying the free trade agreement does more for regional development in Canada than any policy in our history.
I am sure the thousands of people in northern Ontario who have lost their jobs since 1988 find little comfort in the would-be Prime Minister's remarks. I would encourage the minister while she is in northern Ontario this week to visit the communities where the unemployment
rate constantly hits 40 per cent and see for herself how great regional development has been under her party's economic policy. I am sure she will recognize that the free trade agreement has not been a boom for northern Ontario. Nor will the NAFTA agreement.
The defence minister and her colleagues do not understand that the single industry northern Ontario communities are less likely to rebound from a plant closure or mill closing than larger cities in more developed areas of Canada. When a mill or plant closes in northern Ontario an entire region and populace is devastated. Without effective adjustment programs in place, the workers who are affected can only turn to social assistance.
It is time for government to initiate programs that will provide incentives for displaced workers to retrain and educate themselves in order to gain meaningful employment. The federal government must play a vital role in ensuring that all Canadians are equipped with the skills and abilities to adjust and adapt to new employment circumstances no matter what region of the country they live in. Programs must be tailored to different regions. They must provide people with different levels of education and employment background with the skills which will be of greatest benefit to them. It is time for the government to lead rather than sit back and quote rosy economic forecasts from foreign investors who are not trying to find jobs in Canada.
There is much that is wrong with this agreement. However it would be an absolute tragedy to force the people of Canada to fend for themselves without hope or assistance from the people they elected to work in their interests.
The Conservative government has shown its inability to help Canadians adjust to these rapidly changing times and I fear its current leadership charlatans show no signs of changing that. The government did not heed the warnings in 1988 and it is not heeding them now as we prepare for the 21st century.
Today I am proud to support the motion of my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River which will ensure that Canadians have every opportunity to improve their skills and education in order to succeed and find meaningful employment.
May 25, 1993

Mr. Speaker, as we move into these stages of closure on the North American free trade agreement I am proud to speak on this motion by my colleague from Kenora- Rainy River that amends the preamble of Bill C-115 to address social and labour concerns.
As I look at the current round of GATT negotiations, the impact of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and the North American free trade agreement, I have become very apprehensive as to who will be the benefactors of these agreements. For example, if we look at the increased labour costs we have here in Canada, the input costs, our standard of living, our wage rates, our labour and environmental standards and then compare them to the southern United States and Mexico we have to ask ourselves if we can survive.
If the wages in Mexico were to increase to our levels then perhaps we could compete in the long term, but the wages have dropped over the last 10 years because of brutal economic reform.
In the manufacturing sector the total compensation for labour in Mexico in 1979 was $2.89 an hour and in 1991 it was $1.59 an hour. Such a drop symbolizes what is happening in that country to the south of us. Its minimum wage dropped from $1.10 an hour in 1979 to 59 cents an hour in 1989. Those wages are on a downward trend and are not contributing to an increased standard of living in Mexico. They are going to take away from our standard of living if we have to compete.
NAFTA is an economic integration based on an international division of labour in which Canada supplies the energy, the water and the raw resources. Mexico supplies the cheap labour and lax enforcement of environmental health and safety standards. The United States supplies the consumer market. Multinational corporations profit at the expense of wage cuts and job losses for Canadian and American workers.
Canadian employment in manufacturing has declined by over 400,000 jobs since the free trade agreement with the U.S. was signed. Many of those jobs have gone to the free trade zone along the border between Mexico and the U.S. It is a sort of anything goes, mini free trade zone that we all hear so much about. Employment in manufacturing in the Maquiladora has increased by 244,000
Government Orders
jobs since the free trade agreement was signed. In 1992 this was brought out in an economic report in the U.S.
In the European Economic Community, economic integration has been accompanied by massive social funds and a social charter that intends to provide a framework for upward harmonization and safeguards against the kind of social dumping NAFTA will exacerbate.
In the North American context, this amendment by the member for Kenora-Rainy River is an attempt to ensure that a country's competitive advantage is not based upon the violation of workers' rights or labour standards. These provisions are essential not only to protect Canadian and American workers but to support the efforts of workers and others to raise labour standards and the standard of living in Mexico.
I was interested to hear just recently about one of the U.S. congressmen who was very violently opposed to this same agreement. He pointed out that their increased exports to Mexico were mainly in manufacturing equipment that will utilize cheap labour and export low cost products that will take jobs away from Canadian and U.S. workers.
It is also important to have the role of labour recognized, as my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River has done. I am equally concerned that in the U.S. a streamlined inspection system has been introduced in poultry and meat processing.
In the last several years the U.S. has moved rapidly toward deregulation and the lines in the processing plants have been speeded up. Some U.S. inspection processing lines now move at a speed of 90 birds a minute in poultry processing and up to 450 carcasses an hour in beef processing or one carcass every nine seconds.
Some of these plants hire their own inspectors. If one of these inspectors is conscientious, turns down too much product and cannot keep up with this hell-bent push for efficiency then of course his or her job is in jeopardy. As a result this push for lower labour and production costs is placing the health of the consumers in jeopardy. In fact just last January hundreds of children became ill from eating contaminated hamburgers in Washington state. Three died and several now have permanent kidney damage. A year ago, on April 30,

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
ABC's Prime Time Live did a documentary of what is going on in those processing plants in the United States. Now we see our own negotiators turning down a provision allowing us to turn back products not measuring up to Canadian standards, which are the best in the world. Mexican standards not only place the labour standards of this nation under attack from the transnational corporations, but our standards uphold the dignity of Canadian workers and provide them with a standard of living that is not prevalent for the average family in Mexico. They are equally important standards that protect the health of the Canadian people.
I respectfully point out to this House that this agreement should not be passed until, first, provisions are in place that will protect our Canadian people and maintain our standard of living and the health of this nation; second, the deteriorating wage rates of Mexican workers and their labour code are brought up to the equivalent of those in Canada; and third, environmental safeguards are put in place that maintain our standards and bring the two other partners to this agreement up to our standards to protect the health of our people and the well-being of this planet. The fourth point is that the House should not proceed with the passage of this legislation until the side agreements being demanded by the United States are finalized and agreed to by all three parties to this agreement and until we are guaranteed that these agreements measure up to our own Canadian standards here in this nation whether it is labour standards, environmental standards or health standards.
The future of this nation is put in jeopardy by the government's push to bring in this legislation before this House today. It is absolutely absurd that we are pushing so hard at this point when the finalized agreement and the side agreements are not in place by the neighbours to the south of us. Look at the long term implications that this is going to have not only on our people, as I indicated in the labour standards we have here or the health standards of our people, but on the very future of this planet.
I suggest that this is a big price to pay for what we have seen to date and what we do not know about that could very well be a pig in a poke. I am not prepared to vote for this legislation under these conditions and I hope the members of this House will vote against it for the same reasons.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I am pleased to participate in the debate, I would rather not be participating in the debate in that I had hoped that the debate would not take place at all.
Anyone who studies this agreement in detail and understands this agreement will know what we are talking about here today. It is the dismantling of almost everything we know that is Canadian. We are introducing processes that will result in the Americanization and Mexicanization of Canadian society and the Canadian economy.
We are talking about five motions put forward by my hon. friend from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca dealing with the environment. Let us be aware of what is going on in terms of the forces in North America as a result of this pending trade agreement. I think it was presidential candidate Ross Perot who first said it during the presidential campaign when he said that if the United States-to say nothing about Canada-signs the NAFTA agreement then we are going to hear a massive flushing sound as jobs are flushed down into Mexico. As we speak, down in the Maquiladora zone in northern Mexico there are 2,000 big plants with 500,000 people. When one approaches that Maquiladora area one does not have to see it or even know that it is there because one can smell it. One can see it from a long distance because of the pall hanging over the factories. The smell is overwhelming.
What is the smell? There are 500,000 people working in those plants. There are no sewage treatment facilities for those 500,000 people. There is no water in their homes. Just imagine that stench that results from living in those unbelievable, inhuman conditions day after day after day. What are people doing about it? Nothing. One can see the canals going off into the desert filled with toxic and hazardous waste. That is the way they dispose of it. One sees kids playing in the sewage ditches that are slick and iridescent with chemicals. The stories go on and on.
One of the most moving speeches I heard recently was by Ralph Nader, the consumer advocate in the United States, when he looked at this free trade deal. He said that in terms of just the health of people living in North America that this will result in the standards that we have in our provinces and certain states in the United States being pushed down to approximate those in Mexico to keep the level playing field.
May 25, 1993

We are in serious difficulty if this trade deal goes ahead. Let me put it graphically. Let us imagine that my friend from Prince George wins $10 million in the lottery tonight. That would be a nice gesture. He decides he is going to open a new manufacturing facility such as a new processing plant. He is going to create employment for people and eventually parlay that $10 million into a substantial profit. He wants to open his facility where he will maximize profits and where the environmental regulations, labour laws and the cost of doing business will be the lowest.
What about labour costs? My friend from Prince George will have four choices. It will probably require reasonably highly skilled workers so he can locate his new plant where there are trained men and women and pay them $18 an hour. He can instead go down to some of the northern states and for the same level of skills pay $12 an hour. He can instead go down to Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas or New Mexico and pay $6.50 an hour. However, now, under NAFTA, once it is signed and in place, he can go down over the Rio Grande River and pay 60 cents an hour for those same skills.
It does not take much imagination to know that Ross Perot was right. There is going to be a massive flushing sound as the jobs head down into Mexico where my friend is going to exploit Mexican workers at 60 cents an hour, where the regulations for the environment are abysmally low and non-existent, where the labour laws are completely ignored and where the trade unions are working for the company.
That is the kind of future that this person and these people want in this country. What does this mean to our children's children? The jobs of the future will not be in Canada. They will not even be in the United States. They will be in Mexico where they are able to exploit the workers.
My hon. friend from the Conservative side says they want decent wages for the workers in the plants. Of course they want decent wages for the people in these plants. I think it is unfortunate that we hear from the Tories that fair and decent wages are something that we ought not to be fighting for in this country.
Where will the future economic activity be when one can pay $18, $12, $6, or 60 cents an hour? That is why there are 2,000 plants in that northern Mexican zone right now. That is why there are 500,000 people.
Government Orders
My friend asks what is stopping them. I will say what it
is.	Right now there is no free trade deal with Mexico. In other words those goods and services do not flow freely. They cannot get access to our markets.
People say that if we enter into a free trade deal with Mexico then we should think of all the goods that we are going to sell to the Mexicans. What the hell can one buy from Canada if one is being paid 60 cents an hour? What kind of goods and services can one access if that is the kind of income one has?
If we proceed with this then there is going to be a dismantling of what we know as a country. There is going to be a natural movement south. There already is under FTA. Have we lost manufacturing jobs in this country because of the free trade deal with the United States? Yes, of course we have. Have we lost thousands or tens of thousands? No, we have lost hundreds of thousands of manufacturing jobs as a result of the existing free trade agreement and now this government wants to expand that into Mexico.
We are talking about jobs and the fact that Canadians will have to compete with people who are paid 60 cents an hour. These are trained people. The Japanese have said that after three years of operation in the Maquiladora zone their plants are as productive as anywhere else in North America. We are not talking about some unskilled labour force. We are talking about a very skilled labour force that is continuing to reskill and upgrade in order to compete under those conditions. That is just one side of
it.	There are many.
My colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca has put forward a number of amendments. He said: "We do not support this bill at all but the government seems determined to jam and ram and rush this legislation through before the negotiations are even completed". I think it must be unheard of in international trade history that we would join in an agreement when it is still being negotiated and discussed.
Again, I do not like to mention it, but I cannot help saying that I do not think it is right for a government to proceed or for this House to consider legislation when the minister responsible is not here. The Minister for International Trade finds it more appropriate to be outside the city. He is elsewhere.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
It is not as though he did not know the debate was taking place today. We all knew it was taking place today. We have known for weeks.
I want to go on record to say that the Minister for International Trade chose consciously not to be part of this discussion and not to respond to the questions that we are placing to the minister. We are talking to an empty chair. This is probably just as interesting, but nevertheless it is certainly unacceptable.
My friend from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca has put forward some of the most thoughtful amendments that one can imagine in terms of how to protect the working conditions of workers in Canada and elsewhere to ensure that the environment in our North American continent is not destroyed.
He is using Europe as an example. In Europe they were quite prepared to lay out a charter describing what rights workers will have and what environmental conditions must exist as a result of the trade deal there. Does this government ask for environmental safeguards to be part of NAFTA? No, it does not. Does this government ask for training and other operations to be available to all those men and women across this country who lose their jobs as a result of this deal? No, it does not.
Let us be clear. This government is opening up the door to the transnational companies. They are not companies in Canada trading with a company in the United States or with a company in Mexico. It is the same company just trading within itself. That is the kind of trade that most of our companies are into.
It is saying that it is going to open the doors and make it easier for companies to move that part of their operation which is labour intensive into Mexico or into the southern United States. That is what we are talking about and that is why we, as New Democrats, oppose this legislation so strongly.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBIanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on Motion No. 1 which is the amendment to this legislation introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.
These motions are grouped for debate. In this grouping motions have been presented by my colleague from the NDP, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de
Fuca. I had the privilege of sitting with him in committee and dealing with the substance of NAFTA and with Bill C-115 during the short time that this government allowed the Parliament of Canada to even consider this very important and very complex trade and investment agreement. It is more than that.
I found my colleague from British Columbia to be passionate and sincere and a very knowledgeable exponent of his party's position on this issue. He has raised many worth-while concerns which many Canadians share as we rush headlong into this agreement.
Canadians are fearful because of the complexity and the implications of NAFTA in the face of what has happened in the four years since the free trade agreement has been implemented with the many job losses and recession in Canada and with the flood of plant closings and job losses to the United States. They are fearful because of the distrust that they have of this government.
This government has demonstrated time and time again that it does not govern in the interests of Canadians but in the apparent interests of a non-elected, unaccountable and privileged few in Canada and, what is more worrisome, outside of Canada. That is why Canadians are so fearful and so concerned as we rush headlong into this debate on this legislation.
Given the power of the government to impose closure as it will and as it has on this issue, which will stifle a meaningful debate on this issue, there is really not much hope for us here in Parliament to properly address the many concerns. Let me tiy to deal with some of them in the very short time that I have to deal with this particular group of amendments concerning environmental and social issues.
My colleague from Kenora-Rainy River raised the issue of labour standards and the right of workers to free collective bargaining, to form associations and unions and to represent themselves with management. This is a right that is honoured and cherished in Canada and the United States and in many other countries but which is very frequently and systematically abused and denied in Mexico. It is only fair and reasonable that those rights ought to be part of the ground rules and the basic playing field upon which these three countries and perhaps
May 25, 1993

other countries, as is provided for in the agreement, form this trading and investment region.
I want to raise an anomaly because I sat through a fair number of hearings on the NAFTA legislation and on the NAFTA itself. It is an anomaly which appears in the preamble to the NAFTA and in the preamble of Bill C-115 but which is absent in the objectives of the agreement. That is the way in which the agreement treats two different sets of rights and protections.
In the preamble there are clauses which deal with sustainable development, the environment, rights of labour mobility and other workers' rights. These rights are noticeably absent in the much stronger part of the legislation and the agreement which concerns the objectives and which defines the responsibilities and commitments of the respective governments. I will quote the objectives of the agreement because they are interesting. One part of the objectives of the NAITA, part (d) in article 102, says:
To provide adequate and effective protection and enforcement of
intellectual property rights in each party's territory.
It is an interesting anomaly particularly in light of the amendments that have been brought forward by my colleague and by my colleague from the NDP concerning environmental protection, child labour, the rights of collective bargaining and association by workers and many issues which have been debated and which continue to be debated in the United States. It is interesting that the NAFTA should provide protection for intellectual property and provide no protection for workers' freedom of association or provide effective safeguards in the objectives of the agreement for workers and the protection of the environment. They are two issues of very great importance not only to Canada but to the United States and Mexico.
That is an anomaly which appears in the agreement and also appears in the legislation.
The amendment of my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River addresses this in part because it puts it in the preamble which would strengthen the preamble in that respect. It could very well be placed in the objective where it would be even stronger.
Government Orders
Those are the kinds of things which if we had more time to deal with this legislation we might advance to improve and safeguard the measures that need to be in an agreement like this to adequately protect the people of Canada and the people of the other signatories of this agreement. That is my first point concerning this group of amendments.
I would just like to respond to a comment that was made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade earlier today. In full oratorical flight he said that the NAFTA is a trade agreement, it is only a trade agreement, it is specifically a trade agreement, and it is nothing more than a trade agreement. That is all that NAFTA is.
In the time remaining I would like to quote for my hon. friend opposite the testimony given last week before the Senate standing committee on foreign affairs by Dr. Robert Cohen, who is a fellow with the Economic Strategy Institute in New York and is a specialist in the economics of high technology industries. He appeared before the Senate committee to discuss from a U.S. perspective some of the industrial impacts of the NAFTA on the United States, and they are devastating. A reading of Dr. Cohen's testimony would help us understand why the United States is so worried at this point in time.
I will conclude by citing what Dr. Cohen says. He says that it is not a trade agreement but is an investment agreement. He says:
What is created under the NAFTA is not only the ability to open up
trade, but the ability to industrialize Mexico under far fewer
constraints than were offered previously.
He cites all of the industries that will be able to take advantage of this situation.
He is saying in his testimony that the opportunity made available by NAFTA will be to industrialize Mexico under far fewer constraints than were offered previously. That is why we have these amendments.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking in support of the amendments by my colleagues from Kenora-Rainy River and Cape Breton Highlands-Canso I would like to say these few words in the context of two questions.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
First of all, I would like to congratulate them for their excellent input and motions that are on the Order Paper on Bill C-115.
The first question is: Why force the bill now? Why ram it through Parliament at this stage in light of what happened last week in Ottawa when the negotiators did not come to a conclusion on some crucial aspects of this trade agreement?
It is very hard to understand on the part of the Canadian public and for us in the opposition why this bill must go through now when governments in North America which are part of this proposal have not yet finalized their thinking on this important proposition.
It seems to us that there is an agenda which has not yet been explained. It will be the subject of subsequent interventions today on the part of our leader and colleagues in my party. That is because it is difficult to accept the fact that Canada should be the first to race off the mark with approval by Parliament of a very important, substantial, and complex trade proposal when the other two partners have not yet reached an agreement on this matter domestically, let alone internationally.
The second question that needs to be asked is: Have we learned from the free trade agreement? If so, what have we learned before we move on to this new continental agreement phase? It would seem that we have seen that the free trade agreement has brought in its wake advantages for some and considerable economic and emotional harm to many others.
If one were to ask the average Canadian who lives in an industrial town or city whether the free trade agreement has been good most would answer in the negative because they have been hit by some kind of industrial lay-off attributed to the free trade agreement. It is this perception of the damage that the agreement has caused to the daily life of the industrial worker that seems not to have been learned so far.
This is the reason my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River is putting forward a very important amendment on the question of labour. It is really a question that says we must learn to manage the transition for the people affected by free trade. Has the government learned this lesson? Has the government put into place the necessary
programs and measures to provide a shock absorber for the people affected by free trade agreements?
Unfortunately the answer comes down on the negative side, particularly when it comes to older workers and those who are employed in small and medium sized companies who are not benefiting from older worker programs. In other words, we are talking today about the necessity of establishing possibly two commissions. One would deal with the question of labour and the proper management of the transition from the existing trade condition to the proposed one. The second would deal with the establishment of a commission that would deal with matters related to the environment.
Why do we do that? We do that in relation to labour for the reason that I have just given. In other words, we must not allow trade to become a traumatic experience in the lives of thousands of Canadian families who are affected and suffer the results of free trade because their jobs disappear as a result of decisions made by multinational corporations. We must find ways whereby the trade agreement will ensure that the environment, which is the base of our economic well-being, is not damaged by the trade policies that will be allowed under the NAFTA.
What are we talking about here, particularly on the environmental side? Very briefly, we are talking about some common basic principles for managing environmental issues, precautionary principles. In essence we must move to take precautionary measures before we see the total damage and have the final scientific proof that there is damage taking place.
The second is the preventative principle which flows from the first. We are much better off when we prevent damage than when we repair it. The third is the polluter pays principle which has already been accepted for some time in North America, particularly in the United States and Canada. Finally there is the principle of transparency which does not need much elaboration.
We also want to talk about the importance of a commission with respect to environmental standards. We are very concerned that by moving with NAFTA we would lower rather than improve the quality of environmental standards. Harmonization is a very seductive word, but it could lead to harmonization downward not upward. We would like to find a way through the establishment of a commission to permit harmonization
May 25, 1993

of environmental standards upward rather than downward.
In essence we are talking about providing sufficient funds for the construction of sewage treatment plants and water purification systems; to encourage reduction in the use of pesticides; to improve energy efficiency; to facilitate the use of public transportation over private transportation and of course to reduce air pollution because we know air pollution knows no boundaries.
In other words we are talking about two things in these quite publicized parallel agreements and nobody really knows exactly what they will be about in the end. One is the establishment of a commission that would deal with environmental matters along with a very rough sketch I just outlined a moment ago. Of course the question is whether such a commission will have any enforcement powers. If so which enforcement powers will it be given or will it just be an advisory board like the International Joint Commission on the Great Lakes? Therefore some very important questions must be raised within the debate.
Second, are we going to establish a commission to look at the management of the transition from the point of view of the people affected by free trade? The human side of trade must be emphasized and raised at every opportunity.
One factor is related to the economic condition of the family and the other one is related to the environmental and health aspect of the population affected. It is important therefore that we put these points on record today. It is important that these parallel agreements on labour as well as the environment not be limited to advisory roles. Commissions must be created to protect the interests of the people affected and the environment. They will also have the power to implement the recommendations they see fit to define in the interest of the public in general.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in debate. It is very difficult under severe time constraints to appropriately handle the debate in front of us on the economic constitution of this country and North America.
In three short days if the government gets its wish the legislation will be through Parliament and ready for implementation on January 1, 1994. Hopefully if we have
Government Orders
anything to do with it, it will not be implemented and certainly if Canadians had anything to do with it, it would not be implemented.
Mr. Perot talks about the big sucking sound of jobs going off to Mexico. I do not want to quote him too often for fear of being totally associated with him but some of his quotes are catchy if nothing else. He talks about a three-legged one-eyed 40-year old camel that is about to die. He is talking about NAFTA. I am not sure of the analogy but nevertheless it is not bad. I think it aptly describes this bill.
We support some of the amendments that are before the House. We think amendments on the environment, social conditions and training are very laudable. Canadians will support them and we support them.
We also want to say that no number of amendments or side accords that could be brought to bear will ever correct this deal. It is impossible. It is flawed and unacceptable to the majority of Canadians. If they had their way and knew what it was all about they would certainly oppose this bill.
With regard to the side accords and the amendments, we are going to speak to the environment. The government has said: "Well, sometimes we are in and sometimes we are out". In the beginning it said: "Well, we are going to be at the table because we had best be at the table to protect our interests". We know it did not want to negotiate any side accords. However, as time progressed the minister said: "Well, yes we do favour the side accords". Now it is abundantly clear the government will not support them in labour standards or in environmental standards.
One may ask how bad the environment is. Mr. Gephardt, the House leader for the Democratic Party in the United States paid a visit to Mexico. Anybody who has paid a visit to the Maquiladora has a totally different perspective on this issue. I am glad to say I was there. I was not happy with what I saw but it was certainly an eye opener. I would encourage all government members to get down there and have a look.
What did Mr. Gephardt see? His group checked out a polluted site left behind by a U.S. lead recycling plant. Two U.S. engineers, both dressed in protective gear, would not let the congressional delegation near the contaminated grounds. It was a little too dangerous for politicians. But Gephardt saw Mexican labourers at work

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
in the same muck trying to clean up massive piles of toxic waste without benefit of protective clothing or masks. The majority leader added one other detail. Behind the facility was a dairy whose milk was sold to the citizens of Tijuana. A number of cows from the dairy have died from severe lead poisoning.
How bad is the environment? How badly do we need side accords? We need them desperately but we are not going to get them with any teeth and certainly the deal is flawed.
Mexico has great environmental laws and it brags about them. It says it has the best environmental laws in the world but there is absolutely no enforcement.
What I really want to raise in the House today is a recent development reported yesterday in The New York Times. Some of the Canadian papers gave it some play today but not nearly what it is worth. It is suggested that the major drug cartels in the world are going to set up Maquiladoras to front their drug operations. They are going to buy legitimate television and manufacturing outlets to smuggle the drugs into the United States.
One might say this is far-fetched but far from it. In fact the National Security Archive, which is a research group that tries to declassify government documents, has come forward and confirmed it. It has been confirmed that the Maquiladora zone and the NAFTA are going to be used to push drugs through the United States into Canada. There are 1,700 trucks waiting at any one moment at that border that get basic inspection once in a while. The majority of the time there is a five minute wait because the officer says: "Hey it is their business. They have to get through". If they are not being inspected, can you imagine the drug trade?
We just received this classified document by fax a few minutes ago. I think it is worth reading for the record to explain to Canadians that we have a wonderful free trade agreement on everything, including drugs. We are spending millions of dollars to fight drugs, counteract the drug trade and help youth get off drugs and we are going to sign an agreement that will allow the drug dealers of the world to bring drugs into Canada with no problem at all. They can put it in trucks. There are no inspectors at the border.
I am going to read this so-called classified document which is no longer classified. It states: "The Munoz drug organization operating in Juarez, state of Chiapas, Mexico owns the Huersa battery recycling plant. The plant located on the Juariz-Casas Grandes Highway in an area known as the El Espion is being used as a staging point for narcotic smuggling from Mexico to the United States. The plant reclaims lead from used batteries. The organization contracts various trucking companies in the U.S. to transport large quantities of unserviceable batteries from the U.S. to Mexico. The plant is staffed by workers from southern Mexico and not by local workers".
Why? Because it is best if they do not know what is really going on. They are from another area. Talk about a negative environment. I wonder what is in those batteries. They must be super charged. It goes on to say that the plant's main building is being reinforced to accommodate a helicopter. I am wondering what this helicopter is going to do. I guess they are going to fly the batteries from Mexico to the United States and Canada.
It goes on. It is a so-called classified document and the negotiators of the agreement said it was too hot to handle. Why was this not brought up in negotiations? It was too hot to handle. We can understand why.
Of course we support the side accords on the environment and labour standards but no number of amendments like this, even if they were being supported by this government, would make this flawed deal acceptable. As we progress through the debate we find more and more revelations like this that tell us we should stop, step back from this agreement and take a look at it.
We are rushing headlong. We have to get it through in three days. We have to get it through despite the fact, and we have repeated this time and time again, there are absolutely no guarantees this bill is going to go through in the United States.
Leon Panetta who is in charge of the budget of the United States said that if the vote had been held last week the deal would be dead. After our visit to Washington we suggest the majority of commerce people feel the same way. The deal is dead unless there are teeth in the side agreements. The United States is pushing for them but Canada and Mexico are fighting those side accords.
May 25, 1993

We know why Mexico is fighting the accords. It says 80 cents an hour is enough. The government is saying it wants to improve the life of Mexican workers. I toured on a bus with a group of business people from North America and talked to them. They did not know I was a politician. I asked them about the workers in the Maquiladora. One person said to me: "Do not worry about the workers, we know how to handle them. There is no labour strife here. We will look after the workers". I saw how they look after them. It is an absolute travesty of justice. It is out and out exploitation. We laud the amendments but no number of amendments will make this bill acceptable to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the question most people ask about NAFTA and one of the greatest concerns people have is how Canada can compete with Mexican wages which are 80 cents to $1 an hour.
On top of that there is the challenge that Mexico is graduating four times as many engineers and scientists today as Canada. We have also seen over the past four and one-half years a wholesale exodus of industry from Canada, a phenomenon which has been referred to as deindustrialization.
In Canada we have lost about 15 per cent of our manufacturing jobs over this time period. We have lost manufacturing jobs at more than twice the U.S. rate. This applies right across the whole gamut of manufacturing. Canadians have a legitimate concern. If this is what has happened over the past four and one-half years, what will be our record of job losses in our high paying industries in the future, particularly with a NAFTA when Canadians will be put face to face with veiy cheap labour in Mexico?
We have to be realistic about this. Jobs have globalized. Many of these jobs from Canada and the United States went to Mexico long before the free trade agreement was entered into with the United States. The Maquiladora region was established by major multinational corporations which were taking advantage of cheap but good Mexican labour and free access to the American market. [DOT]
The phenomenon of globalization is something with which we all have to contend. We cannot bury our heads
Government Orders
in the sand. Unlike what some people in this House say, is it possible to go backward and re-establish tariff barriers in Canada and make Canadian consumers pay more for the goods we have?
Canada among all the nations of the world is the foremost trading nation in terms of the percentage of its gross national product that comes from exports and from imports. Like it or not, that is reality. Can we automatically go back and create a closed type of environment where our tariff barriers force the jobs into Canada? It is highly unlikely that we could abrogate the treaty with the United States and not suffer retaliation. We would hurt far more than the Americans would were they to erect barriers against Canadian exports. Eighty per cent of our exports go to the United States.
Those are the realities with which we have to deal. Does this mean that we cannot insist in our trade deals on at least a level playing field, on at least the opportunity to compete fairly with not only the Mexicans but also with the Americans?
Much emphasis has been put on a side deal which the United States will cut with Mexico dealing with labour standards. If what the government says is true, that it wants this trade deal because Mexico is a Third World developing country and it is only fair that we give it an opportunity to increase its exports and create a dynamic economy, then this government more than any other should be interested in having the labour standards of Mexico raised to acceptable and tolerable international standards. I am not just talking about wages but worker health and safety, the right to collectively bargain and the right to fair wages.
This, if we can achieve it, will go a long way to reducing the discrepancy between high Canadian industrial wages, which are approaching $14 an hour, and the much lower Mexican wages, which let us say are about $1 an hour.
However, Mexico is not the only concern. As we have indicated, Canada has been losing manufacturing jobs over the past four and a half years at more than twice the U.S. rate. Many of these jobs have actually gone to the United States. We have seen, for example, how Co-Steel and Dofasco are now putting up a $300 million mini mill in Kentucky. One of the many reasons cited by their president for so doing is, among other things, cheaper wages.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
Maybe Mexico is not the only concern in terms of wages and labour standards. Maybe we have to worry as well about whether the United States is playing fair and whether their playing field is level. Do we want Canadian labour standards to be reduced to those in the United States? Six of the states in the United States have no minimum wage laws; in another 14 states the minimum wage is $4 U.S. an hour or less; 20 states have either no minimum wages or minimum wages of less than $4 U.S. In addition to that, 20 states in the United States have right-to-work laws, laws which make it extremely difficult for workers to collectively bargain.
I do not necessarily carry a brief for unions or for big business, but if one of the things that workers want through the democratic process is the right to organize, then why should we allow the United States to deny them that right when we here in Canada grant them that right?
If we are going to have a parallel accord to the NAFTA dealing with labour standards, let us also be aware that we need to have labour standards in the United States which are brought up to our standards rather than lowering ours to theirs.
We find it very difficult to understand why this government is so intent on rushing this deal through. Why the undue haste? Why, when the United States has not even brought these agreements before its own Congress, do we find our bill in Parliament under time allocation without a fair opportunity to debate it?
Is the government afraid of the debate? It is going to say that we have had lots of debate. The United States does not feel it has had enough debate. There are enough concerns where it wants parallel accords, where it wants to make sure that its playing field is levelled out. It will not present it to Congress until it sees the actual accords. We are going to take it on faith.
We have faith that the United States will be able to come up with exactly the type of deal to which we would be happy to accede. We know the free trade agreement was not the best agreement that we could get. It did not have a defined subsidies code. It did not have a provision
to deal with anti-dumping. When our steel industry, in all of its right thinking, thought that it was going to have enhanced access to the United States and for the first few years had to live under a 3 per cent voluntary restraint, why is it now finding that every time it tries to meet American prices in selling to the United States it is hit by dumping? This is not a level playing field.
This agreement with the United States had many flaws, flaws which could have been curbed and cured had we had longer debate and greater discussion in Parliament.
The same applies to NAFTA. We on this side of the House are not against freer trade. We are the party that has historically promoted it. We know over the long term it produces the greatest benefit for all of our citizens. But free trade without a level playing field is selling out Canada's interest. That is what this government is prepared to do. That is why we will never support this NAFTA deal as proposed by this government.

Mr. Speaker, in the moment or two that remain before we break I want to underline the value of the amendment proposed by our colleague from Kenora-Rainy River.
It advances a comprehensive and thoughtful approach to labour standards within the agreement. Equally I would want to support the interventions of our colleague from Davenport and others who have spoken of the need for stronger environmental provisions to be incorporated in or around the North American free trade agreement.
Before turning to the substance of those two issues I want to join with my colleague from Willowdale in deploring the decision of the government to push through NAFTA without adequate debate.
We have the most bizarre situation of the principal trading partner, the United States, determined to wait and see what the side agreements will contain before offering to Congress implementing legislation. What has the Canadian government done? It has said: "No, we do not need to wait. These side agreements have nothing in effect to do with NAFTA. We have been proceeding with NAFTA since it is a stand alone matter and we will put it through the House of Commons this week".
May 25, 1993

We have not had an adequate debate of this major issue within our country. We had it neither in the committee where Liberals consistently urged more extensive hearings, more travel, more opportunity to hear from Canadians about their concerns. Here we have the same situation in the final stage. The government is pushing this important legislation through in a matter of three days. I cannot think that any government acting responsibly could lend itself to such a procedure.

Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate the minister of constitutional affairs on his appointment as UN envoy to the negotiations aimed at reuniting Cyprus and wish him well. He is an ideal person for the job.
For many years Canadians of Cypriot origin have been urging our government to become more directly involved in efforts to find a just and viable solution to the Cyprus problem, but as we have been part of the UN peacekeeping force since 1964 our government has been reluctant to do so.
However, we are now withdrawing our peacekeepers and Russia very recently vetoed an effort to extend the mandate of the entire UN peacekeeping force on Cyprus beyond next month. This makes the constitutional affairs minister's role both urgent and absolutely vital.
Twenty-nine years of Canadian peacekeeping on Cyprus must not be wasted.

Madam Speaker, across the country Canadians of Portuguese origin are celebrating 40 years of immigration to Canada. Historians tell us that 500 years would be a more accurate figure.
Portuguese explorers were among the first to see Canadian soil. Portuguese fishermen caught cod on the Grand Banks, but only a handful settled on the Atlantic coast.
Recent Portuguese immigration began in the 1940s and increased rapidly in the 1950s. By 1991 the number of Portuguese in Canada was estimated at about 250,000. The Portuguese immigrant is well known as a hard worker, a proud homeowner and a self-reliant member of the community.
Portuguese people have made a vigorous contribution to our economy in construction, trade and commerce, the arts, professions, farming and fisheries.
This anniversary prompts us to look ahead to the future and the challenge posed by changing employment opportunities. In doing so the Portuguese in Canada will continue to enjoy respect and admiration in the tradition of the great explorers of 500 years ago.

Madam Speaker, the proposed North American free trade agreement, NAFTA, and the legislation to implement it must be withdrawn.
In the name of free trade multinational agribusiness has sabotaged the farm support system that since the 1930s has protected farmers from the vagaries of the marketplace. If NAFTA is allowed to succeed measures to protect small and medium sized farms and their communities will likely be abolished.
In Canada in the name of free trade we have already lost domestic pricing of grain, the marketing of oats under the Canadian Wheat Board and quality meat inspections at the U.S. border.

Madam Speaker, since her appointment as the chair of the government's subcommittee on poverty the member for Don Valley North has unleashed a series of vicious verbal assaults and accusations against food banks and their many volunteers. Refusing to believe that poverty really exists in Canada she is trying to erase the old poverty line and redraw a new lower one so that fewer Canadians are officially counted as poor.
Last week the chair was reprimanded in public yet again, this time for secretly sending a member of her staff to lie and spy on the Daily Bread Food Bank in Toronto. Posing as a needy student a staff member left with four bags of food. Given the shortages facing food banks this year this act was morally reprehensible and completely irresponsible.
Therefore, I want to add my voice to those who have demanded that the Prime Minister immediately remove the member from her duties on this important committee. The actions and statements of the chair are completely inexcusable and she has repeatedly acted in poor faith and bad taste. She has become an embarrassment, even for this government which knows no level of embarrassment or shame.

May 25, 1993

Madam Speaker, there is a secret political club in this country composed of 100 major corporations. These corporations handle 70 per cent of Canada's exports and they have forged a political deal with the Liberals and Conservatives. Stage one of the deal was the free trade agreement.
It is now well known that the FTA cost hundreds of thousands of Canadians their jobs, families and life savings. Despite a near total media black-out on the North American free trade agreement, Canadians are starting to recognize the roles played by the Conservative-Liberal coalition to sell out Canada to the international profiteers.
It is clear that the Liberals and Conservatives voted together on December 1, 1992 in support of NAFTA in this House. On March 31, 1993, 38 Liberals failed to even show up to vote. NAFTA is 4,000 pages of special deals to cut wages, cut jobs, close plants, cut environmental protection, cut prices on resources, and cut social programs, to in effect remove Canadian sovereignty from every jurisdiction.
NAFTA is all about making the rich richer and the poor poorer, and that is why the Liberals are going to vote for it this week.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, after much criticism from the Liberal opposition a member of the government party opposite has finally recognized the improper conduct of his government and colleagues.
Last Saturday the Conservative member for Portage- Interlake stated in the press:
The last eight years under Mulroney were done in a certain way, a
lot of activity took place and some was questionable.

May 25, 1993
Hear, hear.

He only said some.
What is the cause of this sudden burst of insightful commentary? Quite simply, the Tories know the wrath of the people will soon be upon them. They are now seeking to distance themselves from the present leadership.
Commenting on the hordes of lobbyists who skulk the capital and for years have successfully convinced their Conservative brethren in the Prime Minister's Office not to impose strict laws on their activities the member for Portage-Inter lake summed up the attitude of the government by stating:

Madam Speaker, today is National Missing Children's Day.
Our future as a flourishing and thriving society rests with children. Who among us has not looked into the eyes of a young child without seeing the glint of curiosity, the spark of intelligence or the simple love for life at the heart of the growing and learning process? Who can give us as much joy, happiness and fulfilment as children? The first step, the first word and the first musings, all these stages bond us as families. Children become a reason for being and raising them a main focus in life both for the family and society.
To lose one's child is a devastating incident that happens far too often. Statistics show that 61,000 children are missing in Canada, approximately 45,000 are thrown out or are runaways who need our special attention, 13,000 are unknown disappearances and 432 are parental abductions. I commend the Solicitor General for announcing only today the publication of a manual to assist police in dealing with child abduction and runaway youth. However there still remains the problem of international abductions-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister.
Last week representatives from Canada, the United States and Mexico failed to reach an agreement on the NAFTA side deals. These are the same side deals the President of the United States, Mr. Clinton, says if they are not accepted he will not proceed with NAFTA and will not present the legislation to Congress.
Now that we see the negotiations are not over yet and there is a big impasse, why does the government want a blank cheque from the House of Commons? Why is the government not waiting to proceed with the legislation until we know the results of these negotiations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while it is true negotiations are ongoing with respect to improvements of the labour issues, the environmental issues and others, it still remains very clear from the leaders of all three countries that it is the intention to proceed with the ratification and the implementation of the North American free trade agreement by January 1, 1994, unamended I might say. There is also an undertaking that the free trade agreement will not be reopened.
The leaders of all three countries are on the same wavelength with regard to it and I expect it to proceed in a normal fashion.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance chooses to ignore the very important fact that the President of the United States has clearly stated, as have the Senate and the House of Representatives, that they would not proceed with NAFTA without an agreement on labour conditions and the environment.
Last week we saw a major deadlock in the negotiations of Canada, Mexico and the United States on this question. This morning the Minister for International Trade was in the U.S. He made it clear he could not accept the conditions submitted by the U.S. government last week. Why does the government insist on having us

May 25, 1993
Oral Questions
vote on this bill, when it knows perfectly well that, by this fall, we may have an agreement that is totally different from what we have today?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
