Madam Speaker, I do not share that view. Neither does the Government of Canada nor the other leaders. They have indicated very clearly the agreement would not be opened up and that it was their intention to implement the agreement on January 1, 1994.
The side agreements regarding surges, labour and environmental conditions, things the Government of Canada pursued very vigorously in the course of the discussions, will not affect the over-all body of the deal.
The commitment of all three leaders is that it will be implemented and ratified to take effect on January 1, 1994. We are proceeding on that basis.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that is not what the President of the United States has said. If there is no agreement on labour conditions or environmental conditions, the United States will not be part of the NAFTA deal. It is very clear it will not sign and will not deliver if it does not get its way.
Why is the government forcing us to vote on it when we are still negotiating with them? It is evident there is a big disagreement between Canada and United States so we should wait. Why does the government want to proceed? Is it just to try to make some political gain at the expense of the workers of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member has been around long enough to know that in the course of negotiations certain positions are taken by respective countries to gain what they perceive as the best deal to suit their interests. That is the exercise that is going on now.

Madam Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister has repeated several times today that the United States would proceed with NAFTA.
He must know the President has made it clear that without the two side agreements the United States now seeks the United States will not proceed. He must also know last week in the negotiations in Ottawa the United States made it clear that it would settle for nothing less than trade sanctions as a means of enforcing the so-called side agreements on environment and on labour standards.
Since there is apparently no middle ground between agreements which are enforceable and agreements which are not, can the government now tell us what the chief negotiator meant when he said there were "serious difficulties" for Canada in these proposals? What does it intend to do about these very serious difficulties?

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, what is important is that the President of the United States has made it perfectly clear he wants NAFTA implemented.
As for the side deals the discussions are going on. As occurs from time to time in discussions among different parties these are difficult at times. As indicated last week by the chief negotiator there are some differences of opinion.
The important thing is that NAFTA is not going to be changed and that is in the interest of Canada. We are putting forth legislation that will enable the government when the other parties have done the same to proceed with the implementation of the deal.
As for these discussions they will continue until such a time as they come together and agree to principles that are in Canada's interest and Canada agrees with.
In closing we think it is an excellent idea to have bilateral accords with respect to the environment, labour and the other areas, but not at the cost of NAFTA and not at the cost of Canada.

Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister for International Trade let me direct a question to the parliamentary secretary who is answering for him.
May 25, 1993

Oral Questions
The United States has said repeatedly it would not proceed with NAFTA unless it got side agreements that were enforceable through trade sanctions.
Not many months ago the minister said that Canada would walk away from NAFTA if there were enforceable trade sanctions included. What is the position of the government today? Is that still its position? Can we assume NAFTA is dead in Canada if the United States continues to insist upon enforceable trade sanctions?

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as I indicated in my previous answer, NAFTA and these side deals are separate.
They are not.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Bring in Michael Wilson.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
If the Americans through their political process choose to link them for legislative purposes that is of course their privilege. Unlike our friends over there this government does not set its legislative agenda by rules from south of the border. We set our own agenda in accordance with what is in Canada's interest.
These discussions on environment, labour and the other things will continue to take place until such a time as the representatives of Canada are satisfied that what is being decided is in the Canadian interest and then we will proceed with those.
Madam Speaker, may I first say on behalf of myself and my party that we wish Mr. Speaker all the best and a speedy recovery.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, in the absence of the minister of trade my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
The most relevant quote today must surely have been in The Financial Post: "It has been a great month if you are an American looking for work in a Canadian company". What do they mean? Why? It is because Canadian companies are moving south at a very rapid rate.
Today's Financial Post provides all the evidence the government should need to reverse its views on the FTA and on the NAFTA. The Financial Post cites a series of companies that have moved south and that are making investments of up to $1.8 billion in the United States as a result of the trade deals.
The Deputy Prime Minister knows there are two million Canadians who would love to have jobs with that $1.8 billion Canadian. Will the minister and his government relook at the agreement and tell Canadians why his government wants to sign the NAFTA and have it passed in this House? It is going to sell out the jobs of Canadians to the United States.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member knows very well that the bright spot in the Canadian economy has indeed been the export of goods, particularly manufacturing goods.
Friday's Montreal Gazette alluded to the fact that manufacturing fuels economic recovery: "In fact it may come as a surprise", and I am sure it comes as a surprise to the NDP, "that growth in manufacturing output in Canada has outstripped that of every other major industrial nation in the past year". That is what Statistics Canada stated in its annual report.
The member wants some examples of the advantages of the free trade agreement. Just in the last little while here are some examples of U.S. manufacturing operations moving into Canada or expanding into Canada: Heron Cable, Waterloo, Ontario; Intercity Products Corp., Brantford, Ontario; ISE Limited, formerly Sit-Rite, Mississauga, Ontario; J. L. De Ball, Montreal, Quebec; GTE Sylvania; Hughes Aircraft; Fasco Motors; GM Diesel. I could go on.

I have a supplementary. Canadians are, of course, wondering where the jobs are, since the unemployment rate is now 11.4 per cent and over 13 per cent in Montreal. The minister knows perfectly well the unemployment rate is still going up.
My question is this: Why is the government in such a hurry to sign a new trade agreement that will reduce the standard of living of Canadians even further?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is precisely because we want to create new opportunities, better access to trade and secure access to trade, which will allow our manufacturers and our service oriented organizations to produce for the export market. To create a

May 25, 1993
Oral Questions
market of 360 million people is certainly to our advantage. To establish a set of trade rules with a dispute resolution mechanism that provides for freer trade and unfettered trade is clearly to our advantage because Canada has indeed proven to the world that it can compete with the best of them.
All we need is a clear set of rules, a dispute resolution mechanism and the opportunity to get in there to compete with the best of them and to penetrate those markets. That is precisely what we have done under the free trade agreement and that is precisely what we are doing under the North American free trade agreement.

Madam Speaker, what Canada needs is a fair set of rules, fair trading agreements and agreements that will create jobs here in Canada. That is not what Canadians have received.
It is clear that two-thirds of Canadians oppose the NAFTA. It is incomprehensible to this side of the House why the government insists on pushing through the deal this week.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister: What kind of commitments has this government made? It wants to push the legislation through this week when it has not even been completed in the United States and, indeed, is not even completed. Has this government made specific commitments and if so, to whom? To the Prime Minister of Canada? To the United States? To the international business community? What are the commitments this government has made that necessitate ramming this through this week?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I could say that more than two-thirds of the Canadian people do not share the views of the hon. member's party.
It is 90 per cent.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Perhaps it is closer to 90 per cent, as my Liberal friend suggests. The fact is that individual companies have been in Mexico and have been out there exploiting the opportunities that are there. There are opportunities for western Canada, for central Canada, for eastern Canada. Why not get on with the job and create the proper environment, create the appropriate set of rules, create the appropriate dispute resolution
mechanism so we can deal in a fair and equitable manner with the best in the business.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister of health. Today, the House standing committee on health and welfare tabled its unanimous report on Canada's blood system and HIV. The committee recommends that a full public inquiry be established to look into the medical and social tragedy of the more than 1,000 Canadians contaminated with AIDS-infected blood.
Will the minister respect the will of the committee and establish a full public inquiry today?
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Madam Speaker, I received the report this morning. I accept and endorse the establishment of an inquiry that would focus on ensuring that the blood supply system in Canada continues to be safe.
I believe without question in the safety of the system itself today and the members of the committee have said that we have a safe blood management system in Canada. However, I believe it is time to examine the system itself. Because the provinces are obviously involved in the process I have written to them today. I have requested their collaboration in determining the terms of reference on the form, the composition and the mandate of the committee. I look forward to being able to launch the inquiry itself before the end of the summer. It will have to report within the next year to ensure we have an efficient and quick answer to the problems raised by the committee today.

After repeated questions from this side of the House and now endorsed by the committee, the minister finally has agreed to the request we have been making for the last six months.
I have a supplementary for the minister. The unanimous report also recommends that the federal government revisit the compensation issue and I quote: "as a matter of urgency take the lead in establishing a process to identify and notify HIV-positive blood transfused persons in Canada". Is the minister prepared to tell the House today that he will also comply with the unanimous recommendations on these additional issues?
May 25, 1993

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question today is for the Minister of Justice or the minister taking his place. It relates to a report that I have in hand. The minister is here. I am glad you are here, Mr. Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext: Put your glasses back on.

Yes, by golly, it is him. Is the minister aware of a report written by an intelligence officer of the U.S. embassy? It was released out of the national security archives and details initiatives by two Mexican drug cartels to use the North American free trade agreement as a conduit through the Maquiladora zone factories to ship drugs into Canada and the United States.
Can the minister tell this House whether or not the RCMP has been notified of these activities? What action does the RCMP intend to take?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not quite understand how the hon. member can tie in a free trade agreement, whether it is with the United States or Mexico or anywhere else, with the importation and smuggling of illegal substances into Canada or anywhere else.
In fact the free trade agreement with the United States has allowed our customs officers trained to protect Canadian society from the importation of drugs and illegal firearms, to be on the look-out for missing children, which we endorse today as part of Missing Children's Week, and to be able to apprehend and make more drug seizures at the border and across Canada in co-operation with the RCMP and other law enforcement agencies than before.
NAFTA and the free trade agreement have nothing to do with the importation of drugs other than allowing our customs officers more freedom to be on the look-out for such illegal substances.

Madam Speaker, my question for the minister was as to whether or not the RCMP had been notified of this report done by an intelligence officer for the National Security Agency.
I want to refer directly to the report and read a quote from it so we understand who is making the allegation about NAFTA. It is not I.
"The Rafael Munoz organization along with other well-known drug organizations in the Juarez and Tor-reon areas, states of Chihuahua and Coahuila, Mexico, intend to maximize their legitimate business enterprises within the auspices of the new U.S.-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement guidelines. Their plan calls for establishing Maquiladora assembly plants, free trade warehousing areas, fronted borderland purchases and other developments for future cross-border use. Once in place these operations can be used as fronts for drug trafficking activities into the United States".
This report was prepared for the United States government. Has the United States government made this government aware of the secret report it has prepared to alert police against this activity and what action has this government taken about it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are in constant co-operation and communication, not only with United States customs, but also with United States law enforcement agencies.
I can only repeat what I said in my answer to the hon. member's first question. NAFTA and the free trade agreement have nothing to do with increased importation of illegal drugs, other than allowing our well-trained officers the opportunity to have more time, more resources, more technology and a greater effort in dealing with missing children, the importation of illegal drugs, illegal firearms and other illegal substances into Canada.
Since the free trade agreement has come into effect, we have improved and increased our seizures of illegal drugs coming into Canada. That trend will continue with the signing of the NAFTA agreement.

I would like to state at the outset that I did not release the document to the public and I would like to believe no member of the committee did either.
I believe my colleagues uphold the principle of parliamentary privilege as I do. Naturally I am hurt that a colleague from the government side, the member for Don Valley North, would suggest the possibility that opposition members both in the NDP and my caucus could have released it only because we allowed ourselves to be interviewed by the media.
May 25, 1993

For my part I talked to the media only when called and with the explicit understanding that I could only discuss the testimony of witnesses which is in the public domain and my opinions on the issue. The two issues on which I did discuss my opinions were ones I had already raised more than once in questions in the Chamber for over six months.

The essence of confidentiality on this issue is to ensure equal opportunity of access to reports of the House of Commons by all Canadians. If we release the report ahead in the House all members of Parliament have equal access to this report and therefore all Canadians from coast to coast at the same time.
The parliamentary tradition of first access in the House of Commons ensures that information indeed is equally accessible to all Canadians. I would submit the temptation to be quoted ahead of others is a natural human trait, but in order to sustain the life of this privilege and the principle of equality on which it stands we must guard against the temptation.

this member and other members of this Chamber I will be prepared to make the appropriate motion at that time.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we broke I was underlining the irresponsibility of the government in bringing forward the NAFTA legislation for final disposition this week when we obviously do not yet know what those two side agreements to which I referred earlier will contain.
The United States has made its position very clear that it will not proceed until such time as it is certain of what will be in the side agreements. Yet the Canadian government continues to take the view that somehow the side agreements are irrelevant to the central issue of NAFTA when it must know perfectly well that the side agreements-if they mean anything-will entail differences in how the agreement is interpreted and applied.
In these circumstances we on this side of the House are strongly opposed to the procedure that this government has chosen to follow. It has not provided Canadians with the opportunity to debate or even to understand because it does not itself understand what will be in the two side agreements.
Earlier today my colleagues drew attention to the fact that the central issue concerning how side agreements on labour and environmental standards would be enforced has not been resolved. Only this past week here in Ottawa a major road block was encountered when the United States took the view that the side agreements should have what has been loosely called teeth but in fact are the provisions for enforcement through the application of trade sanctions.
The government has never indicated to the House or to the Canadian people what form such trade sanctions might take. It has merely said through its chief trade negotiator that such trade sanctions are unacceptable.
Surely on an issue of this importance all Canadians should know what the standards would be. Also, they should know the role of the proposed tripartite environmental commission and a parallel commission on labour standards and what those would have as their mandate. Finally, they should know what ability tripartite organizations would have to encourage compliance with the standards.
There are precedents available both in national law and in international law to suggest resolutions of this issue, however, on the eve of shoving and pushing through the NAFTA legislation we do not find any indication from this government as to its stance with regard to enforcement.
It is well known that in the case of Mexico the labour laws and more particularly the environmental laws are of a generally high standard. The issue or the problem has been that those standards have not been applied presumably largely because of the inability of the Mexican government to muster the resources to apply those standards.
It is not beyond the wit of humankind to devise methods of resolution and of application if time is given to serious consideration of these issues. Instead of providing that opportunity for the Canadian Parliament to offer its views and to offer its advice on how best to proceed, the Canadian government is proceeding quite unlike the United States and quite unlike Mexico.
The United States Congress will not be asked to pass judgment on implementing the legislation until such time as the side agreements are completed. It is evident that the Mexican Senate is not proceeding rapidly to endorse or ratify the agreement.
The result is that of the three parties to the proposed agreement it is only Canada which is acting in this precipitous fashion. It is beyond our imagination on this side of the House what possible motive the government must have for doing this.
If the government could explain its position, which it consistently has failed to do, then we might better understand why it is that it is in such a rush. In the absence of such explanations all we can ask is why it is in a rush. What is the hurry? Why is it that the government is proceeding in this precipitous fashion?
It intends to apply time allocation tomorrow. By Thursday afternoon, if it follows that path, presumably the NAFTA legislation will be out of the House of Commons. If we can infer from its actions in the House of Commons what its intention would be in the Senate then we can conclude that the government will apply time allocation in the Senate and we shall have the NAFTA legislation out of the Canadian Parliament by mid-June.
May 25, 1993

By mid-June we will know little more-if anything- than we know today about the intentions of the United States, why the United States has put forward its proposals on side agreements, what its commitment to those specific proposals are and to what degree it regards those proposals as negotiable with Mexico and Canada. Is it that in fact Mexico and Canada are merely spectators at a negotiation between the United States administration and the United States Congress?
Anyone who has had contact, as it were, with the United States Congress in the past will recognize that quite often in international agreements the situation arises whereby the administration, after prolonged negotiation with the U.S. Congress, finally comes up with what it regards as a solution to the problem. Then it says to its international partners: "That is the agreement between the President and the Congress and do not think you or we are going to change one comma or period in that agreement. That is it. Thke it or leave it".
Is that the situation that Canada wants to be placed in? Is that wise? Is that why the government is acting today? Does it seriously think that it is to Canada's advantage to proceed with this legislation when these and a myriad of other questions remain to be resolved?

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am privileged to participate in this debate this afternoon. To begin I think it would be useful for the members of this House and those watching to understand where we are in history and how we came to be where we are now.
Of course in early 1989 the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement was passed by this House. After the Bush administration had been successful in completing that task, it then looked southward to have a trade arrangement with its southern neighbour, Mexico. The Canadian government at that time realized that it was going to be scuppered if it did not try to participate in that trade arrangement with Mexico. It decided to crash the party, as it were. In that arrangement there was a lot of me-tooism on the part of the Canadian government.
Government Orders
Subsequently there was a presidential election campaign in which George Bush went up against Bill Clinton. Bill Clinton had to distinguish himself from George Bush on the issue of the North American free trade agreement. All of a sudden the wisdom of participating in a trade arrangement with Mexico was put in some doubt. However, does Canada change its position in the light of this new information? Oh, no. The me-tooism just carries on. Even after the party has been proven a bust we still want to crash it. This is called sanity gone completely amok.
Before getting into the substance of debating the amendments before us this afternoon, I want to put my comments in context. We are opposed to the North American free trade agreement. That is unequivocal. It is not just the procedures of this government's implementation of this legislation, it is the legislation itself that we are opposed to.
I also have no confidence that any supplemental agreements will adequately address environmental or labour concerns. I feel that the concerns in any trade arrangement that is made on any basis with any group should be embedded within the agreement.
The North American free trade agreement has huge gaps on environmental standards and labour law. Therefore I think it is fundamentally flawed and no supplemental agreements will address those concerns.
That being said, the amendments proposed by my colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca are an attempt in the face of this blind determination on the part of the government to pass the North American free trade agreement to humanize this very inhumane legislation.
To us it is utterly mystifying why the government is rushing to pass the North American free trade agreement legislation. Whose agenda is this anyway? What is the almighty rush?
I was in Halifax 10 days ago and met with colleagues from the U.S. Congress and the U.S. Senate. There is considerable doubt as to whether or not the legislation will pass in the United States. They are concerned that there are inadequate provisions for environmental standards and for labour law. Just this past week we have learned that the Canadian government negotiators have

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
split with their American counterparts on those supplemental agreements.
The Americans very much want strong enforceable tariffs so they can ensure that the laws they bring forward can be enforced. Canada is saying no. No, we do not want them to be enforced; we do not want trade sanctions to make certain that environmental or labour legislation is respected. So the U.S. and Canada have split on this.
The question should be asked; How can this split foster our negotiating stance at the table? Why should Canadians have any confidence at all in the ability of the Canadian negotiators to represent the interests of Canadians?
I know from first-hand experience how little faith there is in Canadian negotiators after the Canada-U.S. agreement. I ask the government why should the fish plant workers and the fishermen on the west coast, or the east coast for that matter, have any faith that the Canadian negotiators are working in their interests? If these negotiators are, as the government suggests, working in the best interests of Canadian citizens, the question of wages becomes a topic for vety real scrutiny.
My colleague from Kamloops has done a lot of research on this issue. He has come up with some frightening figures. As we all know, the map of North America is like an upside-down triangle. Well, the upside-down triangle is very real when it comes to wages. For jobs such as computer technicians or similar skill levels, in Canada the wage rate is $18 per hour. In the northern tier states-the triangle is getting a little narrower here-it is $12 per hour. For the border states, that is, Texas, the southern states, Florida, and so on, it goes down to $6.50 an hour. These rates are for similar skill levels. In Mexico those jobs pay 60 cents an hour.
What kind of logic would say that a negotiator is going to convince any investor to locate a plant in British Columbia when he can make that same investment in Mexico and have workers work for 60 cents an hour as opposed to $18 an hour in British Columbia? When we have negotiators using that kind of logic I am concerned not just as a parliamentarian but as a parent. How can I tell my children there will be jobs in the future when we
have a government that is negotiating that kind of a trade deal?
We are just focusing on the labour costs. I have spoken a number of times on the environmental provisions in NAFTA, but there are frightening pictures of environmental concerns along the Maquiladora where there are open sewers and no environmental standards or no enforcement of any environmental provisions that are there.
The amendments we are debating today relate to environmental and social conditions. This agreement is a bad deal for Canada. It is a bad deal for workers. It is certainly a bad deal for anyone who wants sustainable development in the future. It has no vision or only one that is tainted by the greed of the transnational corporations.
As politicians we have more to answer to than those in the boardrooms of our country. We have to answer to the workers and to future generations. This is a bad deal for Canadians, a bad deal for workers everywhere.

subtopic: NORTH AMERICAN FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with interest that I listen to this debate that concerns not just Canada, but more particularly the people of Canada.
Last Saturday, May 15, there was a tremendous rally on Parliament Hill. About 60,000 people marched in opposition to this agreement. These were ordinary people, people who are part of the Canadian fabric, workers, plumbers and others representing average Canadians.
Those people decided that this deal was not a good deal. They felt that it was premature to talk about free trade with the United States and Mexico. One of their reasons was that because of the free trade agreement with the United States, Canada has lost over 450,000 manufacturing jobs. Those jobs will never, never come back to Canada.
We are not in a position to be competitive with the United States and Mexico. I am not saying that trade as such is not a good idea, but before engaging in a free trade situation, we have to have conditions that allow us to be competitive. Those conditions do not exist right now in Canada.
May 25, 1993

First, our interest rates are much higher than those in the United States. Therefore, the manufacturer that has to borrow money has to pay much more for it. Second, it is a fact that taxation is about 10 per cent higher in Canada than in the United States. Therefore, why would any manufacturer locate a plant here if he knows that people who work in the United States or Mexico have a much lower rate of taxation? These two factors do not allow us to be competitive and as long as we do not have the same level of taxation, whether it is in the United States or Mexico, we will be the losers.
Another factor is that our climate is much harsher and therefore, it is much more expensive to produce goods in Canada. Just to give an example, even though they love Canada, most Canadians like to spend the winters in the south. In the past we have seen industries move to the United States, to Atlanta and the south because production and labour costs are much cheaper there.
All those reasons are not conducive to having a free trade agreement that will benefit Canada.
This particular NAFTA agreement has many serious flaws. 1 would like to cite one. It is on page 16 of the North American free trade agreement and concerns intellectual property: "This section also provides rules for protecting trade secrets generally, as well as for the protection from disclosure by the government test data submitted by firms regarding the safety and efficacy of pharmaceutical and agrichemical products".
This is a very serious matter. Looking back in history, we know what happened to the thalidomide victims. At that time the test data had not been divulged and people were taking thalidomide. As a physician I remember pharmaceutical agents visiting our offices and telling us that this medication was 100 per cent safe. Later the test data showed there were abnormalities in foetuses.
With this agreement the pharmaceutical companies would be able to protect test data showing that pharmaceutical products such as that would be dangerous. For that reason alone we are losing our sovereignty. If we sign this agreement we will not be able to control data that should be available to the general public.
Government Orders
It is known that Bill C-91 concerns pharmaceutical companies which are mostly foreign owned. That bill protects their patents for 20 years. Our generic companies are losing ground. This is not creating jobs in Canada. For that reason and many others working Canadians know very well that this deal will hurt them. It certainly does protect major corporations, but the home offices of those corporations are not in Canada and they do not have the interests of Canada in mind.
What we need are small businesses that are Canadian by nature. We know those businesses create more jobs than any free trade agreement would.
The European Economic Community has a free trade deal, but that deal is completely different. In Europe the countries are closer together and there is very little difference in the pay scales. Therefore it benefits Europe to some extent.
Sweden wanted to get into the European Community but it was decided it could not join. It would not be competitive with the other countries because of its taxation structure and productivity. Therefore it is still waiting as it has not solved its problems inside the country.
I think the same applies to Canada. As long as Canada has lower productivity, higher taxation and higher interest rates than the United States, it cannot be competitive.
Another question I would like to ask is as to how this deal would solve our debt and deficit problem. I am sure it will not. It is going to aggravate that problem because we are in debt. How are we going to pay the debt of $660 billion that all levels of government owe to Canadians and to foreigners? With that deal we will never pay that back and we will become the Panama of North America.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with my colleagues on this side of the House in opposing the legislation as it is proposed by the government for many reasons. I would like to share with you as well as with the public a few of those reasons.
The free trade agreement came into effect on January 1, 1989. There had been a lot of promises on the part of the government. One of its promises was that when the agreement had taken effect a lot of adjustment programs

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
would be put in place in order to deal with displaced workers. There would be programs to train and retrain the work force and so on.
We have seen a lack of initiative on the part of the government in those areas. In fact we have seen the opposite since the signing of this deal. While the Canadian and the American governments have agreed on the elimination of trade barriers, unfortunately we have seen a lot of discrimination when it comes to Canadian products such as softwood lumber, steel, wheat and meat.
One would suggest that those products were discriminated against by the Americans basically because there has been no agreement on the definition of a subsidy. Having said that, unless the subsidy question is resolved I would suggest that the same sort of scenarios will develop if and when the North American free trade agreement is implemented.
The subsidy question is still up in the air and the different parties are dancing around it without being able to tackle it head on. That is one problem we are faced with.
The second problem we are faced with is that there has been no guarantee in the event the North American free trade agreement is put in place that a multilateral committee would be able to resolve all of the trade disputes between different countries. There is no guarantee that committee would be able to do so without a proper definition of what forms a subsidy and what does not form a subsidy. Our work is cut out for us.
On the other hand, the government is rushing this legislation through at an incredible speed, way over the speed limit, to pass it through the House of Commons and pass it through the Senate. Only then will it stop without giving it final approval. Royal assent will not be given to the North American free trade agreement until both the American and Mexican governments have received approval of the North American free trade agreement from their legislators.
It has already been stated by the President of the United States that this deal will not go through the United States Congress and the Senate without having a parallel agreement along with it. On the other side, our government is saying that is not the case. As members of
Parliament who are representing the people of this country we should be given the clear goods in terms of what the position of the government is in the event the parallel agreement does not go through.
What is the position of this government in the event that the American government does not approve the free trade agreement over the next few weeks? I might suggest that the government will end up with egg all over its face. Simply put, there is no reason for us to be in the position we are in to push for a legislation when we have absolutely no clear indication or a clear statement on the part of the American government that it will go through.
Unlike our colleagues in the NDP we do not want to see walls built around Canada. We do not want to lock ourselves in. We are a party that believes in fair and freer trade. At the same time we do not want to see ourselves in a position whereby we are giving everything away without trying to put the fundamentals in place in order to protect the interests of Canadian business and the people of Canada as a whole.
I might suggest that this particular agreement, and the way the government is handling it, is not in the best interests of Canadian business, the Canadian public or the government.
The government will have no credibility after June 15 or June 23 when it goes to the negotiating table when the Senate and the House of Commons have already approved it. The government will have played the last card in its hand. Our negotiators will not be in the best position they could have been if the government had waited to have the legislation approved by this House and by the other place.
It is gambling at the expense of both Canadian business and the Canadian public, gambling that is not going to be in the best interests of Canadians.
There are a lot of things we would like to see happening to both the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and eventually the North American free trade agreement. We must have a clear and unequivocal statement on the question of subsidy codes. We also must have a clear understanding and a clear statement on the question of the anti-dumping code.
May 25, 1993

We also must have an effective dispute resolution mechanism because obviously what we have before us now is not solving the question of disputes and is not really dealing with all of the disputes before us in an effective manner.

We also must have similar protection when it comes to energy, as they have in Mexico.
However our position on the North American free trade agreement as it stands right now is unequivocally clear. We will not be supporting the legislation as it is proposed before the House of Commons. It has voted that it will not support any free trade agreement, not this free trade agreement, not the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, not any agreement. When someone is opposed to any trade whatsoever, one would question the motive.
On the other side, the government has decided to give away everything without tiying to protect the interests of the business community and the labour community in Canada, as well as people at large. We have those two extremes.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly will be addressing some of the issues raised at the end of the previous speaker's speech because the implication that New Democrats are opposed to trade is one of the most spurious arguments that has come up of late.
I would like to start by congratulating the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca for having made the amendments he has to the proposed legislation by the government. In this particular group he has proposed an

amendment affecting a matter of labour adjustment. There certainly will have to be labour adjustment because if this agreement goes into effect the dislocation of wage earners in Canada, not just hourly workers, is going to be phenomenal. We know that there was literally no adjustment at all. The committee set up to look into it proposed that there was not that much of a dislocation and adjustment was not needed. He is also proposing that we address the matter of a social charter as it relates to the further dislocations which occur in our society and workers' protections for certain programs. I do hope I will have time to address some of these issues in more detail later.

I cannot help but reflect not only on the legislation before us right now but also the whole legislative process that has gone on since I came into this House. The first item we dealt with, certainly myself anyway, as new members of the House of Commons was the free trade agreement with the United States. I would suggest that what we really have seen not only since I came into this House but since this government became elected was the imposition on all Canada of the same kind of a period which has become known in Quebec as the great darkness.
The great darkness refers to that period in Quebec when the government was so tremendously oppressive of its people that there was very little opportunity for any kind of democratic action to be pursued and it was very difficult for people to express their human rights and function in a normal democratic society at all. I suggest

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
that what we have in Canada now is the same as it was in Quebec. It is best described as the great darkness.
The very fact that this legislation is being pushed through as hastily as it is without any real evidence that it has to be done as quickly as it is being done marks the very epitome of the kind of oppression which was so extant during the great darkness in Quebec. We certainly have it here now.
The basic assumption is we have a contempt for people. That was certainly symptomatic of what was happening during the great darkness. That being the case, I would suggest that it would be in the interests of all Canadians, and certainly it would be in the interests of the government, perhaps and most likely for its even potential re-election aspirations, to give Canadians the opportunity to be able to go through the economic constitution with the same thoroughness and receive the same amount of information and debate-I am referring to the North American free trade agreement-as was given to the Constitution.
There are a number of issues, as I pointed out earlier, to which some very close scrutiny must be given to the effects of what this agreement will do. But if we are looking at the legislation, we have to do the best we can to make proposals to it which will make it as humane and as acceptable as possible to all Canadians. Yesterday I was talking to some people who asked: "Ron, how are things going in Ottawa," and I had to reply: "Not very well". When they asked what was the matter I had to tell them that this was the week when the North American free trade agreement was going to be passed in the House of Commons. Mr. Speaker,
I wish to add my voice to this debate and to thank my colleague, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, for putting forward this motion. It is the first motion and talks about a number of very important aspects of this free trade agreement. I want to highlight some of these.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is trying to make sure that when the government signs the free trade deal or goes into a free trade deal, the rights of Canadian workers, indeed of all Canadians, are protected. The hon. member and I do not feel this is actually taking place.
In his amendment he asks us to respect the freedom of association and affirm the role that free and independent, public and private sector unions play in the conduct of democratic governance. He wants to honour the rights of working people to organize and to bargain collectively and the right to strike. He wants to encourage an open dialogue between management and labour in all decisions affecting the future of the work force as a result of this agreement.
Prior to this agreement, this country entered into the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. In that agreement we found that labour was shut out of the process. In fact there was not that negotiation and as a result Canadian workers were left out of this deal. They feel their demonstration on the Hill a few days ago shows their rights are not being protected and are not even being addressed by this government.
Finally, what my hon. colleague, the member for Kenora-Rainy River, wants is the adjustment programs that were promised by the Prime Minister and the Minister for International Trade.
After the last deal these same requests that the Americans are addressing, that President Clinton has said are important and he will bring in in his country for American workers, are programs that somehow the government has forgotten about. It says it cannot bring in adjustment programs because it would discriminate against those workers in industries that are closing down not because of free trade. How would you make it fair to
Government Orders
address the concerns of those workers who have lost their jobs because of free trade and those workers who have lost their jobs simply because of the downturn in the economy?
I do not buy that argument. My friend, the member from Rainy River, does not buy that argument. My friend, the member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso does not buy that argument and the member for York West does not buy that argument. On a daily basis the government provides funds and programs for certain sectors of the economy such as the fishing industry in my friend's riding. He may argue that the government does not provide enough and he is probably right, but there are specific programs directed toward specific aspects of our economy and specific industries in the economy that are hurt.
The government came up with the de Grandpre report as a response to this. It was really set out to justify its inaction. The government has done nothing with the recommendations of this report which would have gone,
I would suggest, a long way in dealing with some of these problems.
That is what the hon. member is asking for and I do not think it is an unreasonable request. I hope that the members opposite, as few of them as there are in this House tonight, will take a serious look at supporting this amendment.
I will be talking on this bill at a later occasion. I just wanted to address some of the concerns of my friend. I want to say that a lot of constituents in my area of Haldimand-Norfolk, when I was at the Jarvis parade yesterday came up and said to me: "Bob, how can this government be passing this legislation? I thought they were still in negotiations. Is it not still negotiating the labour aspects of this bill and the environmental aspects of this bill?" I said it was. They said: "Well will this not have a major impact on how this bill will influence Canadian labour codes or influence Canadian workers or influence the environment of Canada?" I had to agree. They said: "Why the heck are you passing this bill at this time?"
I will be talking a little later when the environment motions come up about my concerns on how this government did not address environmental concerns in this legislation. I want to read a news story from Southam News where it states: "Canada seeks limits on NAFTA environmental powers". I am sure it relates in the same way to the labour code which my hon. friend has been

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
talking about. It reads: "The confidential Canadian position paper, reprinted by Inside U.S. Trade"-we had to get it from Inside U.S. Trade because we did not have access to it here in this House-"shows that Canada could curb the powers and propose a three nation monitoring system. Canada proposes that the commission act more as a mediator producing recommendations that may assess parties to reach a mutually satisfactory resolution in any dispute", rather than putting some teeth into that.
Canadians really want to know what this issue is because there is a question of sovereignty. It is a question of how much sovereignty do we give up as a country in order to get some sort of fair trading practice with both the United States and Mexico.
The report also states that the government said that Canada would allow the commission to look at complaints from citizens or environmental groups only if they received backing from their home government.
It seems to me they want to mute some of the concerns of these groups before they go to these commissions. The whole idea of the commission is to make sure that Mexico for instance which has the same environmental and labour laws as Canada will enforce those laws.
If it does not enforce them, products coming into this country from countries that do not have the same environmental or labour standards as this country will have a tariff or possibly may not be allowed into the country.
That makes a lot of sense. How can we as Canadian farmers stop a Mexican product on which DDT was used? We cannot use it in this country because it is not environmentally sound. How can we allow those products into our country without first making sure those unsafe pesticides and herbicides are removed?
That is the crux of this issue. It is an issue of labour standards also. Why should we as a country allow our workers to lose jobs to Mexican workers and employers who do not have the same standards as we do in Canada? There is a way to stop that. We can make sure that
products coming from those countries are not allowed in this country if they are not playing by fair rules.
I think we as a country need to get away from being the boy scouts of the world. We need to take some strong trade actions to stop this material from coming into our country. Canadian workers, farmers and businesses have no fear of competing against anyone in the world. I believe we as a country can compete as long as we have a level playing field.
We do not have that level playing field now under the Canada-U.S. free trade deal. This NAFTA deal is even worse than the one we now have with the United States. If we do not have a subsidies code, if we do not have similar anti-dumping legislation then there is no way we as a country can compete fairly with the other countries. Let us have fair trade and not this so-called free trade.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to have as many members in the House as possible for the words I have to offer all of us today.
Government Orders

Debate has just begun on the report stage to look at numerous amendments that could extend for hours if not days simply on the amendments that have been brought before us. Before this debate even begins the government walks in and announces it is going to move a closure motion to shut down the debate.
As you will recall, at second reading of this bill we also had a closure motion that effectively cut debate on this important bill to just a little over two hours in this Chamber. When the committee studying this legislation sat down to have a look at it the government members moved the motion that essentially produced a closure in committee. The very first motion they discussed set a specific timetable for the committee. Committee debate would end on a given day whether it had finished its study or not. Now at report stage and prior to third reading after only a couple of hours of debate in the House, the government House leader has once again come in and imposed closure on us.
There are important things we have to talk about here. The parliamentary secretary earlier today accused members on this side of the House of not wanting to debate the bill because we kept talking about process. We are forced to discuss process because the government continues to cut off useful debate on this issue.
The member for Kamloops put it quite clearly earlier today that all the debate in the world is not going to change the opinion of the New Democrats in this House of Commons. We do not agree with the North American free trade agreement or the legislation that is being brought in to implement it. We are very strongly opposed to this legislation because of its failings.
This government does not want to listen to the debate that puts forth the failings of this legislation and gives it the opportunity to have second thoughts about this poor piece of legislation it is forcing upon the Canadian people. As an opposition party in this House of Commons we have an obligation to talk about its inability to listen to what the people of Canada have to say, the experts throughout the country and the people who are speaking for those who oppose the agreement itself.

Government Orders
We have heard over and over again from Canadians from coast to coast to coast, from people who have studied this legislation and from people who have studied the implications of the agreement how bad this legislation or agreement really is and the devastation it is going to cause to the people of this country. One of the things that is not discussed frequently either in this Chamber or anywhere else is how this legislation will impact on ordinary people in all three countries, in Canada, the United States and Mexico, working people, people concerned about the environment and people who live off the land. These are the people in Mexico, the United States and Canada who will be adversely affected by this legislation. This government refuses to take the opportunity to listen to this debate and maybe take a second look and recognize what it is doing to this country.
It is a very important debate. The government should be sitting here listening to it with all its ears. Earlier today members of my party brought to the attention of the Chamber the fact that during this important debate on a bill that is 4,000 pages long, the minister responsible for this legislation has chosen to be elsewhere. In fact quorum had to be called just a few minutes ago because there was only one member of the government party in the Chamber.
I know that it is not proper etiquette in this place to talk about the presence or absence of a member but, my goodness, this is a debate that is dealing with the economic future of our entire country. This is a matter that is going to affect the future of hundreds of thousands of Canadians tomorrow, the next day, the next month and for the rest of the life of this country however long we have to exist as a sovereign nation.
This bill implementing the North American free trade agreement rewrites the economic constitution of this country. This morning the hon. member for Kamloops gave a very eloquent speech in which he talked about the economic constitution of Canada and how the North American free trade agreement essentially restructures the entire economic framework in which we operate.
Where does this come from? I am asked this over and over and over again in my own constituency. What is the rush? What is the urgency? What is the need for an agreement of this nature? I took a copy of the very large
North American free trade agreement to one of the high schools in my constituency just two weeks ago. I took that agreement in because these young people were saying: "We need to establish better trading practices between countries". I agreed with them. We do have to trade in a more elaborate fashion that allows for Canadians to be employed, to earn wealth and to create revenues for the running of the country, their communities and their households.
When one puts that agreement in front of persons and they intelligently flip through it and read it, they notice that this is more than simply a way in which we are going to trade goods between one country and another. It is a brand new economic structure for North America and it comes from the corporations who operate with no political boundaries in mind.
Who is asking for this agreement? It is not the small business in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan or the mediumsized manufacturing company in Cut Knife, Saskatchewan or the produce company in Meadow Lake, Saskatchewan. These are not the companies that are pushing for this deal. They are the companies that are the friends of the Conservatives such as the multinationals who are already getting the tax breaks and the corporate breaks and who are treating their friends to tax-free lunches in SkyDome boxes while they watch the Blue Jay games. These are the people who are going to benefit from the North American free trade agreement and not the working people or the farmers in Mexico, the United States or in Canada. Not on one's life.
We have an opportunity here today to debate reasonably and effectively some veiy important amendments to this legislation which, while it will not correct the problems, if this government is bound and determined to barrel ahead with it, it will in fact smooth the water somewhat for the people who have to live with it after the fact.
We have side agreements which are being negotiated that this government seems to be ignoring. My goodness, there is just no logic to what is happening here.
Mr. Speaker, I see you have given me the one minute signal. I am sorry that I only have 10 minutes to speak. I do want to indicate that as it stands and as this legislation exists today as a restructuring of our entire economic framework, I and most of my constituents and my party cannot support the legislation or the agreement.
May 25, 1993

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-115 which is the free trade agreement for North America.
It is really incredible that this bill is only the implementing legislation for an agreement that is at least six inches thick and that the government treats it in such a cavalier way. It whipped through the whole public hearing process with very few witnesses and no hearings across the country.
We are going through a charade here in the House of Commons this afternoon and tomorrow. The entire legislation implements a free trade deal that not only involves the United States and Mexico, but makes provisions for all the nations of the North and South American continents to join in. The government hardly has a minister or any members in the House. It is as if this was tissue paper and did not really matter.
I think it is incredible that the government would negotiate a deal like this and go to all the effort that is involved and the political downside. Canadians are opposed to the deal two to one. Then the government members do not even come into the House to bother defending it or to argue in favour of the bill.
I have the distinct feeling that we are facing the same situation as in 1987-88 where essentially the vast majority opposed the government yet it implemented the FTA. In the 1988 general election something like 57 per cent of the people opposed it. We have this situation today where the North American free trade deal is being rammed through the House in a matter of 12 hours with no participation by the government to speak of at all. Speeches are being made by the members of the Official Opposition and by the NDP to try to call on the government to take some responsibility to treat this matter seriously.
Our party is in favour of freer trade around the world. In the 1988 general election we supported expanding our trade with countries including the United States, Mexico and all other countries through the GATT agreement. We did it simply because we believe that Canada has a better opportunity to negotiate a freer trading arrangement with the rest of the world through multilateral trade arrangements rather than through the FTA.
Government Orders
Clearly if there ever was a trade deal that turned out to be veiy bad it was the FTA. It is impossible to count the number of jobs that were lost. Some say it is 400,000 due to the FTA. Clearly thousands and thousands of Canadians are not working today because of the FTA combined with the fiscal and monetary policies of the Government of Canada during the ensuing three or four years since the FTA was first signed in 1988 and came into effect in 1989.
I guess the part of the NAFTA agreement that I find offensive is that the government has the experience of the FTA with the problems of multiple trade remedy law attacking Canadians and Canadian products, the problems of the anti-dumping duties imposed against the steel industry and the countervail duty on hogs, pork and other commodities. Yet the government is sitting down to negotiate this.
Let us be clear about this. The same guy that signed the FTA is the same guy that signed the NAFTA agreement. The Minister for International Trade, who was Minister of Finance back in 1987-88, is the same negotiator. He was aware of the deficiencies of the FTA. Yet in the NAFTA he did not move to correct it. He did not try to get a subsidy code. He did not try to get an anti-dumping code. Look at every other international trade agreement around the world, whether it is the European Economic Community or the Australasian agreement with New Zealand and Australia. He did not try to correct those problems and so those are two very major problems.
The fact that we are reducing tariffs in some ways will be beneficial to Canada because essentially we had a type of one way free trade deal with Mexico where we were allowing most things from Mexico into Canada but it had quotas and all kinds of trade restrictions on our exports. However, the obvious things are those deficiencies in the FTA which the government made no attempt to correct as far as we can see.
There is the whole question of labour standards. If there are people working for $1 an hour manufacturing things in Mexico and they are working for $12 or $15 an hour in Canada then it is going to be very hard to compete. If there is a plant that can turn out plastics in Mexico where there are no environmental standards to meet and the waste is discharged into rivers, streams, or landfills then it is very hard to compete.

At least there was a change in government in Washington last January 20. If there had not been a change then that would have gone on. At least the Clinton administration has a concern with that arrangement such that it is demanding side deals related to labour standards and the environment.

It proposes to make remedies to the problems relating to labour standards and the whole social milieu and the arrangements in that regard. I compliment the member for Kenora-Rainy River in putting this motion before the House. It is one of several being debated in this group.
It is incredible that we are debating this legislation today. The United States has not even introduced the legislation in Congress, either in the Senate or the House of Representatives. We have no idea about the companion pieces of legislation relating to labour standards and the environment which are very important.
We are not only dealing with the environment as an economic cost in the manufacture of things, but there is also, from the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex, a motion relating to the chemical residues in food and agriculture products which are so important. We want to trade with Mexico. We want to trade with all nations around the world but we want to do it in a safe and healthful way.
We are opposing this legislation today not because we do not want to expand our trade with Mexico and the other Latin American countries, but we are concerned with the situation where legislation is rushed through the House. We do not even know when the companion legislation will be negotiated or if it ever will be negotiated with regard to the environment and human health and safety or labour standards.
This is really being rushed at us. It is not having the proper consultation with Canadians. Canadians are very concerned about it. They are very frustrated by the process and they want to see this legislation put off until it is better organized and better arranged and until there is a more complete consultation with Canadians so that we do not buy a pig in a poke as has happened so often in the past with so many of the things the government has brought forward.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like first of all to add my voice to those on this side of the House who are condemning the government for ramming through a bill which has not even been negotiated by the Congress of the United States, the Parliament of Mexico and indeed the negotiators here in Canada.
I find it incredible that a few short moments ago the House leader of the Tory party once again, for the umpteenth time in the course of this Parliament, came in and invoked closure. The Conservatives will go down, when they die as they will in a few short months, as the government that invoked closure the greatest number of times in Canada's history.

speechtext: The most obstreperous opposition in the history of Canada.

The member says obstreperous opposition. It was not the Liberal Party that brought in the tactic of bell ringing. When we had the discussion of the Crow rate back in the early eighties there were literally hundreds of hours of discussion in the House. The Conservatives of the day, who were in opposition, charged the chair. The current government House leader was known for grabbing the mace and attacking the Speaker. In 1988 Canadians were asked to sign an agreement. They were asked to take a leap of faith by a Prime Minister who promised them hundreds of thousands of jobs were going to appear as a result of the free trade agreement. At that time we had some warnings for the Canadian people. We said that the steel industry was an industry potentially at risk if the free trade agreement did not contain a proper definition of what constitutes a subsidy and if it did not foresee an integrated steel market patterned after the pattern set by a Liberal government with the auto pact.
Five years ago we were accused by the government of being obstreperous. We were accused of being fear mongers. We were accused of all sorts of things. Five years later the only question that remains is: When can we get rid of this government?

Government Orders
In the city of Hamilton employees at Adpak today received notice that another Hamilton manufacturing plant will be closed. The people of Hamilton know that the promise of the Prime Minister about the free trade agreement has not materialized. In fact what we have is a trade deal that has gone in one direction. Now we are not even being asked, we are being told to ram through a NAFTA deal, a 4,000 page document, that has not even been negotiated by the three parties.
Why is the Prime Minister and his government so desperate to get this trade agreement through in the next 15 days? Could it be that it has more to do with his intention to rewrite the history books than it does with his concern for Canadian workers?
Any objective observer who analyses the last four years of economic decline, particularly in the manufacturing sector, can only conclude that the free trade agreement has not worked for Canadians. It has sent Canadian jobs and Canadian companies south of the border. With the holes in the current NAFTA we can expect more of the same.

There are gaping holes in it concerning the definition of subsidy and concerning labour standards.

That is why I am happy that the member for Kenora- Rainy River has introduced a very constructive amendment that would deal with one crucial issue and concern for Canadian workers: Under the NAFTA, under free trade, will Canadian labour standards be protected or will we see Canadian wage rates, Canadian working conditions, and the Canadian right of free association being pulled down to the lowest common denominator?
I am sure members on the government side of the House will be standing over the next few hours, because that is all we have since the government is insistent on ramming this through, and giving chapter and verse about all the wonderful trade laws and environmental laws that exist in Mexico. It is true. Mexico has reasonable labour and environmental standards on the books. There is only one problem, which is that they are respected in the breach.
Anybody who witnessed the absolutely horrific environmental disaster of that liquid oil leak which occurred last year in Mexico, where an industrial company that was making cooking oil was pouring the extra cooking oil into the sewers of Guadalajara, will know that all the labour laws in the world will not help if they are not applied.
In its current form this bill has absolutely no protection for Canadian workers, for Canadian labour standards or for Canadian environmental standards.
We are being asked by this government to buy a second pig in a poke. We bought a pig in a poke in 1988. Remember the Prime Minister's promise: "Sign this trade agreement and we will create hundreds of thousands of jobs".
The jobs have been created but they have not been created in this country. In my own community in the last three years we have lost over 10,000 jobs in the steel industry alone and the steel industry was supposed to be one of the winners in the free trade agreement.
If one is a smart business person and has undergone an expansion-and that is essentially what we did in the first round of free trade agreements. We expanded our capacity to trade but did not do the proper cost benefit analysis to Canadian workers and Canadian companies in the first phase of free trade.
The amendment by the member for Kenora-Rainy River requires that this agreement respect freedom of association and affirm the role that free and independent public and private sector unions play in the conduct of democratic government.
This agreement must honour the rights of all working people to organize, to bargain collectively and to have the fundamental right to strike. This agreement must implement retraining and adjustment programs for workers displaced as a result of this agreement. This agreement must encourage an open dialogue between management and labour on all decisions affecting the future of the work force.
The Prime Minister of Canada promised that in 1988 every worker who lost her or his job as a result of the free trade agreement would get government assistance. What happened? The government struck a commission and the commission came back and said: We are sorry but we made a mistake. We made a promise but we are

not going to deliver. There is not a single program that this government has developed specifically to respond to those workers who have lost their jobs as a result of the free trade agreement.

The same Prime Minister promised us in 1988 that there would be adjustment programs for workers who lost their jobs, but what is he doing now? If the government believes that its document is good, if the government believes in a second stage of free trade, why is it forcing us again to vote on a bill which has not even been negotiated by the three governments concerned? Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this amendment, which I find very laudable. I hope that the political parties in the House of Commons will support it.
Let me first review the Liberal policy with respect to NAFTA. We as a party want a common set of trading rules and a level playing field. We want a definition of subsidy and we want it now. We want a definition of dumping and we want it now. We want to ensure that there are appropriate labour and environmental standards before we proceed and we want that now. We want the same deal on energy as Mexico has secured from the U.S. and we want it now not later. We need sovereignty over our natural resources.

When I made my speech in 1988, as we began this trip with the United States, I remember asking at the time that we obtain a basic guarantee for Canadian workers to have training and retraining programs which would help those who lost their jobs find new ones. You will no doubt remember that, Mr. Speaker, because I know you have an excellent memory, just as your colleagues opposite who are going along with everything I am saying now.
During that election campaign, we were told we would have the best training and retraining programs in the world. But what happened in fact? Well, Mr. Speaker, you know as well as I do that there were no such programs. Nothing like that happened, so the country is in worse shape.

Today we talk about 1.6 million Canadians unemployed, but some people suggest there are probably twice as many because some people have given up. We talk about over 2.2 million Canadians on social assistance, perhaps even more than that. We talk about over two million people being fed in food banks this year in Canada, one of the richest nations in the world. We talk about a country that once looked after its poor and those who did not have enough in such a way that they could get back into the work force. This is what has happened to our country because of these policies.
This proposal that we ensure free association, that we can continue to have unions involved, that we can assure workers that their bread and butter and their jobs will be protected is an essential one. Perhaps even more important, we can not only state that there will be the best training programs available in the world but make sure that anything we can do to make sure that this happens will be done.
We do not want to fall into the same trap we fell into before. We went forward with an agreement and found out later that we were totally unprepared and now thousands of Canadians are in the unemployment lines, thousands of others are receiving social assistance and thousands of others are being fed by food banks.
In this country, and we could quibble about definitions of poverty, there are close to five million Canadians living at or below the level of poverty, most of whom are

women and over one million of whom are children. This is really deplorable.

They are making changes to the Canadian Wheat Board and they refused to bring the commissioners of the Wheat Board to the committee. It is as if they were making changes to Air Canada, or to CN, and not bringing some of the directors of those corporations before a committee. It did not happen.
When we asked to hear the advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat board, a body elected by producers to represent producers at the wheat board, we were denied. We had Professor Carter before the committee and we asked for an extension of time. That was denied because the government does not want to consult.
We need some real consultation and this is where consultation should take place. The Canadian Wheat Board should be reviewed. It was set up in 1935. There have been changes made to it. A board cannot remain stagnant. The way we market grain has not been stagnant. Surely if we are going to make changes we should do it in an open fashion.
The purpose of setting up the Wheat Board in the 1930s was to help market surplus grain the countiy could not get rid of. That was its purpose and it did a good job. In fact when the Canadian Wheat Board was first set up it was going to be set up as the Canadian Grains Board but in the debate that followed that bill in the House there were changes made. In fact it was reduced to simply wheat and at that time there was a dual marketing system. For a few years the farmers had a choice of hauling their grain either to the Wheat Board or to market through the private grain trade. That did not work.
What happened was when the initial price for the Wheat Board was higher than the so-called spot market the grain came to the Wheat Board. When the price was lower grain did not come.
The argument on the other side has been that if we open up barley and have a dual marketing system farmers will have a choice. That is not a choice because the nature of the Canadian Wheat Board requires that it have a monopoly in marketing grain because of the pooling system. If you are going to maintain a pooling system you cannot have a situation where the Wheat Board does not know how much grain is coming in, when it can market it and so on. If this is going to work it is going to work on a monopoly basis or not at all.
This bill is inadequate. It only calls for barley to be given the same protection under the wheat board as wheat is. There are more aspects to the Canadian Wheat Board and the future of grain marketing than that alone.
A number of areas could be looked at. One of the key aspects of this bill and of the Canadian Wheat Board is that we have to remember the Wheat Board is paid for by farmers. If we remove barley from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board, it is not going to save the taxpayer a penny. The taxpayer will not gain anything because the taxpayer does not pay for the Wheat Board, farmers pay for the Wheat Board. Those people who have permit books, those people who grow grain, those people who are hauling to the Wheat Board, are the ones who pay for the Wheat Board. It is not going to

make a more efficient government by taking barley away from the Wheat Board.
