It is important because the way the various representatives of the various parties put their position forward should be indicative of their attitude toward rural Canada.
I would suggest that in rural Canada the primary resource sector, whether it be fishing, forestry, mining or agriculture, is key to its future. We are going to need diversification and development in other areas, but the primary resource sector is the key to the future of rural Canada. How a federal government approaches the primary resource sector is going to be the key on how rural Canada is developed.
The way that this government has moved with respect to agriculture should send shivers down the spines of most Canadians. We can look at other primary resource sectors. The fishing industry is in peril in Atlantic Canada. The future of mining and mining communities which become deserted after years of people contributing in a particular area, the future of forestry with respect to clear cutting and other areas, all of these issues are important for rural Canada.

Private Members' Business
The Canadian Wheat Board, which is important to western Canada, is one of those industries that is important to the rural community in that part of the country.
I would like to conclude by saying that I am looking forward to hearing what other members and the government have to say. I am also very pleased that this bill has reached the floor of the House and that we are finally having a debate on the Canadian Wheat Board, a debate on agriculture and a debate on the future of rural Canada. It is an important issue for all rural Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to join the ongoing debate that has been held several times in this House and in committees of this House about issues that are relevant to our rural constituencies in western Canada. I really welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate today.
I would also like to note at the outset that the specific role, mandate and potential of the Canadian Wheat Board has been the subject of a lot of discussion both here in the House of Commons, in the agriculture committee and in farm organizations across western Canada for a long time.
The proponent, the member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, has stated that he wants to see an agricultural sector that is self-reliant. He wants clear rules from the government. This government in the last few years has been working hard to ensure that there are clear rules for agriculture, that there are fewer regulations for agriculture and that the whole agrifood sector is capable of competing internationally against those people and interests that we have to compete against in the world. We cannot hide from competition in the world today and this government is making sure that the agrifood sector is as competitive as possible.
Let me start by reflecting on a success story that has been remarkable. That is the success story of oats that has developed since 1989. Let us look at the facts. The facts are pretty clear. For the 10 years between 1977 and 1987, under the Canadian Wheat Board marketing monopoly, oat exports were 110,000 tonnes per year. In the four years since, 1989 the average has been more than three times that; over 350,000 tonnes in exports per year. This year there will be more than 600,000 tonnes in
exports. That tells me that is quite an improvement. That is more than six times the amount of oats that was exported in the 10 years from 1977 to 1987.
Now let us talk about the whole agrifood export chain. There also happens to have been three new processing plants on the prairies, one in Manitoba, and two in Alberta. Those processing plants have the capacity to handle 170,000 tonnes and 75 per cent of that goes for export. That is 170,000 tonnes capacity in these processing plants on the prairies. That is compared to only 110,000 tonnes in total exports in the 10-year period prior to 1987.
This is a remarkable growth in the market. This has come about in part because Canadian farmers have been offered the choice and they seized the opportunity to choose to find their own niche markets or to market their oats privately and that has been a tremendous success. I do not think anybody could argue the contrary, although I am sure that my colleagues on the opposition side will try. However, as the facts really speak for themselves, it is impossible to argue the contrary.
Look at the facts. Look at oat prices today. The price for oats today is up about 25 per cent over what it was last year. It is a very positive market for oats producers. Farmers were given a choice. They took that choice and it was possible to develop a very important market for those farmers who took that opportunity. That is a big success story.
I remind members of the opposition that nobody is proposing that barley be taken away from the Canadian Wheat Board. The proposal out there is simply to allow both private marketing and marketing through the Wheat Board. Farmers will have the chance to choose how they will be able to market. They would have had the opportunity to market barley into the United States only, incidentally. In the continental market they would have that opportunity to choose.
The world marketplace has changed dramatically over the years. With those changes there is a real need for change in the government and in the way in which those in the Canadian agrifood industry deal with the challenges before them. They have to ask themselves some questions.
May 25, 1993

What grain marketing structure can best exploit market opportunities? That is the first and most important question the industry must ask itself. The Agriculture Canada regulatory review held last year is an example of government and industry working together to answer this question.
Of course this bill we are talking about was introduced in September 1991 prior to the launching of the regulatory review. To a large degree events have overtaken it, but this does provide us with an opportunity to put some facts on the table which are critical to understanding what is going on in the marketplace.
The review asked whether those regulations governing industry were enhancing the competitiveness of Canadian farmers or whether those regulations were hindering it. Numerous changes to regulations have already been made and more are coming. These changes will reduce paper work and lessen costs for farmers.
Part of the review of the regulations was an examination of the concept of a continental barley market. During the regulatory review some members of the agriculture industry asked that this specific issue be reviewed and examined further. Some said they wanted an opportunity to sell their barley on the open market within North America, while others endorsed the continuation of the Canadian Wheat Board as the sole marketer of Canadian barley to outside markets.
It was pretty clear that the issue of barley marketing was one that needed further study. Mr. Speaker, I think you will understand that the bottom line for everybody involved was to examine what was best for barley producers.
A study was commissioned and was chaired by the associate deputy minister of grains and oilseeds. An industry round table of 19 members was put together for the study. This group included representatives from the Canadian Wheat Board, the Canadian Grain Commission, Prairie Pools and other farm organizations and grain-trading companies. The round table agreed to the selection of a consultant to carry out the analytical work. After the consultant was agreed upon, the group also agreed to the terms of reference and the methodology for the study. Round table members were encouraged to
Government Orders
provide their input to the consultant and the consultant then reported back to the round table through his study.
It is important to put into perspective Canada's barley industry.

Mr. Speaker, before the debate was interrupted, I raised the following question: Why rush this particular piece of legislation? I advanced the hypothesis that the government was trying to position itself for the election. We all know there needs to be an election this year, whether the Tories want it or not. There will be one and the Canadian people will render a verdict on all of their policies.
Mr. Speaker, you understand this particularly well. If the government can get it through now it could create a bit of space between this legislation and the election. In doing so it hopes that Canadians will have forgotten that this legislation, as inadequate as it is, was forced through by a majority government.
Another hypothesis has been advanced. That is that the Prime Minister will be leaving that office shortly. He no doubt wants to go down in the history books as someone who has made some substantial contributions to his country. Why in the world would he ever want to be remembered as the person who pushed forward the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement with all of its inadequacies and then NAFTA which'repeats the weaknesses of the previous one, I will never know. But then it is difficult to understand the logic of the Prime Minister.
I recall time and time again the government saying that it created all these jobs, but it forgot to say that the jobs that have been created have been south in the United States.
What really amazes me is that whenever government members talk about the creation of jobs they never talk about the other side of the ledger, the kinds of jobs that have disappeared. Has anyone heard that figure? They talk about the jobs they have created. Do they talk about the kinds of jobs that have been created? Are they long-term jobs? Are they well remunerated? Do they have benefits that we expect of Canadian jobs? Of course those questions are never addressed.
It is really unfortunate that we cannot put the cards on the table and look at both sides of the ledger in an objective way. If we did that, the government knows full well there would be a net deficit. There would be a loss of jobs for Canadians over all and a loss of good jobs for Canadians in comparison to those that have in fact been created.
My colleague from Kenora-Rainy River has advanced an amendment which contains two very important points. In a sense, he asks the question: Will collective bargaining be adversely affected by NAFTA? He has concerns about that.
Looking at Mexico's labour standards one knows why he is asking that question. Not only are the wages substantially lower, not only are certain benefits that we enjoy non-existent there, but there are also very few resources for monitoring whether or not those which they have in legislation are in fact happening. This is documented in an article I recommend to all members of Parliament with respect to the economic implications of NAFTA. It talks about child labour laws, minimum wages and maximum hours and it goes on to very significantly document the present weaknesses in Mexico.

A wide gap exists between these labour laws and what we have here in Canada.

The other question my colleague raises is on training and retraining. I know, Mr. Speaker, that you would agree with this particular point. While the government promised in the election campaign that it would have the best training and retraining programs in the world, of course that never did happen. As a consequence of that thousands of Canadians have lost their jobs and have lost hope of finding other jobs. It is a really sad situation out there.
I repeat that what the Liberals want is a level playing field, a definition of subsidies, a definition of dumping. We want to make sure that there are appropriate labour and environmental standards. We want the same energy deal as Mexico got from the United States. We want sovereignty over our natural resources.
May 25, 1993



Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I would ask the government to act responsibly and to look very carefully at an amendment which, in my opinion, is very worth while.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to say a few words in support of the motions presently before us. The content of Motion No. 1 which was moved by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is actually covered in Motions Nos. 30, 31 and 32 moved by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca.
Nevertheless, it is worth reminding ourselves that in dealing with this legislation there is always the concern as to what we are going to lose. Motion No. 1 refers to the rights of trade unionists, freedom of association, freedom of workers to associate, to affirm the rule of free and independent public and private sector unions and the role they play in the conduct of democratic governance.
I recall one occasion when I was a member of the B.C. legislature. The attorney general at that time, a Social Credit member, the Hon. Robert Bonner, said that the people in British Columbia had the highest standard of living of any province in Canada.
He said the reason for that was that we had the strongest trade union movement. It was the action of the trade union movement in improving the standards of the workers in that province that obliged the employers to improve their technology so that they could compete nationally and internationally. The only way they could do that was to be more efficient in their production and they were able to accomplish that and still pay the highest wages in the whole country.
When people talk about the New Democrats imposing this and wanting to keep the level of the people in Mexico down, it is not that at all, but neither do we want to drop our standards. We want to maintain ours as they are and we want the rest to come up to ours rather than ours going down to their level.
Our concern is that without adequate safeguards the NAFTA legislation before us will result in a decrease in the standard of living of Canadians. There is no need for that. We want to protect it. That is why we support
Government Orders
Motion No. 1 as advanced by the member for Kenora- Rainy River as well as a number of amendments moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca.
In part Motion No. 7 reads:
Nothing in this Act or the Agreement shall be interpreted so as to prevent or limit a Party to the Agreement from establishing a tax on any good imported from the territory of another Party to the Agreement to fund any labour adjustment program or environmental program made necessary by reason of the Party's trade with that other Party or as a result of the production of that other Party.
We will recall the government of the day promised when the FTA came into effect that there would be a training program. There would be money provided for a training program so that people who lost their jobs as a result of the free trade deal between Canada and the U.S. would be trained to take up other vocations where there were opportunities for employment.
We will also recall the government decided to cut back on expenditures to save money. It decided that one of the things it could do without was this promised training program, the program that was going to make us train our workers to take up the new job opportunities.
If the government does not have the money to fund it there should be some other way of funding it. What way would be more appropriate than to apply a tax on goods being imported, goods which we could very well have produced in Canada were it not for FTA. Soon there will be NAFTA, the way things are going.
It makes sense if we have to raise the money somewhere to raise it on items like this one. Once we have done that and once we have the money for the training program, we could agree to reduce that tax. We are a sovereign nation. We should have the right to do that if we choose when there is a specific purpose such as the retraining program, something that is going to improve our workers, to educate them to the extent they will be able to take up other job opportunities.
Motion No. 27 is also before us at the present time. It actually deals with clause 242 of the free trade deal as do several other motions here. In this case we are adding something to it, that NAFTA will not come into effect unless the legislative bodies of the NAFTA countries have adopted a charter of fundamental social rights for North America modelled on items 2 through 12 of the

Government Orders
charter of the European community. What has been accomplished there is a good example.
We have had discussions in the Elouse previously wherein members have referred to the European Community and said: "If it is good there it is good here. If they are doing it in Europe, then to compete with what is happening in Europe we should be prepared to adopt the same procedure here in North America and have a North American free trading zone".
If we are to go that route then let us go the same route as the European community did by bringing in a charter of fundamental social rights for North America. The government talked about a level playing field when it was bringing in the free trade deal. Let us bring this level playing field into effect with respect to the charter of social rights for North America and let us agree to adopt Motion No. 27.
Motion No. 30 is the next one in the grouping before us at the present time. Again it is an amendment to clause 242. In this case it is covering all the ground raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River but a good deal more explicitly. We will not go along with the NAFTA implementation act:
Until the Secretariat of the International Labour Organization states, in writing, that it is satisfied that the United Mexican States and every state in the United States of America is complying fully with the following conventions of that Organization:
(i)	Convention number eighty-seven guaranteeing the freedom of association and the protection of the right to organize.
Certainly in this day and age in Canada we can agree that is a fundamental right that should be protected in the legislation we are discussing at the present time. It continues:
(ii)	Convention number one hundred and five abolishing forced labour.
(iii)	Convention number one hundred guaranteeing equal remuneration for men and women workers for work of equal value;
(iv)	Convention number one hundred and eleven abolishing discrimination in employment. [DOT]
agree to that. However I think we should send a signal out to everyone who is aware of this legislation on what we are doing in North America, that we not only believe in these things but we are prepared to put them in writing and to agree to them as part of the agreement among the three states or there will be no NAFTA.
Motions Nos. 31 and 32 deal with material similar to that moved by the member for Kenora-Rainy River. Certainly there is nothing in them that anyone here is opposed to. I just cannot believe anybody would be opposed to any of it.
I would urge the House to approve these amendments to NAFTA. It will not be good legislation but at least it will not be as bad as it is now.

Mr. Speaker, I want to put a few remarks on the record with respect to the NAFTA.
The NAFTA as currently written is the embodiment of neo-conservative trickle down economics. There is a notion behind the agreement, the way it is written now, that if we get government out of the way, lower tariffs, remove the border between Canada and the United States and give much more sovereign power as it were to the large corporations, to the multinationals and transnationals, something miraculous will come out of it. The notion is that something great will happen; that there really ought not to be any role for government if something goes wrong; and that there ought to be no co-ordination among the private sector, government, unions, volunteer agencies and so on. The notion is that is not our business, that we should leave the business of trade to the private corporations that will do their thing and we will benefit.
All one has to do is look at the economic carnage wrought by this government over the past eight to nine years and one will know that trickle down neo-conservative economics just do not work. We should ask the 350,000 manufacturing workers who lost their jobs in the last several years whether trickle down neo-conservative economics work and they will give us a resounding no.
Is there anyone in the House who would oppose any of The NAFTA as written is terribly flawed. It builds that? Is there anyone in the House who would not agree upon an already flawed document called the free trade that this should in effect be the practice of the three agreement, the bilateral agreement between Canada and countries entering into this agreement? I think we all the United States. If we try to build something on a
May 25, 1993

flawed base, regardless of how good that something is it too will be flawed.
It is interesting to note that we are involved in debate on the very crucial issue of whether to enter into a trilateral agreement with Mexico and the United States. The proposed agreement raises hundreds if not thousands of questions, and what does this government do? It moves time allocation. In other words it wants to limit debate. We have to ask ourselves what the government is afraid of. What is the rush? What is going on? On something as important as this issue one would think the government would be providing more time for debate, not less.
We also have to ask those questions in the context of what is happening in the United States. The Bush administration approved the NAFTA with Canada and the United States, but there is a new occupant in the White House.
There is now a Democratic administration in Washington. Democrats in the main have some serious questions about NAFTA and the way it is drawn up. All indications are that NAFTA will not survive the political debate in the United States unless there are some substantive parallel accords applying to labour standards and environmental standards. In other words, the message that we get from the United States is that if the NAFTA is not beefed up, if it is not strengthened through parallel accords on the environment and labour standards it is a no go and NAFTA will not survive Congress in the United States.
That is the message that we get from the United States, yet this government appears to be totally oblivious of what is going on across the line. It is saying to heck with that. It is just proceeding. It has already signed the document and now it wants to shove it through Parliament, ram it through Parliament.
What is the rush? What is this government afraid of? One would think that the government would want to put the brakes on the process here in Canada and wait until developments move forward in the United States but that is not happening.
One of the great boasts of this Conservative government about the FTA before it was passed and after it was implemented was that it gave Canadian manufacturers
Government Orders
access to the United States. The government said if we could just get into that U.S. market then it would be just great. It said that manufacturing would shoot up, there would be all kinds of jobs created, and it would be heaven again.
Ask the people in the steel industry about that. Ask the people in the pork industry. Ask the people in the softwood lumber industry whether there has been free, unfettered access to that great U.S. market. The answer is no. They have another experience to tell us. There have been all kinds of harassment because that so-called access to the United States is not as great as this government would suggest.
One of the reasons for that is that we have a bilateral agreement that involves two countries, one that is much larger than the other. It is 10 times the size. When one is that big it can play around with the agreement. It can bully the smaller partner in the agreement. It can ignore all the legalese of the documents that should be guiding trade and commerce between the two countries. That again was ignored by this Conservative government.
Therefore we have an FTA that was poorly negotiated. It is flawed and now this government is trying to build upon on that flawed document with still another flawed document called the NAFTA. There has to be a renegotiation. There have to be improvements made.
We on this side of the House have stated over and over again some of the things that have to be done, some of the minimal conditions that have to be met. For example, we must have a subsidies code. We must have an anti-dumping code.
Right now each country lives according to its own internal rules. We do not really have a common law when it comes to subsidies or when it comes to dumping and we need that. Our experience since the FTA was implemented tells us that we must have common rules for each country to live by. Those are two things that we want, a subsidies code and an anti-dumping code.
We also want a much more effective dispute resolution mechanism. The way it is now the Americans can come up with almost any kind of trumped up charge against the way the FTA is working and drag various sectors of the economy through all kinds of examination, litigation and so on. Therefore we must find a better way of resolving our disputes.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
Consistent with what is happening in the United States now, we need agreed upon labour standards. If we are going to have the Mexicans involved in a trade pact with us we must have agreed to labour standards. We also must have agreed to standards when it comes to the environment. There are simply too many questions on this side of the border about labour and environmental standards as they are in place right now in Mexico.
We ought to have the same provisions under NAFTA when it comes to energy as do the Mexicans. That is not the case now. They have a stranglehold on their energy supplies in that country and we do not in this country. We have to share our energy supplies with the Americans.
This is a flawed document. It must be renegotiated if we want to be fair to the workers in this country who have a lot of questions about NAFTA.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to stand here and participate in this debate. There are several issues at stake here and it is appropriate that the House take extra time tonight to discuss these issues.
For those who were in the class of 1988 the issue of trade is one that has preoccupied us since the day we were elected. First we had to immediately deal with the free trade agreement. The Official Opposition warned that it was one thing to trade with the United States but another to trade properly. However our interventions, amendments and arguments against the government were all rejected in favour of the free trade agreement. Subsequently we have gone through five years of horrendous economic decline which the city of Winnipeg has felt in an especially difficult fashion.
My constituents want me to participate in this debate to ensure that the government understands that in their opinion the North American free trade agreement is every bit as bad, if not more threatening, as the original agreement.
My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg-St. James, just finished an eloquent speech in which he outlined the reasons we oppose this free trade agreement.
I would like to use this first opportunity to participate in this debate to focus on one or two issues that are of
relevance to the whole country and particularly to Manitoba.
My colleague from Kenora-Rainy River, who I must also take this opportunity to thank for his very wise participation in discussions in Winnipeg on aboriginal training issues, has moved amendments to the legislation.
Most Canadians do not realize that the piece of legislation that we are dealing with is an immense document, the workings of which the opposition has been given no assistance to understand. Nor have we had an opportunity to fully discuss the ramifications of this act with different experts.
Having said that I think it is very appropriate to start by looking at the preamble. What the preamble does ignore, and what the member for Kenora-Rainy River wishes the House to amend and accept, are the labour conditions that exist in Mexico and the difficulties they will create for the Canadian labour market.
It is quite obvious that the burden of the original free trade agreement has been felt by Canadian workers in union and non-union shops. They will be made vulnerable to changes in the labour market.
One of the interesting differences in the trade strategy of the Liberal Party dating back to the 1960s and the trade strategy of this government and the NDP is that the Liberal Party has a long tradition of making the right deal at the right time.
Occasionally we get laughter from the NDP but the people who benefited most from the free trade agreement are those in the Canadian automobile industry. Who has benefited the most from that but a man named Bob White? He is up there marching back and forth saying that he does not like trade agreements. Has he ever asked his workers about the trade agreement? Never. Why? Because they are too busy making money.
It is the recognition of the trade movement itself, and not its leaders, that a reasonable trade strategy is the way to go. Notice all of a sudden that those members are very silent. All of a sudden there is dead silence. They are thinking: Oh, yes, those are our cheques. We had better be quiet for a few minutes.
May 25, 1993

Liberal members recognize that a reasonable trade strategy is the way to go. The international trade agreements we have struck in the past, the ones that we seek to reform, are the appropriate way to go.
The North American free trade agreement fails in the fundamentals, in terms of labour. For that reason we oppose it.
My colleague from Kenora-Rainy River has moved to make the following amendment in the preamble:
"respect the freedom of association and to affirm the role that free and independent, public and private sector unions play in the conduct of democratic governance,
honour the rights of all working people to organize, to bargain collectively and to strike,
encourage an open dialogue between management and labour on all decisions affecting the future of the work force as a result of this agreement,
implement retraining and adjustment programs for workers displaced as a result of the agreement, including support for those wishing to become self-employed-"
The purpose of this amendment, which the Official Opposition fully supports, is to recognize that labour conditions in Mexico and parts of the United States are fundamentally different from the labour relations we have set out to achieve in this country by provincial and historically although not currently by federal legislation. It is also to recognize that the conditions in Mexico have to be dealt with more directly than has been proposed.
I would like to quote a government document. It says: "Labour abuses are widespread in Mexico. The weak enforcement of Mexico's labour laws has been cited as a strong argument against freer U.S. trade with the country. Mexican resources for enforcement are scarce. Work place inspections are infrequent, particularly for border operations, and only in rare cases are sanctions applied by inspectors. Inadequate safety conditions contribute to industrial accidents in smaller firms and at construction sites".
My colleague from northern Ontario knows full well, as do I, the conditions in the mining industry and the lumber industry, for example, and how many years it took through stringent provincial and federal legislation to ensure the protection of workers.
Government Orders
When we enter labour agreements with other countries we have to ensure that the governments of those countries and the companies operating in them have a commitment that is appropriate for ensuring the safety of workers. This is not a natural process but requires a strong-willed government.
I think we are all disturbed by the news in the last couple weeks about what is going on in Mexico. We have to ask whether there is a strong-willed government that can create the best working conditions for its people?
For example, there are child labour laws. The child labour laws are observed in large and medium sized manufacturing and commercial establishments in Mexico but they are not well observed in small shops and factories and they are virtually ignored in the informal sector.
The statutory minimum age for employment is 14 years. Mexican children between 14 years and 16 years of age may work but are subject to special legal protection and shorter working hours.
According to a study by the Cato Institute an estimated 10 million children work at least part time in Mexico supplementing an adult labour force of about 30 million. The huge number of child workers reflects generalized poverty and inadequate enforcement of child labour laws. Therefore we are competing with a labour market in which children are very active. That is totally contrary to everything we strive to achieve in this country.
When we have already undermined the financial and income security of Canadian families through several actions taken by this government and other provincial Conservative governments, can one imagine the insecurity felt when they are competing against children from other countries? People will wonder why they cannot compete the same way. Why can they not bend the rules? They will wonder why family firms cannot have children working in them when after all they are relatives.
We have drawn a line because of experiences in Europe and elsewhere. We have drawn a line that says we are not going to allow child labour. We cannot then enter agreements with other countries which have turned away from these problems and pretend they do not exist.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
When we talk about Third World labour conditions, we must in our deals set out what we expect. This party believes that unless we deal with the issues of child labour laws, minimum wages and maximum hours, these conditions will be exacerbated.
I do not think we are doing the Mexican labourer or skilled tradesperson any favours by offering access to a market under working conditions which are so poor. There will be no incentive among the companies involved with these labour markets to improve the working conditions of these people. Conversely there will be tremendous pressure, some of it actually very legitimate, by Canadian companies saying they cannot compete with $1.23 or $1.25 an hour and they must have an equal playing-field.
The only way an equal playing-field can be achieved is through a tremendous depression in the wage structure in Canada and this party has stood for proper working conditions for all Canadians for generations. When this party was the government, the minimum wage for workers under the jurisdiction of the Government of Canada was the highest in the country. It is now the lowest.
The proof of the commitment of the Liberal Party on trade issues and working conditions for Canadian workers is unparalleled and the Liberal Party is very proud of that.
For these reasons we believe the act has to be amended not only in the substance, which we will return to later in the debate, but in the very preamble. The veiy way in which the act is framed is contrary to the interests of Canadian workers.
I fully support my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River who understands the conditions of working people in this country and has brought forth to the House very fine amendments.

Mr. Speaker, I too wish to take part in the debate and speak to the report stage amendments on Bill C-115, an act to implement the North American free trade agreement.
Before I start I want to comment on what the government is doing here because it is not getting the message out to the people.
In my riding of Kootenay East some Americans came to Cranbrook and interviewed some of the businessmen with regard to the NAFTA agreement and what they thought about it. Most of the businessmen said they were not too concerned about the NAFTA. They were more concerned about the GST and its effects.
The Canadian people have to understand that the goods and services tax is a part of the free trade agreement. The manufacturers could not compete with the Americans and the other industrial nations with a manufacturing tax off, so the government took it off the manufactured goods, put it on the consumers and said: "There you are; now we are on a level playing-field".
The patent drug legislation is another area where the Americans complained so the government brought in patent drug legislation to answer their needs.
The Prime Minister said our health services would not be affected in Canada and that was not part of the deal. Why did it cut back on the equalization payments to the provinces? Why is it quietly saying it is going to be okay that we might have to bring in some user fees? Why is the new leadership saying that user fees could be something of the future? To beat the requirements of the free trade agreements. That is what it is all about. To downsize what we have in Canada so the government can say we can compete. Let us get it clear here what we are talking about.
I want to specifically talk about the environmental aspects of free trade. In my riding the situation is almost an environmental disaster. It was created by the Liberals in 1965 when Prime Minister Pearson was trying to bring about the Columbia River Treaty and some of those arrangements. We have a reservoir there called; Kooca-nusa: Kootenay, Canada, U.S.A. That is why it is named Koocanusa. It says "recreational reservoir". Twenty years later come to the Kootenays and have a look at that reservoir now. It is nothing but a dust bowl.
The Americans are siphoning the water out of there so fast when we are supposed to be storing it for flood control and hydro electricity. They are using it for irrigation, tourism and fish enhancement. They are going to flush it dry this summer and kill all the fish on the Canadian side of the border to meet the needs of the Americans.
May 25, 1993

I want to go a little further with regard to The Equinox which has put out a very good report called Diverting Interests: To Keep the U.S. Southwest Blooming, Visionary Engineers are Proposing to Replumb the Waterways of Canada.
Francis Dale, a Los Angeles lawyer who was Richard Nixon's ambassador to the United Nations who states: "We'll pay you for it. It will not take any water away from you. It is a path through from Alaska so to speak". His thesis is that to survive and flourish as a common market of North America, Canada and the United States must develop more co-operative and profitable uses for our fresh water resources. He confesses that the Americans are guilty of shameful over-consumption and notes that the United States uses three times more water today than it did 30 years ago.
I could go on with regard to another aspect of it. Bill Clancey, president of Multinational Water and Power Inc. of Vancouver is the dapper silver haired person behind the latest proposal to sell Canadian water to southern California. Claney, who describes himself as a business facilitator and public relations consultant, worked for and became a close friend of former B.C. premier W.A.C. Bennett during the Columbia River Treaty.
He talks of the North Thompson diversion which is another hare-brained idea to divert the North Thompson into the Mica reservoir, a salmon-bearing river in British Columbia, and bring it down into the United States to meet its needs.
They also talk about:
diversion, according to Clancey, would cause little or no
environmental harm to the North Thompson River since salmon
runs occur primarily in the fall, reasons Clancey,
They told us they were going to store the water in the Kootenays during the summer when there were high run-offs. Then in the fall they would take it for their hydroelectricity.
These are ramifying things that are happening here. If this government was really concerned about trying to protect our water instead of saying it is only selling bottled water it would put other terms in the treaty.
In the heat of the 1965 federal election campaign with massive river diversion schemes in the air such as the
Government Orders
North American Water and Power Alliance, then Prime Minister Lester Pearson spoke promisingly of arrangements with the United States by which some of our water resources would be moved to the south. Our Liberal member says he applauds what the Liberals were doing in those days. We know what they have done. We see it every day in the Kootenays.
Opponents of water exports say there are a number of legal manoeuvres that can be undertaken to blunt the possible effects of the trade pacts. Wendy Holm would like to see an official memorandum of understanding signed by both Canadian and American trade officials limiting the free trade agreement and NAFTA to only bottled water. If that is what they say it is, draw it up that way. As well, Canadian intentions can be clarified. At present large-scale export of water is against federal government policy but not against the law.
In August 1988 the government introduced Bill C-156 to prohibit large scale water diversion but the bill died on the Order Paper. When the federal election was called it was never reintroduced.
We do not need it.
The hon. member for Calgary says we do not need it. Come to the Kootenays and tell the people in my riding you did not need it.
Nobody trusts you.

They told us 20 years ago when the Columbia River Treaty was being debated that we would not need it because we would store that water during the summer and when it was winter it would be covered with snow and we would not notice the difference. Yes, that lasted for 15 years. But now the Americans are taking that water and leaving the dust and the wind. Salmon are being caught in little pools of water to die in order to feed that desire of the Americans and their water systems.
They want to flood cities such as Bull River and Invermere and transfer our fish-bearing North Thompson River into the Columbia. The hon. member for Calgary says we do not need it. The Canadian people better wake up to what is happening with regard to these agreements because 20 years from now it will be too late. They will come and say they are going to take it. In my

Government Orders
riding the people know. They clearly know when they see that reservoir being drained.

Mr. Speaker, I very seldom commend anybody from the unofficial opposition. There were certain elements that struck home with me but I am not going to dwell on them.
I am speaking to a bill that involves 4,300 pages and there is no way that can be covered in 10 minutes. I intend to speak on this again. I want to draw the memory of a lot of people in the House to what happened during the last campaign. It involved the free trade agreement. The way I approached it with my constituents was to tell them we were dealing with the future. We did not know what free trade was going to do. There were certain things I was concerned about but I did not know for sure. It was like playing a game of poker where $500 could be lost but only $50 could be gained. I do not like playing those kinds of poker games. I have no objection to free trade. Free trade is a good thing across the world and we are looking at globalization. I am not an opponent of free trade but this free trade agreement failed at the 11th hour. We get all the concessions that are now causing this trouble with respect to subsidies, definitions and a better idea of what we are giving away, what we are getting in return and in particular, the protection of jobs and the training for jobs lost that was going to be accomplished in a relatively short time, certainly in the length of this Parliament and the level playing-field that was discussed in general terms.
As I stand here today, I find it very ironic and paradoxical that when we came into this House, those of us who were elected in 1988 and some are in this House tonight, the very first debate we had at the opening of that Parliament was a free trade agreement that was not definite. There were things in there that even the government confessed it did not know how they were going to work out. But it felt by and large it was going to be good for Canada. A percentage of the Canadian people took the government at its word.
Now it is veiy ironic that as we are about to close this session of the 34th Parliament we are now about to go into another agreement that is larger and has more uncertainties that compound the uncertainties we had
before. But we are better off in one respect because we know some of the promises made in 1988 were not being kept and we know where we are now. I want to mention some specifics that I have been tracking very closely.
To begin with, the difficulty was how many jobs were going to be lost and gained. They ranged from 450,000 gained to 100,000 lost. Nowhere in the wildest imagination could anybody realize that the jobs lost would be somewhere in the vicinity of 300,000 manufacturing jobs alone in four years. I have not addressed the service industries and I have not talked about other aspects of Canadian industry. Consider a labour population that is in the vicinity of 13 million. When we talk about one sector losing 300,000 jobs, that is a large percentage of the entire labour force. It is not lost temporarily but lost never to be regained. We know it is not plus or minus anything. We know that in one sector alone it is over 300,000 jobs.
I want to talk about level playing fields. I agree with some of my colleagues who have said that the goods and services tax was related to the free trade agreement. The manufacturers' sales tax cost 9 cents to the dollar. For every dollar collected the government could use 91 cents for whatever purpose. However, it had to be traded in for the goods and services tax that affected not only the 30,000 businesses that the manufacturers' sales tax affected, but the 1.3 million small businesses in Canada. It cost them anywhere from $7,000 to $9,000 to implement and cost the Canadian taxpayer 56 cents out of every dollar to collect.
It is 10 times more inefficient than the manufacturers' sales tax, to say nothing of the fact that it has gone on 1.3 million small businesses. Every individual in Canada is being haunted by this goods and services tax. That was not envisaged as part of the free trade agreement.
Consider social programs. One of my concerns was that it would affect unemployment insurance. In the province of Newfoundland and in my riding, which the last time I checked had the second highest unemployment rate of the 64 regions in Canada, it was a major concern. My constituents were told by the minister representing Newfoundland and the Prime Minister that they had no worries about social programs. They were a

Government Orders
sacred trust and, in particular, unemployment insurance programs would not be touched.
Today the government contributes zero to the unemployment insurance program. Bill C-21 changed it completely, took away the job development programs and rearranged the whole business of how unemployment insurance takes place. It has upped the ante by almost 50 per cent to those paying and those employing. If that is not a change then I do not know what is.
Nothing was going to happen to our medicare. That was only four and a half years ago. The major candidates who are now trying to be Prime Minister of this country and leader of the Conservative Party have been talking about a medicare that is not being financed by the government. Is that not the beginning of the end of what we considered to be one of the major pillars of Canadian society? It is what makes us so different from other countries in the world. It was a program that was introduced by Liberals. In four and a half years we have gone from: "It is not going to be a problem," to "It is already a problem". In Newfoundland alone we have lost $750 million in the last few years from transfer payments and EPF. A lot of that money lost has gone to reducing hospital services. If that is not the beginning of the end in a relatively short time, I do not know what is.
These are promises that were made four and a half years ago: "Nothing is going to happen". Well, it has happened and what are we gaining? We were supposed to gain free access to the American market. We have not gained free access to the American market. We have been hit time after time and the hit list has included Canadian exports in softwood lumber, steel, wheat, magnesium, pork and the list goes on.
I am standing here tonight and the government wants me and my colleagues on this side of the House, and I think some disbelievers over there, to accept that the North American free trade agreement as an adjunct, add-on, an extension to the free trade agreement is going to be good for Canada. I do not accept that and my colleagues do not accept it. I do not think anybody in their right mind would accept it for the very reason that the promises made for the free trade agreement with the United States were not kept.
There were jobs lost. There was no compensation program. There were no job training programs put in place to compensate for it. Unemployment insurance has been changed. We still have no definition of subsidies. We are looking at the beginning of the end of medicare as professed by the leadership candidates for the Conservative Party. We have lost somewhere in the vicinity of a half million jobs. Now we are being asked to sign on the dotted line to involve another country where the labour costs are less than a tenth of what they are in Canada. We are looking at a minimum wage that is out of sight. I believe it should be out of mind.
On top of all that we are looking at labour standards and environmental standards that have not been discussed. I find it incredible that we were being drawn by the Americans before and the relationship between the Prime Minister and the President of the United States certainly was great grease for the skids to get this going.
Now we are all alone in this. The Americans are saying that they are not sure they want to pass this so we are rushing to get this completed before Parliament ends. We are going to be sitting all alone with this agreement if we allow the government to go ahead and sign this. There will be nobody else to sign it. The Americans will not have it signed. Parliament will be dissolved. We will be into an election. Where will we stand then?
This is the most ludicrous thing that has happened certainly in my relatively short time here in Parliament and I am sure in the lifetime of many who have been here for 25 years. I have spoken to them. They cannot believe that this scene is taking place tonight.
I hope they have the opportunity to speak in more detail on more specific subjects concerning this atrocious deal in the next day or so.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to speak to Bill C-115 at report stage.
It seems to me that it was only a few years ago that I stood in this same House shortly after my election in 1988 to speak against the free trade agreement. Here we are after countless other disastrous pieces of legislation have been passed by this Conservative government speaking to another trade deal.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
This is report stage and one of my colleagues, the member for Kenora-Rainy River, moved an amendment which speaks to protecting the people of Canada. It is in fact quite a j ust amendment and I think we should all, including members on the Conservative side of this House, support this amendment.
The people of Canada are frightened, desperate and confused. They listened to the Conservative government telling them time and time again how they were going to be well-served by the policies of this government.
The free trade agreement came in. There were massive losses of jobs. Many of those jobs were lost because of the original free trade agreement that was signed and voted on in this House in December 1988.
The Conservatives opposite say that perhaps not all jobs were lost as a direct result of the free trade agreement. I would say perhaps not. A lot of it might also have to do with this government's very high interest rate and tight monetary policy and a whole host of other terrible Conservative policies which have devastated the economy in Canada.
Now it is rushing through this other disastrous piece of legislation while the Americans and our own negotiators look at parallel agreements. We do not even know what is going to be in them but we are going to agree to a trade deal.
Has anyone ever told this Tory government that one does not agree to things until one knows what is in them? I remember when I was a young girl and somebody said: "Do not worry. Trust me". My mother always said that the first time somebody tells you that then one should worry and not trust. That is exactly what this Conservative government is saying to us and to the people of Canada: "Do not worry. Trust us". By golly, nobody can trust this government. It has had it. Not only that, it is at the end of its mandate. Why this huge rush to approve a trade agreement when we are not quite sure what is going to be attached to it?
I suggest that we not rush into it, but it has never listened to anything that we have ever said. After all, it seems to believe that it knows it all at the expense of the Canadian people. If the government so sure that it is doing the right thing then it should bring in this amendment. It should consider the well-being of the people of Canada who have elected us to serve them. I believe this Conservative government has time and time again forgotten that it is serving them.
Right now we hear that there is a recovery on the way. I ask this Conservative government to go to the people and tell those who are out of work and underemployed where that recovery is because whatever recovery there is, it is a jobless one.
Our first duty is to the people of Canada to ensure that they can afford a livelihood, raise their families and have a decent way of earning a living. This is not happening. This has not happened since I have been in office. As long as those members have been sitting opposite us I can truly say that this economy has really gone from bad to worse especially when it concerns the workers of Canada.
I wonder about this Conservative government that is so prepared to rush this NAFTA bill through. For one thing why is no one standing up and speaking to this amendment?
Knowing what has happened in the past I can say that it of course will not approve these amendments. There are a host of other amendments which also speak to the social well-being of the people of Canada. Why is it that none of the Conservative members stand up to speak to this motion one way or the other? Either tell us why the government will vote against this motion or tell us if it will support this motion. I think that the people of Canada, the people who elected them, want to know why they are so determined to have a vote on this bill this week.
They want to know that. They want to know before the vote actually occurs. Remember, as I said just earlier in my few brief remarks, the people are desperate and frightened. They want some kind of word on what is going to happen to them. What will happen to them if we end up agreeing to a NAFTA that has side deals? We are not even sure what is in them.
I beg this Conservative government to at least support these very well thought out amendments. It is an absolutely worth-while endeavour to support these amendments. It would not hurt it to show a little compassion perhaps, once in a while, although I know it is difficult.
May 25, 1993

Mr. Speaker, it is intriguing to me to hear a member from the Liberal Party first of all point out that there is nobody in the House from the Conservative side and when she leaves, as she is doing, there will be no Liberals left. Beyond that we are going to get into this all night.
What is more important is where will the Liberals be when the vote comes? This bill is now before us at report stage. It has already received first and second reading, second reading being approval in principal. At second reading the vote on the bill was 113 for and 94 against; 113 being Conservatives and 94 being Liberals, New Democrats, Bloc and Independents.
What was intriguing was that while 42 out of 44 New Democrats were here, one being absent because of a death in the family and the other being in Europe at the time on parliamentary business, there were 38 Liberals missing. The vote at second reading was carried by the government by 19 votes.
The opportunity of defeating the government and defeating this legislation was the best that there had been in this Parliament. The government only won by 19 votes yet 38 Liberals ducked that vote; 38 Liberals were not here to stand up for Canada and for their country.
The member for Vancouver Quadra who was the Liberal leader in the last election said that free trade was the fight of his life. He was not here to vote, joined by 37 other Liberals who ducked the vote.

You cannot talk about who is not here. You know that.
Government Orders

We are allowed to talk about who is not here for a vote. The member opposite suggests we are not allowed to say who is not here. We are not allowed to suggest who is not here sitting listening to this fascinating debate and the speech that I am making.
We are entitled and will over and over again point out to the people of Canada that if they want to defeat the North American free trade agreement and its legislation they have only one choice in the next election and that is the New Democratic Party. If they want to keep it in they are going to have to vote for the Conservatives because the Liberals have no position that could be relied upon by the people of Canada. Those who sent them here to defeat the free trade agreement would have to be disappointed on the vote at second reading because that was an opportunity to defeat this legislation and to defeat this government.
When this bill passes, as it will, because the government has the majority in this House, it still remains for the United States Congress to enact legislation implementing the North American free trade agreement. All the information that is coming out of Washington is that is a very problematic proposition.
If it is approved in the United States, as it will be regretfully by this Parliament, and it is approved by the government of Mexico, the free trade agreement will come into force on January 1, 1994.
However, the agreement will have in it a provision that it can be cancelled by the government of any one of the three countries on six months' notice. We say to the people of Canada that if we have the opportunity prior to January 1, 1994 we will cancel the North American free trade agreement.
I say to the people of Canada that it is critically important that they understand what is at issue in this bill. First of all this bill reinforces the free trade agreement and free trade regime which was put into place on January 1, 1989. Now Canadians have had experience with that bill, that legislation and that regime.
The NAFTA takes the free trade agreement and makes it worse. It adds Mexico, a country that not only has a fascinating history, with many citizens and residents we applaud, but has a government that has stamped on the human rights and civil rights of its

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
people. It has one of the worst records on the continent in terms of human rights. It has no effective legislation in place in respect of the environment. It has wages one-quarter to one-tenth of what they are in Canada. It has no social legislation which compares one iota to the social legislation we have in this country.
The first problem with the North American free trade agreement is that it pairs us up with a country whose standards in economic and social policies do not compare to ours. It offers, to corporate investors an opportunity to take the resources from this country and move them, not only to the United States as the free trade agreement does, but all the way to Mexico. With it will come that gigantic sucking sound of jobs going south that Ross Perot referred to in the last election in the United States. That is the first problem.
The second problem with the North American free trade agreement is that it turns over to a dispute mechanism the sovereignty of our Parliament and our legislatures. It gives to a trade dispute mechanism the authority to override legislation adopted by this Parliament or by the legislatures in territories of our country if those laws conflict, in the opinion of this disputes mechanism, with the terms of the North American free trade agreement.
Our government has negotiated a deal that takes away the sovereignty of this Parliament, turns it over to a body which will be appointed by the three governments which will meet in secret and whose mandate is to ensure that the economic interests of private corporations in North America override the interests of the democratically elected institutions in our country.
It may seem like a ludicrous proposition that which I have just stated because why would any government do that? Even more, why would a majority in Parliament, members of Parliament who are democratically elected and accountable, go along with it?
The answer goes back to a speech of Ronald Reagan prior to the 1980 election in the United States when he set out the neo-conservative agenda for North America. That agenda said that we have to begin to break down the barriers and open up the resources of North America to corporate America.
The barriers he referred to were barriers that were erected originally ironically by a Conservative government, the government of Sir John A. Macdonald. Those barriers were erected to develop what he called the national policy. Those barriers were erected to protect our society in what was then called British North America, to permit us to develop north of the United States a society which was different from the United States. He recognized, and the people of his time recognized, that it was essential if we were to have a sovereign country, we had to have our own economy. This government and the Conservative members who support it have sold this country down the river, not once with the free trade agreement but now a second time with the North American free trade agreement.
We will vote against this bill. We will fight this bill every step of the way, tonight, tomorrow, the rest of this week and into the election campaign. We will ultimately, with the people of Canada, win the fight to keep this country sovereign.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to join the debate this evening on the first part of the amendments dealing with the North American free trade agreement. My remarks will be general because the amendments specifically deal with the environment and social policy.
We heard much from the Conservative benches during the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement debate and now in dealing with NAFTA about the changing nature of our world, globalization, the need for international trade, et cetera. I have no dispute with much of what they say as indeed we have seen a tremendous globalization, particularly starting in the 1960s, picking up speed in the 1970s and then well into the 1980s.
We see both positive and negative results. We see the positive side where there has been tremendous economic development in parts of the world particularly in parts of Asia where tremendous growth is occurring. There is no doubt about that. The People's Republic of China, Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, India and I believe very soon
May 25, 1993

Vietnam, will experience a tremendous increase in their rate of growth.
Yet one also has to stand back and wonder what benefit this growth has been to the ordinary people in many of those countries. I had the occasion to visit some of those countries. I saw the huge skyscrapers going up, apartment buildings that in terms of the rents are comparable to those in downtown Vancouver, Toronto or New York. There are the very expensive clothes and the Mercedes. But in the shadows of it all is the beggar. There are people who are still working for the equivalent of $1 to $1.50 a day. Much of their so-called prosperity is on the backs of the poor.
When it occurs and when the workers are able to demand a little bit more as they now are in Korea and Taiwan, those industries are being moved to mainland China, to Thailand, to Vietnam or to North Korea. There is this continuous shift searching for very cheap labour, as though that is the important component.
Of course with globalization, we have now opened our borders to these countries and now our Canadian workers have to compete against them. We see Canadian companies, the large retail organizations, setting up their own manufacturing units. The hammers, other tools, clothing or whatever are all manufactured especially for them under contract to what essentially are sweat-shops so that they can provide Canadian consumers with supposedly cheap goods. I imagine the mark-up between the factory gates in the Third World and the time the item reaches the consumer here is quite substantial.
We are asked to continue this with this agreement, to have our own North American version of an Asian backwater so to speak, our own source of cheap labour. That is what this is all about: the ability of our ownership class to have access to cheap labour.
The government has the gall to suggest that this is good for Canada, that this is good for the men and women who work, make and produce the things we need in this country, who pay their taxes and keep this country going. This government claims that this frontal assault to the average Canadian is a good thing. [DOT]
We have seen the results of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. We have seen hundreds of thousands
Government Orders
of jobs leave Canada. Of course it was the combination of the free trade agreement and the high Canadian dollar that priced our goods out of the market and allowed this huge exodus of capital and manufacturing jobs out of Canada.
What I do not understand about the Tories is that there is a simple thing they have never figured out. It is that people need to earn incomes in order to buy the goods and services the businesses are offering. If Canadian men and women cannot earn the dollars in good jobs, then they cannot buy. It is no wonder we have this recession. It is no wonder we have lost the confidence of the consumers. It is no wonder we have the deficit. It is because more Canadians are out of work and are not able to pay taxes. Instead they are drawing UI and welfare.
That is a recipe for disaster. Why is this government acting against the self-interests of Canada, of this nation? It has a job to protect and govern this country. Why in Heaven's name is it so adamantly on this course that is going to do further harm and cripple our country?
The government is of course driven by ideology. I would suggest in some ways the neo-conservatives over there are the purest ideologues left in this country. They are driven by ideology. They are not driven because something is good for the country or because it makes common sense. They are driven because they feel this is the right thing to do.
Therefore, we are down this neo-conservative path that the Americans have finally rejected. I suspect that the Americans will not pass this agreement because they have come off the neo-conservative binge and have assessed the damage it has done to their country. They have seen the type of economic malaise that exists in the United States in the numbers of unemployed and the deficit they have. They have come off that. It is a question of time a matter of months before finally we in Canada can get off this same ride the neo-conservatives have put us on.
What a ride it has been. We have the highest per capita debt in the world. We have the highest level of unemployment of the industrialized countries. They have crippled this country. Of course in one sense we can understand it. These people believe in little or no government. They will leave behind a government and a

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
country so in ruin and laden with such a weight of debt that the government will not be able to do anything.
These people have succeeded in down-scaling government and one would almost think they did it deliberately. In fact, there are some who suggest that David Stockman who was the budget bureau director under Ronald Reagan is now openly admitting that they ran up the deficit in order to justify cutbacks to social services down the road. It was part of the neo-conservative agenda to destroy government. That is what these people have done. What a record.
Of course when we deal with NAFTA that is part of the scenario. It is part of the grand design. They burden us with huge amounts of debt. They deregulated so that now we do not have any viable transportation system left in this country. They have done it with communications. They have done it across the board. They have weakened our cultural institutions. They have tied our hands with the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. Now I suppose the height of their accomplishment is NAFTA where Canadian workers are going to have to compete with the Mexican workers who earn $1, $1.50 or $2 an hour.
What an accomplishment in eight or nine years of various governments, including past Progressive Conservative governments as well as Liberal governments often crowded by the CCF and the New Democratic Party. We have built institutions in this country to help protect and enrich the lives of Canadians and to make this one of the most decent, civilized countries in the world. In nine short years these folks driven by neo-conservative ideology have brought us to our knees. They have crippled Canada. I am afraid it will take a long time to heal from the abuses inflicted on us.
I am not against international trade. There are some good models we could follow. The Conservatives during the 1988 election said that we should look at Europe. I agreed. The Europeans got together and formed a social agreement. It was not just an agreement on trade but an agreement on social policies, labour standards and the environment to ensure that the whole matter was not dragged down to the lowest common denominator of
Greece, Spain and Portugal. There are plans afoot to raise those countries to higher levels, but in this agreement there is no such guarantee. We will be forced down to the lowest common denominator.
For that reason my party and I are opposed. We will do everything possible to protect Canada, our way of life and our standard of living.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too would like to participate in the debate tonight.
As I listened to the hon. member for Regina-Qu'Ap-pelle I was struck by the passion with which he spoke. I actually contrasted it with my own mood tonight. It is one of despair to some degree. As once again we are debating something that has been compared to a constitutional debate changing the economic constitution of North America under the threat and indeed the reality of closure.
When the government moved closure on second reading of this legislation I asked the Chair at that time to intervene on behalf of Parliament, to protect Parliament from becoming a rubber stamp and to protect Parliament from the tyranny of a majority that simply regards any prolonged debate on something of this importance as a nuisance. There was a time when closure came after the opposition had dragged the debate on for a while. Now the government House leader if we are not prepared to agree to limit the debate before the debate starts feels justified in moving time allocation. If we do not agree before the debate starts we get a motion of time allocation.
That is not the purpose of closure or time allocation. If at a certain point the government feels the debate has gone on long enough it does not take it long to move time allocation. It can take the political risk of cutting the debate off. The opposition can take the political risk of dragging the debate on. We do not even get to do that. We do not get to let the Canadian people make some kind of judgment about whether or not the debate has gone on for too long. Right off the bat we have time allocation, and all of this at the same time as we are allegedly down in the United States negotiating parallel or side agreements to the very agreement we are seeing rammed through the House at this particular time.
May 25, 1993

It is embarrassing to think the Canadian negotiating stance is that we are negotiating but in the meantime we are going to pass the bill and the implementing legislation as is. It is only embarrassing if one looks at it with any kind of national self-respect. I guess it is not embarrassing if one looks at it through the eyes of the Conservatives because the fact is that they like this agreement just the way it is. They really do not want to improve it. It is so transparent. They like it the way it is because the idea of putting in tougher environmental standards or tougher labour standards goes against their particular view of the world.
That is where the hon. member for Regina-Qu'Ap-pelle was right on when he said this was an ideological fixation on the part of the government. It is fond of thinking that somehow the New Democrats are the ideological ones, but this is the most ideological government we have had in Canadian history. It has rewritten the ideological fabric of Canadian society.
What the government is doing in these agreements is trying to enshrine its ideology beyond its own political existence as a government so that regardless of what happens to it its particular view of the world will be enshrined in these agreements for a long time to come, particularly if we get a Liberal government after the next election because the Conservatives will have done all the dirty work for the right wing of the Liberal Party.
These agreements will not be changed and, as I have said before, they will outlast the Conservatives. They will go far beyond the reach of their political life as a government.
The Minister of Finance said it well this morning when he was answering questions in the House respecting the North American free trade agreement. He said: "Why are not people out there exploiting these opportunities that the North American free trade agreement creates?" Creates for whom?
I want to say two things. I think the word exploit tells us a lot. These agreements are really all about exploiting the people of Mexico, the people of Canada and, for that matter, the people of the United States. It is about exploiting the working people of those three countries by pitting them against each other in a new form of so-called competition. The opportunities are not for Canadian workers. The only opportunities they have are to be faced with ultimatums from their employers to take
Government Orders
a $3 an hour cut in wages or lose their jobs as is the case with a number of firms in my riding and in Winnipeg generally. Those are the only opportunities that exist for Canadian workers.
The opportunities are there for Canadian exporters of a certain kind: people who are willing either to export or to relocate in Mexico and take advantage of those low wages. Those are the opportunities, but what are the opportunities for? They are opportunities for exploitation. We should just reverse exploiting opportunities and talk about opportunities for exploitation because that is what it is.
All the statistics about how Canada is benefiting from the free trade agreement only have to do with exports. They do not say anything about jobs. They do not say anything about social well-being. They do not say anything about the environment. All they talk about is certain kinds of export statistics.
Theoretically we could have a handful of companies in Canada employing only a handful of people who are very successful at exporting all kinds of things to other countries. This would make our economic statistics look great except for the fact that a whole lot of people who used to have jobs do not have them any more. I suggest to the minister that to the extent he believes these statistics, and I am not sure he does, he is suffering from what the famous philosopher Alfred North Whitehead once called the fallacy of misplaced concreteness. That is investing certain abstractions with a reality that hides what is really going on. To have the Minister of Finance, the minister of trade, or whoever does it from day to day here get up to talk about these wonderful export statistics is a good example of the fallacy of misplaced concreteness.
The concrete reality is that Canadians everywhere have either lost their jobs, are losing their jobs, are being asked to accept a lower wage, a wage rollback, or in a variety of other ways are being asked to forfeit the standard of living and degree of social justice we have achieved in the last 40 years to 45 years in the name of competition.
I had my nomination meeting a week or so ago within about 48 hours of the tragedy in Thailand where a factory was burned and somewhere in the neighbourhood of 250 women died. It struck me that there was a competitive

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
factor, a factory that was a good investment according to all the rhetoric we hear on the other side. It probably was very productive. It probably had very high productivity, low overhead, cheap wages and no union. The list goes on of the ways the factory in which those 250 women died met all the standards of competition, efficiency and productivity. This was a place for people to invest, invest in death.
That is what we are being asked to applaud time and again in this House, the fact that we are turning the world into a place where decisions to invest in places like that factory in Thailand are called good when they should be called bad.
I rise on a point of order. I am just clarifying, Madam Speaker, that I will be speaking on the next motion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes. The hon. member has spoken on this group so I will have to recognize somebody who has not spoken on it. Otherwise we will have to put the question on the first motion.

Madam Speaker, about 10 years ago the Prime Minister was first elected to the House of Commons. As a matter of fact I think it was in his very first speech in the House that he said: "Give us 20 years and you will not recognize this country".
The Prime Minister has had less than 10 years and already if we look at the economic situation in Canada we are fast becoming a Third World economic basket case. It is quite a legacy to have left us; it is quite a legacy to have left the Canadian people. Although the Prime Minister may soon be gone that legacy will indeed live on through the enshrinement of the policies and the ideological commitment of this government in both the free trade agreement and the proposed North American free trade agreement.
These agreements are a way of enshrining the government's corporate agenda. None of us on this side of the House has any difficulty with the idea of reducing trade barriers, reducing tariff barriers, increasing opportunities for Canadian workers or increasing opportunity for Canadian business.
These free trade agreements really do not have a lot to do with that. What they do have to do with is opening up
