Mr. Speaker, I am very happy my socialist friends over there on the left are awake so they can hear some sense instead of the nonsense we have heard for 10 minutes. Instead of talking about the substance of this bill all we heard was phone numbers. Let us get some substance into this debate instead of some nonsense.
May 25, 1993

I was speaking with my wife at about 11.45 this evening and she asked me what I was doing in my office at that late hour. I pointed out that the House was still sitting, and she asked me why. I said very simply that we had to debate throughout the night because the government was going to close debate on the North American free trade agreement.
She asked me why, what was the hurry? I had no answer for her because there was no answer to that question. There is no hurry. There is no reason we should be here at 1.45 a.m. talking about this agreement. There is ample time for us to talk about it between now and the time it should be implemented on January 1, 1994.
I ask Canadians who are listening and who read Hansard to consider whether this is a reasonable use of the time of the House, of members of Parliament, of House management and of the pages. Is this something we need to do? Do we need to go through the night talking about issues that need a tremendous amount of study and consideration?
Why would I say that? I am not the first person to have lifted up this volume. It is the North American free trade agreement. However I am sure that constituents in Scarborough West and people across Canada would be very interested to know, if they were looking for something in the North American free trade agreement, that it has no index. It has a table of contents but it does not even have an index. We are expected to go through a document of this nature when looking for things we want to find.
For example, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca moved three motions concerning sovereignty. If one wants to look in the North American free trade agreement to see where sovereignty is dealt with, good luck. There is no index.
If we look in the table of contents there are a few generic terms. Are we going to spend the next day and a half going through this huge agreement page by page? That is what we will have to do. Otherwise we will not be able to find out what is in the agreement. Interestingly enough that is not what we are talking about, although in reality we are. What we are talking about is Bill C-115, another hefty document. It has approximately 193
Government Orders
pages, all of which is the legislation to implement this giant agreement.
We have to go through this particular piece of legislation to implement the NAFTA now because once this debate is over this evening we will be voting on all the amendments we are talking about. Then we will be into third reading and it will be over because the government has imposed closure. There will be no more debate. One of the most important pieces of legislation we have had to face in the last four and a half years will have passed through the House of Commons with virtually no debate.
Is there any precedent for it? It is typical of the Tories. They did exactly the same with Bill C-91, the drug patent legislation. They rammed that bill through with about 17 hours of debate. When we add up all the time spent debating, even with us sitting all night, it is going to amount to a negligible amount of time in comparison to the dramatic effect this agreement will have for Canadians and for Canada.
What kind of a deal are we talking about? What kind of sovereignty are we talking about in these motions? I went back to release No. 165 of the Government of Canada on August 12, 1992. I want to read two short excerpts from it to remind Canadians what the government thinks this deal does:
Canada's primary objectives at the NAFTA negotiations were to secure better access to the Mexican market, safeguard and improve the gains made in the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement and maintain Canada as an attractive investment location in North America.
"The NAFTA talks have been a success for Canada", Mr. Wilson said. "We have improved parts of the FTA without giving up any of the gains we already achieved under that agreement. This NAFTA deal is FTA plus."
This is the recommendation on which we are supposed to pass the agreement, that the NAFTA deal is the free trade agreement plus. He has the nerve to say it improves the free trade agreement.
We passed the free trade agreement in 1988, 24 hours to 36 hours before Christmas. That was four and a half years ago. We still do not have a definition of subsidy. We still do not know how anti-dumping is going to be treated. Those are two very fundamental aspects of the free trade agreement. Yet at that time the Minister for International Trade said that they had improved the gains they had made in the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
I say nonsense. That is not true. That is simply not accurate because there is still no definition of subsidy.
There is still no question about what is going on with dumping. What about the clause that provides that we have to guarantee supplies? Suppose there is a national emergency in Canada and we decide we need all our natural resources for a particular time. We cannot do that under the North American free trade agreement. We have to commit a certain amount of that to our trading partners, notwithstanding what is in the best interest of our country at a particular time.
Does that make sense? Not to me. Does it make sense that we would be debating it at a quarter to two in the morning? Not to me. Does it make sense that we are ramming it through with two and a half days debate? Not to me. I dare say that it does not make much sense to most people.
What could the rationale be to do this? The deal is not going to come into force until January 1,1994, so there is no hurry there. We have lots of time. So far as I know no comparable legislation has been tabled in the United States, so there is no hurry there. We are apparently way ahead of the Americans on this yet we are still being forced to deal with it quickly.
There is one other interesting factor that is going to intervene, something that has happened in the United States. In the United States there was a general election and the people of the United States were given the opportunity to vote for their representatives before the North American free trade agreement was put to those representatives by their President. In fact it still has not been put.
We have not had that opportunity yet we know that before the implementation date of the North American free trade agreement we must and will have a federal election. Let us have the federal election. We know it is coming. It is inevitable.
This issue can be one of the issues of the election and then we will still have enough time, depending on the results of the federal election, to pass the implementing legislation and get the deal in place by January 1, 1994, if that is what the people of Canada want as expressed by their votes in a general election. Is it because the government is afraid to do so that it is imposing this undemocratic closure of debate before debate has even begun?
I have to leave that question to those people who are listening and those who are reading Hansard, but I think with great respect that the answer is clear and self-evident. There is no confidence in this government and it is trying to ram things through in an undemocratic fashion because it knows that if and when it goes to the people with these issues it will not be able to convince them that its vision is correct.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for the second time in the last eight hours or so to have the opportunity to speak on the second group of amendments on behalf of northern Ontario and members of the Liberal Party from northern Ontario.
In the 10 minutes that I have I would like to speak specifically about the resource-based industries of northern Ontario and the effects of both the past free trade agreement and the one we are talking about now, which is the NAFTA.
We really have to put this in context. One of the things I would like to do is talk to people who are still up this morning listening to this debate about the small amount of trade that Canada does with Mexico and the reason that we as a party felt very strongly that it was to our benefit as a Canadian government and a Canadian people to be present at the table to negotiate the agreement that we have before us, the NAFTA.
One of the things we have to know is that Canadian exports to Mexico in 1991 totalled a measly $440 million and imports from Mexico totalled $2,574 billion. As it stands now 80 per cent of trade between Canada and Mexico is duty free. The remaining 20 per cent has an average tariff of only 2.4 per cent. This is the average duty rate of imports from Mexico because Mexico qualifies as a less developed country and enjoys a general preferential tariff.
Based on that scenario that I have laid out the members opposite and Canadians at home would be wondering why the Liberal Party and Canadians in general would be opposed to the NAFTA agreement if the amount of trade we do with Mexico is so small that it seems to be of no consequence to our over-all trading situation, to our imports and exports as a trading nation. Our concern is that the past free trade agreement is being superseded by the NAFTA and in the past agreement there were some major concerns with the agreement that we as a party needed to have addressed in order for us to be able to support NAFTA in its entirety.
May 25, 1993

Let me give some examples of the five areas that we have earmarked for concern which Canadians should look at before they can even consider agreeing to support this legislation. The first area is that of a subsidy and anti-dumping code. We have asked for secure access to the American market. That was the Mulroney government's key objective in the free trade agreement, one that it failed to achieve. There is still no subsidy and anti-dumping code in NAFTA, making Canadian industries sitting ducks for future U.S. actions like the ones slapped on softwood lumber, steel and magnesium.
The action taken by the U.S. has cost northern Ontario hundreds and hundreds of jobs in the softwood lumber industry alone in the last few years since the 15 per cent export tax was placed on softwood lumber.
The government agreed to the memorandum of understanding but then it decided after a number of years because of the fact that it could see jobs being lost in resource based industries as fast as it could count that it would make some significant changes. It decided it would tell the government of the United States that it no longer believed that the memorandum of understanding applied and therefore it was not going to continue with that particular agreement.
We are still to this day dealing with U.S. duties on Canadian softwood lumber. We have said that we are not engaged in unfair trade practices but the Americans continue to suggest that we are.
I use softwood lumber as a perfect example. If there was a definition of subsidies, a definition of anti-dumping codes, that particular loss to a very productive industry in northern Ontario, a very productive industry in Canada as a whole, would not have happened. Almost one million jobs depend on softwood lumber and the forestry industry in Canada.
As I spoke on the first cluster and as my amendment suggested earlier this evening and now this morning, we had also asked for adjustment programs. In 1988 the present Prime Minister promised massive adjustment programs to help Canadian companies and workers adjust to the FTA. Where are they?
We have lost 400,000 jobs since the FTA came into force in 1988-89, 400,000 jobs lost in this country. Members opposite will suggest that those losses can all
Government Orders
be attributed to a very deep recession and therefore none are the fault of the free trade agreement.
On the other hand, on numerous occasions the Minister of Finance, the Minister for International Trade and the Prime Minister have said in this place and outside this place that the cabinet restructured the economy with the free trade agreement and is presently preparing to restructure the economy even further with NAFTA.
Let us be quite frank in this place at 1.55 in the morning. We cannot have it both ways. If we are in the process of fundamentally restructuring our economy then we are obviously going to have some job losses because of it. If we are going to have some job losses because of it we should be prepared as a country, as a government, and as members of Parliament to understand that we need these adjustment programs in place to help those who are going to be displaced because of the new global economy we are entering into. To this day we are still waiting for adjustment programs by the present government.
We have also asked for environmental protection. As we will see with further amendments down the line at report stage this is another issue that is being looked at and asked for in order that we, who have one of the best environmental records of any country in the world, can make sure that environmental situation we now see ourselves in will still be the envy of the world after NAFTA is approved and after we continue on with the present free trade agreement.
We well know what is happening with the negotiators and the present government. They do not want any side deals on the environment. They do not want any protection, any kinds of regulations with teeth in order to make sure that other countries will adhere to the kind of environmental regulations that we as Canadians expect and have always worked very hard to try to put forward on behalf of future generations in this country.
We are also looking at a dispute settlement. For our party the dispute settlement mechanism is the ability to look at the problems that will occur in a regular negotiated collective bargaining process between two sovereign nations that have very different legislation and rules.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
We need a dispute settlement mechanism that is effective, not one which takes months and years such as the one we have had to deal with at the present time, one that was supposed to be implemented as an interim measure until the government was able to negotiate a dispute settlement mechanism that was effective and very quick for all concerned.
I think these amendments that are before us have some merit. These amendments make all of us as Canadian parliamentarians think about some of the flaws that are in the NAFTA. I would urge the members who are still awake this late in the evening to consider looking at them very seriously before they make the same mistake they made with the FTA and before they put the same flaws in the NAFTA that are in the FTA.

Mr. Speaker, this is an historic debate in the House of Commons on the North American free trade agreement. This debate is about an attempt to display the kind of arrogance this government has demonstrated to Canadians through the invoking of closure, cutting off debate on this very important document.
The arrogance does not just extend to the debate here in the House. We have been giving out the phone number for the government lobby. It is 613-996-7441. We have heard that on numerous occasions this evening people have called and have not been treated particularly well by government members. People have called our phones to let us know.
People want to be heard on this issue, and this is their opportunity to be heard. I hope they will call the government members at 613-996-7441 and give their views on the North American free trade agreement. It may be the only chance they will get.
Debate has been constricted on this very important issue. This legislation is over 4,000 pages in length and substantive debate up to today has been limited at second reading to two hours and nine minutes.
People might wonder why members of Parliament would be debating at two o'clock in the morning. It is because we want people to have the opportunity to hear the reasons why we oppose the North American free trade agreement. It will substantially change not only any
trade arrangements we have but it will change the fabric of our country and it will change the fabric of government.
We believe that we are speaking out for the people who elected us. We are not speaking out for the transnational corporations that are behind this deal. We are speaking out for the ordinary Canadians who think that members of Parliament should be working for them no matter what the hour.
The myth that those of us who oppose the free trade agreement and now oppose the North American free trade agreement are protectionists is just that-a myth. We believe that there should be a freer trade arrangement but it should be sectoral, fairer trade which considers sustainability, human rights and and labour concerns. In short it would work for the people and not for capital and not for the corporations. It works for those people who are doing the work.
There is another aspect of the North American free trade agreement that is too little considered particularly in this part of our country. In British Columbia our major trade links are not north and south but with the Pacific rim. The Pacific rim trading partners that we enjoy in British Columbia do not see this trade agreement as trade enhancing. They see it instead as trade constricting.
How will this benefit British Columbia trade? That is what British Columbians are asking themselves because we have really found out firsthand what the Canada-U.S. Free Trade arrangement did to us.
I remember clearly the first speech that I gave as a member of Parliament in this House in the dying days of 1988 when the government was once again ramming through trade legislation. It was the Canada-U.S. trade legislation. I alluded to the farmers in my riding who would be losing their ability to make a living on their farms. Some of them are still clinging to their farms. Some of them are still selling their produce but they are doing so with the onslaught of U.S. agribusiness.
This will only be exacerbated by the North American free trade agreement. If we really believe in sustainable development as this government has espoused in some of the rhetoric that was cited in Rio last June then we had better work to that end. This does not do it with the North American free trade agreement.
May 25, 1993

The Tories need to hear what Canadians think about the North American free trade agreement. We have lost over 500,000 jobs under the Canada-U.S. deal. It would be nice if some of those people could just spend a little bit of money and phone the government and tell it what they think of the North American free trade agreement.
In the U.S. it is no sure thing that this deal is going to pass. I was privileged to meet with members of Congress and the U.S. Senate both in Washington in mid-March and just last weekend in Halifax. We were told at those meetings that Congress does not have the votes to pass the North American free trade agreement. There is considerable concern within the United States for support of supplemental agreements on both the environment and labour. However, there is also considerable concern that no matter what kind of supplemental agreements are passed there is a faction within the Congress-they call it the anti-NAETA caucus-that will not pass NAFTA. They have heard what we have said about the loss of jobs, the concern for the environment and about the kind of food processing that will be done in Mexico and shipped across into the United States and then into Canada. Sustainability means that we have the ability to manage our own resources and that is not going to occur under the North American free trade agreement. It is a bad deal for Canadians. I want to refer to a very specific concern I have which is related to the motions before us. I think it is going to come back to haunt us in this agreement in a very serious way. NAFTA does not allow countries to recognize in their regulations-I am talking about environmental regulations-harmful production processes as wrongs, unless the process is related to the nature of the problem.
What does this mean to Canadians? We would not be able to outlaw products that were made using severely ozone depleting characteristics such as CFCs or halons, or those whose production process-I am not talking about the product-generates toxic pollutants like dioxins and furans and the chlorines in paper production, or whose development involve inhumane treatment of animals. The citation for that comes from NAFTA chapter 9, as well as article 103.
Naturally we would like the government to organize the standards, which are as important as production standards. These standards should be national. There should be no way that the NAFTA could be superior to our own national standards when it comes to the environment on the process side.
What does this mean? Here is a government that for the last five years has made the green plan one of its central pieces of government policy. I have said in this House before that conceptually the government was on the right track. The implementation process is, of course, where we can see and where I am sure many of them feel terribly frustrated because they have not implemented nearly as much as they set out to do in terms of their agenda. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to speak to the amendments which basically concern a whole series of issues that really relate to Canadian sovereignty.
The first amendment sets it out very clearly. The issue is that in the agreement proposed by my colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca the Canadian law shall prevail which is the reverse of the NAFTA in which it says that American law will prevail.
Motion No. 4 deals with the question of the export of raw materials. I want to spend my time basically talking about those two proposed amendments. There are other amendments that are equally important, but those two have particular significance to my riding of Surrey North.
Most Canadians wish to live under Canadian law. We have a significant immigrant population and those people have come to Canada and have chosen Canada as their home in order to live under Canadian law, under Canadian sovereignty. A number of them have been quite shocked to find that we are entering into an agreement under which the ultimate authority is no
longer going to be Canadian law but American law, or agreements dictated by the North American free trade agreement.
I do not think the government and even the cabinet ministers understand the significance of this measure. I want to refer to an exchange that took place in the House this morning between myself and the minister of health. I asked him about generic drugs and their relationship to the NAFTA. He responded by saying that there was no relationship. He did not see any relationship between NAFTA and generic drugs and Bill C-91.
If he had read the NAFTA he would find out under intellectual property-I believe it is section 1709-that the NAFTA directs Canada and will prevent future governments in Canada from passing legislation limiting the patent protection for multinational drug companies. It not only binds the current government but it prevents future governments from exercising sovereignty over our own laws. It prevents us from passing legislation bringing back compulsory licensing or the licensing of generic drugs. It frightens me when the minister of health, who is responsible for our health care system and for drugs, does not know that within the NAFTA there is a clause that would prevent the return of generic drugs and that the whole implementation of Bill C-91 was to comply in advance with the NAFTA.
If that minister of the Crown does not understand what is in the bill and NAFTA and the devastating impact that it will have on Canadians and the Canadian health care system, I wonder how many other things are also in that bill which other ministers do not understand that will have an impact on Canadians and Canadian sovereignty.
One of the other reasons I am particularly interested in Motion No. 4 is that it deals with the export of raw materials. British Columbians know that the export of raw materials means the export of logs. Raw logs are one of the raw materials that the United States has repeatedly been attempting to get its hands on. The whole issue of the tariff against softwood lumber is in fact a dispute over the export of raw logs to the United States.

The United States is now in a critical position in which it has a shortage of wood. When a number of New Democrat MPs went to Washington to meet with congressmen about the softwood lumber tariffs they were told bluntly and up front that the way to get rid of the lumber tariff was simply to allow the export of raw logs.

It was one of those victories where one may have won the battle but lost the war. In that judgment also was a statement that showed that it considered the fact that Canada refuses to export raw logs to the United States a trade restriction and a trade barrier.
Forty-seven per cent of our exports to the United States in 1992 was raw materials. The largest group of these, 12 per cent, were wood, pulp and paper. This is going to grow as the populations in Canada and the United States grow and particularly with the fact that in the northwestern United States there has been overcutting of timber and there is a dramatic shortage. There is increasing pressure on Canada to continue to export material.
Surrey North is situated on the Fraser River. It has a number of small and medium sized lumber mills on its own shores. Adjacent to it in New Westminster and on other parts of the Fraser River are some of the biggest historical wood and plywood mills in Canada. There has been a dramatic drop in the last few years in employment within the IWA, the International Woodworkers, and within the forest industry. One of the things that is causing that is of course increased technology but also there is the whole issue of the export of raw materials. We have had problems with exporting raw logs to the Orient and of course there is still the pressure increasing from the United States.

That is trying to span both sides of the issue at the same time. Of course the reason for that is the transnational corporations which support this proposition which are being sought by the Liberal Party to bankroll their next election campaign. The transnationals support the trade agreement, therefore the Liberals will not oppose it.
On the other side of the coin, the Liberals know that it is going to be a very destructive election campaign for them if they do not in fact oppose the agreement. Here we find them in the House trying to span both sides of the issues and of course they are going to be exposed in the next federal election.
Again the final conclusion on this item is that the people of Canada in the next federal election must be the ones to make the decision not the the House of Commons. We have exercised enough debate on this issue. It is time that we moved this issue forward into the
Government Orders
next federal election and allowed the three clear choices to be put before the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I want to deal particularly with Motions Nos. 2 and 5 in this debate, a debate in which the New Democratic Party is the only party solidly opposing the North American free trade agreement.
I want to point out that Motion No. 2 in the name of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca would have us insert into the law a protection of Canadian law. The protection is there in American law. It is already there in the North American free trade agreement which is carried forward. In the North American free trade agreement it says: "No provision of this agreement nor the application of any such provision to any person or circumstance which is in conflict with any law of the United States shall have effect." We want the same provision, an equal provision to say that no provisions of this agreement nor the application of any such provision to any person or circumstance which is in conflict with any law of Canada shall have effect.
It is very important that this kind of amendment be put forward and adopted. Any act of Parliament or any act of the Ontario legislature or any other legislature in Canada or any decision of a city council or even of a hospital board under the North American free trade agreement can be struck down or made of no effect if it is in conflict with some act of any legislature in the United States. We want the same right to be applied to any act of any legislative body in Canada.
We should have the right to acquire food quality. Food imported from the United States or food imported from Mexico should meet Canadian food standards. We should have the right to control the entry of food into Canada in which there is undue presence, for example, of pesticide residue. We have the right to make those laws now without the interference of the North American free agreement. When this is put into effect, if Canada says you cannot import vegetables that have been poisoned by the pollution of the land and the water that is used to produce those vegetables in Mexico or in parts of the United States, the producers of those would be able to use the North American free trade agreement to strike down that prohibition.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
In the same way if we said, as for example Toronto city council does, that we will not accept a certain product because it is produced by child labour or because it is produced by labour which is not free to organize a union as is required by the International Labour Organization in its conventions, we have the right as a sovereign nation to prohibit the entry of that product into Canada. If we want to have production of goods produced under fair labour conditions or goods that are produced under healthy environmental conditions, we have that right as a sovereign nation. That right will be endangered or even destroyed by this North American free trade agreement because it does not respect laws of Canada as it respects laws of the United States.
If we let this North American free trade agreement go through without this amendment, we are destroying the chance for Canadian producers of food or Canadian producers of equipment for our hospitals, Canadian producers of bed sheets for our publicly owned and publicly operated senior citizens homes, anything like that. If they are produced under unfair or unsanitary conditions we would lose the right to prohibit their import into Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: What clause? That is not true.

The hon. member says that is not true, but the fact is the American law prevails. They can put up any law they want to to prohibit Canadian imports. We cannot put up the same sort of law to prohibit American imports.
The North American free trade agreement is going to be an attack on our general sovereignty as well as an attack on the quality of our food and working relations. Producers and owners of industry in Canada will prefer to produce in a country where they are not required to produce healthy food. They will be allowed to produce food poisoned by the violation of what would be Canadian food quality standards.
Contaminated fruit and vegetables will be imported into Canada. We will not have the right to inspect them fully because they will strike down a Canadian law that would ensure that right. Therefore Motion No. 2 is absolutely necessary to protect us if this North American free trade agreement goes through.
Motion No. 5 is an amendment by the same hon. member and our trade critic.
Nothing in this act or the agreement shall be interpreted so as to prevent citizens of Canada, either individually or in groups, from appearing before any dispute settlement body established pursuant to the agreement where that individual or group wishes to do so.
The original amendment as put forward by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca also included the words: "nothing in this agreement shall be interpreted so as to prevent citizens of Canada, either individually or in groups, from initiating a dispute settlement before any dispute settlement body established pursuant to the agreement."
In other words we need the right to both initiate a dispute and appear before the body that is handling that dispute because this is a right we have now in Canada. If people feel they are being wronged, have bad goods, are being offered bad goods, or bad goods are being brought into the country in violation of Canadian standards and competing unfairly with Canadian produced goods, we have the right to appear before the appropriate bodies in Canada.
We have a right to hear how that dispute is conducted. We have a right to participate in and initiate arguments before these regulative bodies in Canada and that is a right we have to preserve. It is our sovereign right as a sovereign nation.
If this amendment is not adopted Canadians will find that decisions are being made about the quality of our food, much of which is imported from the United States or Mexico, and we will not be able to control the quality of our food. We will not be able to attend the bodies which are making the regulatory decisions.
Those meetings are going to be held in secret behind closed doors. They will not have to even publish their reasons. They will just agree or disagree with a proposal. The argumentation used will not be made public. There will be no possibility of an appeal to a Canadian body, a Canadian regulator or a Canadian legislative body operating according to Canadian custom and Canadian law with the right to know what is being said.
These secret agreements will be used to constrict or destroy any attempt by Canada to prevent the importation of goods that are either harmful to be consumed or produced by unfair competition through violation of basic human rights.
May 25, 1993

In Mexico, 5 million to 10 million children under the age of 15 are being forced to work in the factories. They are paid less than the adults and even the adults are badly paid by our standards. It is in violation of a basic principle of Canadian law that children should be forced to work in factories. That children should be forced to leave school to work is in violation of Canadian law.
Canadians should not have to accept on equal competition goods that are produced in violation of that fundamental human right of children. The only way to protect our right to refuse such goods is to pass this amendment, Motion No. 5. It would give citizens of Canada not only the right to object to a certain import or to appear to initiate the dispute but also the right to speak in the dispute, hear everything that is said and appeal to a higher court.

Mr. Speaker, this debate this evening is typical of what we have seen from this government since it came to power in 1984. There has been excessive use of closure to stifle debate on issues that will affect the long term prosperity of this nation. Decisions have been made that will undermine our workers, the long term stability of our resource sector, and the ability of this nation to make its own decisions. This debate will go down in history.
It is sad that closure is being used again. It has been used more by this government than at any time in the history of this nation to stifle debate in this House. I just have to point out that at 4.07 in the morning on May 26, it is a sad commentary in the last days of this government that it should be taking action such as this.
This important issue has not yet been resolved by the United States or Mexico and is being opposed by many of the members of their governments because they see the fallacy in the reasons that have been given to us.
This North American free trade agreement cannot benefit Canada in the way it is presented. I am speaking here at report stage of this debate that is covering Motions Nos. 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. I just want to deal with a couple of these tonight.
Under the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement the U.S. people were assured by their former secretary of
Government Orders
trade that in the event of a dispute United States laws shall prevail. This was in an address given by the secretary of trade to members of their Congress at the time. Yet in our Canada-U.S. free trade agreement we had a whole multitude of changes to legislation that effectively gutted our ability to make decisions here in Canada that affect this nation and the way we continue to build it.
This amendment simply spells out that under the North American free trade agreement Canadian law shall apply in the event of a dispute. This motion would allow us to put in place provisions to ensure that Canadians would be able to protect their country and their resources from further plundering by interests outside of Canada.
It is interesting to note that in the North American free trade agreement energy was not placed on the table by the Mexican negotiators. However, here in the North American free trade agreement the Americans have equal access to our resources and in particular our energy in the event of a dispute.
We recognize that we have tremendous reserves of oil, particularly in the tar sands in Canada but our conventional reserves are being depleted much quicker than they are replaced or new reserves are being discovered.
It may seem logical to sell off what we have when we have such huge reserves in the tar sands or Hibernia, but we are selling off our cheaper energy and Canadians will have to pay the piper for the more expensive energy after we have spent money on research and developed the technology to make it available. We are going to be paying the high price and again we will be placed out of competition in terms of the cost of production. Whether it is in manufacturing or the resource sector our input costs, as they already are now, will be much higher than they are in the countries to the south of us.
I am further shocked that this government saw fit to take away the amount of reserves that can be held in abeyance to protect the future interests of this country. The National Energy Board used to require a 15-year supply of natural gas reserves before we exported any. I was reading the other day in one of the media papers that another new natural gas contract has been signed with the country to the south of us.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
I was quite shocked one day when I was approached by an American senator who asked me why Canadians were selling off their natural resources. He said that natural gas going to California was being pumped back into the ground to replenish natural gas fields that have been depleted. Twenty years from now the Americans will have the natural gas and we will not. What are we going to do? That is a question that is only fair to put to this government. What is it going to do after our reserves are depleted and what about the future generations of Canadians?
Motion No. 6 is simply a safeguard against the U.S. or Mexico demanding access to our water. The government did not spell out water under a separate section but disguised it in the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement as one of the goods under agriculture. Therefore it is there and it is not simply bottled water.
This particular motion spells out that water is not included in the North American free trade agreement. Water transported by a pipeline or by the diversion of a river is not covered. I have to agree wholeheartedly with this particular motion put forward by one of the members of the opposition in this House. If we are going to prosper as a nation we have to make the best use of our resources and make sure they are used for purposes required in Canada for the prosperity of this nation.
I am deeply alarmed about the lack of water that is quickly developing in the U.S. not only for the production of food but also for watering their lawns. Their cities require huge volumes of water.
We heard earlier today about some of the reservoirs in the Columbia River system that are practically empty. It only makes sense to me that under an agreement like this the first obligation of this government is to look after the needs of Canadians first. It is in that context that I have to support Motion No. 6 at the report stage of this bill.
We have all heard about the grand canal scheme to divert water from the lower end of James Bay across the prairies and down through the Great Lakes system. Some of the dams that are already in place were encouraged to be built by the U.S. corps of army engineers who were probably in a lot of the hearings. They already have some of those reservoirs in place to
begin the diversion of waters from Canada to the nation to the south of us.
The creation of life is dependent on water. I look at the continuing lowering of the aquifers in the plain states of the U.S. where they have to rely on irrigation for the growing of food or the irrigation in the state of California, subsidized irrigation I should point out, used for the production of vegetables and then those vegetables landing back on the Canadian markets at a price well below that of Canada but produced with cheap labour, a lot of it in that country illegally from Mexico, and then we expect the Canadian people to compete economically with such measures.
This is not a free trade agreement when you see a situation developing like that. We need to have our resources here in Canada and use them in the interest of this nation.
I wholeheartedly support spelling it out very clearly in this agreement. I am sure it is no accident that we had to bring forward a motion to achieve that objective, a motion that was left out of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico trade agreement, not left out by accident but left out on purpose because those other nations were demanding access to our precious resource here in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity to rise in support of the amendments that have been provided by my colleague, the hon. member for the Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca area and particularly with amending Motion No. 6 that nothing in this act or this agreement applies to any water transported by a pipeline or diverted by reason of the diversion of a river.
We have been debating for some time. As a matter of fact this debate goes right back to before the last election in 1988 as to whether or not water is in fact a commodity or good that is included in both the original free trade agreement and now the proposed North American free trade agreement.
The government has argued that there is nothing in either agreement which compels us to sell our water and it is technically correct in that regard. There is nothing in the agreement which compels us.
May 25, 1993

The point is that there is nothing in either agreement, the original FTA or the proposed NAFTA, which expressly forbids or prohibits the export or large scale diversions of water as commodities of trade under either of these agreements.
Canada's chief trade negotiator, Gordon Ritchie, has in fact conceded that nothing in either the free trade agreement or this proposed North American free trade agreement would prevent, and I want to highlight and emphasize the word prevent, governments or individual entrepreneurs for that matter from redirecting water south of the border under the provisions of these agreements.
Mel Clark, the former senior trade negotiator for Canada with some 30 years of experience, a strong opponent of both of these agreements, has argued emphatically that the North American trade agreement and the original free trade agreement endanger Canada's control of its water resources.
Dr. Frank Quinn, the senior federal policy adviser for the inland waters directorate for the Government of Canada, has said: "Under the FTA and the NAFTA market forces will inevitably result in the diversion of Canadian water. Sooner or later Uncle Sam will force us to open the tap."
It is only this government that continues to mislead the Canadian public with its line that water is not included in either agreement. It is only this Tory government that refuses to see how its failure to negotiate specific exclusions for large scale water diversions and bulk water exports has in fact endangered Canada's water resources and has severely compromised Canada's sovereignty with respect to this particular resource.
I want to read from an article entitled "NAFTA and Water Exports", a submission by the Rawson Academy of Aquatic Science dated April 1983. It talks about water inclusions in the North American trade agreement. Reading from this article, it says: "Without an exclusion, water is certainly part of the agreement. Any good or service covered by a tariff heading annexed to the NAFTA agreement is subject to the rights and obligations set out in the agreement itself". Tariff heading 22.01 of the NAFTA is as follows: waters including natural or artificial mineral waters and aerated waters, ice and snow.
It has been argued by the federal government that this tariff heading which is the same as that annexed to the free trade agreement does not cover water and river
Government Orders
systems as this is not considered a good in the commercial sense. Tariff 22.01 covers only bottled water, they have argued, because it is found in a chapter entitled "Beverages, Spirits and Vinegar".
They go on to argue. They say: "This argument, however, has proven groundless by the interpretative rules accompanying the tariff schedule of the NAFTA agreement. Interpretative Rule No. 1 states: the titles of sections, chapters and sub-chapters are provided for ease of reference only. For legal purposes, classifications shall be determined according to the terms and headings of any relative section of chapter notes".
It has been upheld and recognized and respected Canadian experts in international trade law have agreed that naturally flowing water is indeed covered under tariff heading 22.01. Even the Ottawa law firm that the federal government referenced in the original water debate in 1988 has acknowledged this. It quotes from this firm: "A review of the tariff items in chapter 22 reveals that chapter 22 is directed at beverages, however, nothing in the wording suggests that the word waters is restricted to waters used as a beverage or waters that are not of large scale quantities as would be required for diversion".
It is pretty clear from the comments made in this document, the comments made by senior trade negotiators for Canada, the comments made by senior officials in the Ministry of the Environment, water is indeed identified as a commodity, a good in the North American trade agreement. Because the agreement does not specifically exclude the possibility of large-scale diversions of water for the purposes of trade, then these agreements subject Canada's water supplies, our natural surface waters, to exploitation by commercial interests.
We want to talk about the interpretive clauses of this agreement and how they affect the possibility of accessing Canadian water supplies. Article 102 sets forth the objectives of the agreement as they are written to eliminate barriers to trade and facilitate the cross-border movements of goods.
Goods of a party are identified in article 22.01 in the agreement and these are identified as products, as understood in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trades. I have a copy of the agreement here as it is written up in the harmonized description and coding system. Article 22.01 is in fact in this original GATT agreement which references both the NAFTA and the FTA. Article 22.01 is identified as ordinary natural water of all kinds other than sea water. That is a pretty wide-ranging definition that pretty much encompasses all natural waters of all kinds.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
The only conclusion that you can reach is that water is included as a good under the provisions of the North American agreement and because it is included as a good, it is subject to the provisions of these agreements if in fact a commercial contract was entered into to transport or divert the flows of Canadian waters to south of the border.
The North American trade agreement is very similar to the free trade agreement with respect to its over-all architecture. We find in the North American trade agreement that the government was not totally asleep at the switch. It did make provisions to specifically exclude the export of raw logs and it made provisions to specifically exclude the export of unprocessed fish from Quebec and the maritimes. Somehow it forgot there was a west coast fishing industry but that is not unusual because it always forgets about British Columbia anyway.
It managed to include exclusions for raw logs and exclusions for unprocessed fish but the North American trade agreement is absolutely silent when it comes to the possibility of export of water resources. There is no specific exclusion which exempts trade in water exports. That is why, regardless of any the purported benefits of these agreements, unless we can get the specific exclusions in the agreements this document should not be supported.

Mr. Speaker, at this untimely hour of 4.30 in the morning, one rises to speak to a series of debates which are intended to tie in and provide clarification to the North American free trade agreement. One begins to see a mirror image of the debate that occurred during the 1988 election dealing with the Canada-United States free trade agreement. One begins to wonder whether or not anyone is actually using any original material. That is perhaps an opportunity for the opposition to engage the government in debate and tie up the business of this House, particularly when we look at the vast amount of legislation we have to deal with, particularly in the justice portfolio. I hope this House will allow some time for the passage of that before this House rises.
I want to take this opportunity to address particularly the aspect of the loss of sovereignty, which is simply not true. I have a series of statements the opposition has made which are simply not true.
I would like to begin by talking about water, which we have just heard some reference being made to. You will note how carefully the speech structure was put together whereby it was said that nothing would prevent the exportation of water in large amounts. Perhaps it is quite true that nothing would prevent it but on the other hand, nothing in the North American free trade agreement or the free trade agreement with Canada and the United States compels Canada to export its water.
I would suggest that if we are looking at a trading arrangement, far be it for those who are traders to keep the doors open. Should governments of the future wish to export certain amounts of water that would be their prerogative. It is the desire and wish of this government that not be the case but we do not need that written into law.
We have seen time after time where GATT has had the matter of trading water in large volumes explained. It is not a matter dealt with in international trading terms as a substance that would be considered as a trading entity by GATT. So there is no truth in the allegation that the North American free trade agreement compels the partners to trade water with each other.
There was another non-truth in this debate with respect to the fact that this whole matter has been rushed. There have been 27 meetings recently by the committee, 203 witnesses have appeared and 95 submissions have been accepted by the committee. As well, the Subcommittee on International Trade has had 29 meetings. It has listened to 124 witnesses. It has accepted 95 submissions, 23 exhibits and four appendices. The committee has visited nine cities.
The matter of the North American free trade agreement was raised at least once in the House of Commons in a period of 234 days; in Question Period 300 times; Members' statements, 22 times and it was the subject of petitions 14 times. To say this matter has been rushed again is a non-truth.
May 25, 1993

I recall during the 1988 debate that my opponents in the constituency of Regina-Wascana were using the scare lactic that if we were to enter into the free trade agreement with the United States we would be forced to harmonize our social programs with the United States. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, being astute as you are in following the news you would find that if anything there seems to be a mini stampede toward harmonizing all right, but harmonizing American standards with those standards we enjoy in Canada. For people to try to frighten the stampede of social thought into thinking that harmonization would occur as a retrograde step is certainly not telling it as it is.
I recently sent a questionnaire to my constituents asking a series of questions. One was with respect to the public's acceptance of the North American free trade agreement. I must tell you in all honesty that the constituency is pretty well split on the subject. I would think that being a technical trade matter the average member of the public is not aware of what is required to become an international trader. The matter of international trade is not a matter that affects the bread and butter of the average citizen in the community. In spite of that I am quite pleased that at least 50 per cent of the constituents support further expanded trade on an international basis.
The opposition's scare tactics are working to a degree but not to the benefit of this country. From an economic point of view, a job creation point of view, the job stimulus and economic stimulus point of view those kinds of tactics are hurting the economics of our country. I hope the opposition will take the time to sit back and just ask themselves what they are contributing to the economy of this country by uttering these phrases that contain so many non-truths.
There is another item that I heard used so often in the 1988 election and I hear again dealing with our loss of sovereignty. This is the contention that if we have a dispute with the United States we will have to solve it by its rules. If that is the case then tell me why, out of nine disputes we have had with the United States using the binding trade dispute settlement mechanism, have we won nine of them? It seems to me that yes indeed, the mouse has made the elephant roll over.
Government Orders
I think that with the inclusion of Mexico and the elimination of these non-truths I have highlighted from the debate we will find that Mexico to NAFTA is quite a bit like Portugal was to the European Economic Community. Portugal was deemed to be a backward country from a technological point of view. What did the rest of the European Economic Community have to gain? They gained the evolution and development of an economy of a country that is now contributing toward consumerism in the European Economic Community. The contribution of the Mexican people and economy will do the same thing for as Mexico becomes a stronger trading partner its expectations for a higher standard of living will grow and that in turn will make its people better consumers.
NAFTA and future trade evolutions can provide all of us with a much higher standard of living as a trading bloc. Perhaps we can step over the Pacific Ocean and develop a trading bloc with the Pacific Rim countries. We have learned from the example that has been given to us by the 360 million members of the European Economic Community.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to hear the member opposite attempt to defend the impact of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and suggest that what he sees as gains under that agreement will be fortified by the North American free trade agreement with Mexico.
He talked about the criticisms of those opposed to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement in the 1988 election. It is worth remembering that we in the New Democratic Party talked about the threat to our social programs, our health care system and our economy. If we look at what has happened to Canada since 1988 we will see that as a result of actions from the federal government our health care system has never been under more serious threat.
Our social programs have never been under more serious threat. We have seen quite blatant and open responses with regard to patent drugs following from the North American free trade negotiations and pressure from United States drug companies. We have 4.2 million Canadians living on unemployment insurance or social assistance.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
If we have benefited from the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement as the member opposite has suggested surely we would not be in these circumstances today. Surely we would not be in the situation where 16 or 17 per cent of Canadians are not part of the productive work force of this country. As a result of the economic and social policies of this government which are exemplified in both the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and the Mexico free trade agreement these Canadians are just thrown away to lead lives which do not provide them with the dignity work would provide.
Anyone who looks at the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement or who is part of that 4.2 million unemployed would find it difficult to believe what the member opposite is saying about the benefits under the North American free trade agreement.
It is worth remembering that most Canadians are opposed to this agreement as they were to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. The government and people of Saskatchewan, my own province, are opposed but this government goes ahead anyway.
Why are they opposed? They are not opposed because they are afraid to compete. They are not opposed because they are afraid to trade in the world economy. Saskatchewan farmers, natural resource producers and manufacturers have survived by trading over the years. With a population the size of Saskatchewan's there is no choice. The economy has been entirely export oriented.
It is also worth remembering that Saskatchewan has contributed to Canada. Most of what separates us from the United States is in terms of policy initiatives from the New Democratic Party and the CCF before it on pensions, health care, social programs and a Canadian way of dealing with economic problems. We all know how important the co-operative sector is to the province of Saskatchewan. That is a Canadian-owned solution to problems of the economy.
Why would Saskatchewan have responded in that way in the past? Why would it be opposed to throwing the economy wide open to market forces to decide everything that will have an impact on Canadians as this government would want?
Saskatchewan in the context of the Canadian market is far from most markets. It has a small population and suffers from many geographical disadvantages, although it experiences some benefits in terms of its resource base and agriculture.
Left to its own devices trying to fend off market forces and do what was best for Saskatchewan and its people it had to take on those corporate interests which were only concerned with making profit and not concerned with the people of Saskatchewan. Consequently it developed in a rather different way than the United States.
If we are close to markets and have a large market we can benefit more effectively from more open barriers. We will recall that Britain was a big advocate of free trade when it had the upper hand. However countries that do not have the upper hand, the market benefits or the industries developed to take advantage of the breakdown of national interests must take matters into their own hands. Here we have an agreement that is giving up more sovereignty rather than claiming back sovereignty. We have a situation in which Canada under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and under the economic policies of the government opposite has lost the power and sovereignty and the ability to make the decisions which are best for Canadians.
What we need in this country is not to give up power to multinational corporations and to other countries. What we need is to develop a strategy which works for Canadians. We need to chart out Canadian solutions for the challenges that we face.
I am sure that it is striking to most Canadians that the free trade agreement we are here discussing makes it impossible for Canada to pass legislation in conflict with the free trade agreement which would be in the interests of Canadians. This would include for example legislation which would encourage or even require the manufacturing of raw materials rather than allow those raw materials to be shipped out of Canada without being processed or without being turned into something with a higher value added and thus lose jobs to Canada.
I would like to close with one point which would also be disturbing to most Canadians. It has to do with the action on the Mexican border of drug smugglers who are setting up factories, warehouses and trucking companies in Mexico to exploit the cross-border commerce which will be expected under the North American free trade agreement. Is this what we are to expect from this North American free trade agreement? It means easier access to cocaine and other drugs to Canada to further erode Canadian society. Under this agreement the export of Mexican products in Mexican trucks will be vastly expanded.
May 25, 1993

I know from trucking companies in my riding how dangerous they feel this to be. They are already under serious threat as a result of the Canada-U.S. agreement. They are already seeing their share of the market cut back. As more and more American trucks come across the border they are now going to be faced with more and more Mexican trucks coming across the border with Mexican truckers being paid Mexican wages in contrast to our Canadian truckers being paid Canadian wages.
These trucks as a result of this action by drug smugglers in Mexico are more and more likely to contain drugs to undermine our own society. It will be very easy for Mexicans to travel to anywhere in Canada within the next 10 years. If our observance of border crossings and so on is anything to go by then we know that we have just given up control over things such as meat packing and meat inspection to American inspectors rather than to our own. I think we can see a major problem arising in that area too.
It is alarming to me that any government would want to further erode Canadian sovereignty rather than to build up Canadian sovereignty. Why would we not want to be able to make Canadian-made decisions in Canada for Canadians is beyond me and beyond the people of Saskatchewan and beyond the people of Saskatoon- Clark's Crossing. This government should be ashamed of the way in which it is undermining Canada's ability to do what is best for Canadians.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this second grouping of motions having to do with Bill C-115.
I am particularly interested in Motion No. 4 which is of great importance especially to the sections of our country that deal with natural resources. Motion No. 4 asks that:
Nothing in this Act or the Agreement shall be interpreted so as to prohibit a Party to the Agreement from requiring another Party to the agreement to process raw materials or raw resources before exporting such materials or resources.
That is basically because a lot of the raw materials come from northern Ontario and affect in particular my riding which is a great exporter of minerals.
Government Orders
As we well know, especially in the mining industry, the trade agreements do not have a very large effect on them. They do trade on the international market now and that is the way their prices are set.
I think it is especially important that we have a clause like this which would not prohibit the additional value-added benefits that come from much of the manufacturing and processing of the different raw materials that can be done in Canada.
It has been a very big problem that a lot of our raw resources have been exported in their raw state so to speak. As such we have missed out on many opportunities at creating good-paying jobs in Canada rather than seeing all of our jobs move south of the border and perhaps even into Mexico. I think it is a safeguard that is extremely important to all of the people of Canada.
As I said in this same debate concerning the first grouping, the people of Canada are worried. They are afraid because they see all of their jobs that have fled south of the border. No matter how many times this Conservative government repeats that we are into somewhat of a recovery, it is very much a jobless recovery. People want to know when they are going to be able to expect to get any kind of employment and I think rightly so. As the representatives of the people of Canada we always have to remember that they are the ones we serve.
I think the original free trade agreement which we debated some four and a half years ago has caused some pretty serious effects on the lives of Canadians. Many of them are unemployed now.
In a place like Sudbury one would think that it is such a big mining industry and mining trades on the international market, however, many small companies that were producing equipment or a number of components for the mining industry have closed down because perhaps there was a parent company in the U.S. and they suddenly decided that it was cheaper to process the goods in the U.S. instead of having another place somewhere else. These companies have rationalized their operations so now they ship the goods because they think it is a cheaper way of doing it and there are no restrictions on that.

May 25, 1993

We have a host of small companies that have closed their doors basically because of the free trade agreement. Even though the people of Sudbury thought that it would not have as big an impact perhaps as in the manufacturing centres, it has still had a severe impact.
I have had people come to my office such as men in their forties who are unemployed and have been unemployed for some time basically because their company closed its doors. It is now producing whatever it was producing in the Sudbury area somewhere else and shipping it instead.
It is very difficult for these people to comprehend why this Conservative government would push through another NAFTA or trade agreement with North America when it has not really addressed the problems in the first deal that they told everyone was going to create jobs, jobs, jobs. It has not done anything to help those people that it has affected.
I think that it is a sad legacy that this government will leave us when it leaves office as I know it will because the people of Canada are not about to allow this government to continue the devastation of its economy and the devastation it has wrought on the lives of Canadians. I think that is the key.
If one watched the election returns in the early evening out of Nova Scotia one will know that there was a Liberal sweep there. The Liberals won 40 seats. The Conservatives managed to keep 9 seats from a previous 35 seats and the NDP stayed at 3 seats.
If that is any indication of things to come then I think the people of Canada know exactly what has happened to them and they want some ray of hope no matter what this Conservative government tries to do or whatever kind of race it is having.
I say that because somehow we are in a recovery but there are no jobs to this recovery. For all of the jobs that the Conservative government tells us are created, twice as may are lost. Every time we turn around we hear of someone else who has been laid off. We know that the jobs that have been created are not the high-paying
full-time jobs of the past. They may be part-time jobs. They may contract jobs. People do not feel secure.
If one has a contract job it may be for three months or it may be for four months. One knows that at the end of four months one is not going to have a job unless one is lucky enough to get another contract. Not only that but one has absolutely no benefits paid. When one has a contract job one gets paid as if one was an entrepreneur.
