Mr. Speaker, I just want to mention a couple of things and put a couple of things on the record about the North American free trade agreement and Bill C-115.1 think it is important that we talk about some of the positive effects that have taken place and that are about to take place as a result of this agreement.
One of the things that we must not fail to recognize is that the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States has produced NAFTA. It is built upon the free trade agreement and has created a new climate for trade and commerce between Canada and the United States.
Canada has really been the big winner when one looks at the merchandise trade flows and one sees the increase that Canada has accomplished in that area to the point that now we are probably exporting about $120 billion to the United States. That is somewhere in the area of a 10 to 15 per cent increase. That is pretty substantive when one thinks of the way the world economies have been lately.
I think it is very important to recognize that. Also it is very important to recognize that our trade with Mexico is about $2 billion or $3 billion. It is very minimal compared to what our present trade is with the United States.
The fact is that Mexico is a developing country. Its demands have increased very substantively in the last three or four years. Its market is expanding very rapidly. It has some 80 million or 85 million people who are learning to become more productive in a developing country. They are learning different aspects of the economy and giving themselves the ability to be more productive, more successful and create more wealth within the country.
I think it is very important to recognize those facts before we get into some of the details. I do want to talk about some of these amendments. It is important that when we get into a trade agreement like the one that we are talking about today or the base of it which is the free trade agreement that we have a set of rules, a dispute settlement mechanism or whatever. There should be a neutral referee who is able to look at the two sides of an issue.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
When there is such a large partner as the one we have which involves the largest trading arrangement in the world somewhere along the line you have to be able to protect the smaller partner. I think we have been very successful in that.
It was alluded to by my colleague from Regina earlier about the success rate that we have had with regard to dispute settlements and one thing or another with these panels. It is very important to recognize that. We have to recognize that if we are going to build an economy, if our economy is going to grow, if we are going to protect the social programs that we talked about earlier, if we are going to protect our health care system and if we are going to do all the things that are very important to us as Canada then we have to increase our gross domestic product.
This is the opportunity to do that whether it is small business, large business or what have you. Those businesses are going to have to take advantage of these new opportunities and when they do their businesses will grow and expand. They will employ more people, the circle will continue and we will be able to resolve some of the employment problems.
One of the few things we would all agree with in this House is that the level of unemployment is unacceptably high and until we have everyone in this country working we are not going to be satisfied as members of Parliament. We all have that as a goal.
We may have different philosophies as to how we are going to get there but certainly it is a worth-while goal. This kind of opportunity for agreements with other countries and economies can help us build our economy and also quite frankly it can help those economies to build.
We are dealing with a Third World country that has struggled but now seems to be moving in the right direction. I think it is to its advantage and Canada's advantage to work with this country. I think it is also incumbent upon us to set the stage for further development in the southern hemisphere. If Canada can make this kind of arrangement work with Mexico effectively it is certainly going to be to everyone's advantage.
In speaking to the four amendments that we grouped together we are talking about the prevalence of Canadian law and what that means under these kinds of agreements. It has been suggested that we provide a new Canadian law that will prevail over NAFTA in case of conflict. I think most people will recognize if they study this that under international law an agreement entered into between states is binding as between those states.
It is incumbent upon the individual parties to implement domestic laws and set up the appropriate laws within their own countries. Under Canada's system of constitutional law we do not recognize international agreements as part of our domestic law.
Contrary to what one of the members suggested earlier about municipalities, school boards and everybody else making their laws to agree to NAFTA, that just does not make any sense at all. Anyone who has studied this will recognize that. Of course we are going to have to have agreements within our own country to implement this and the laws accordingly but that in no way affects other organizations or other levels of government within the country.
The other area I want to talk about is the processing of raw materials. This is one of the amendments. It has been suggested that because of NAFTA we would not be able to process our raw materials. We would have to send raw logs to the United States or maybe even to Mexico and have them shipped back as finished products.
I think anyone who has studied and read the regulations will understand that Canada has the right to maintain its log export controls. When it comes to any other natural resources the same thing would apply. Canadians would have the right, obligation and opportunity to maintain control. Quite frankly, Canada should be taking advantage of improving its natural resources and putting the added manufacturing and processing on to them. I think it is important to recognize that.
There was also a suggestion made that the subject of the dispute settlement process has come up under Motion No. 5. It suggests that an individual would not be able to appear before a binational panel on anti-dumping and countervailing duty matters. That is just not the case.
Certainly when it comes to settlement panels created by governments for the resolution of government to government disagreements or what have you, the Government of Canada would be the one to represent the interests of the country. That is only to be expected.
May 25, 1993

It is also very noteworthy to recognize that individual experts can be brought in for their expertise, knowledge and capabilities in bringing these people forward to help settle the issue. As has been mentioned earlier, Canada has been very successful in maintaining that by bringing those people in and providing the expertise necessary. As a result we have been very successful in that regard.
I know I am running out of time, but finally I want to deal with the amendment suggesting that we have to include a special clause to stop the export of water. In reading this legislation we all know there is no attempt at that. There is no hidden agenda. There is no suggestion at all that rivers are going to be diverted or somebody is going to pull the plug on the Great Lakes to allow the water to flow south or anything like that. It does refer to bottled water, water in tanks, processed water or whatever.
That only makes sense to anyone who has looked at it. We can look at the success of some of these natural water companies. We wish them all well and we encourage them. They are taking advantage of a market that is there. These amendments do not improve the bill. I just want to suggest I will not be supporting the amendments as presented.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of the amendments moved by my colleagues. They are important amendments. If we are to proceed with the agreement the proposed amendments would certainly make it much more acceptable to us.
Let me deal with the first amendment in this group. We have to take a look at the United States-Canada Free Trade Implementation Act as it was passed by the United States. The act states:
The Uniled States law is to prevail in conflict. No provision of the agreement nor the application of any such provision to any person or circumstances which is in conflict with any law of the United States shall have effect.
We assume that a similar provision would also be included in the NAFTA legislation when it goes before the U.S. House of Congress. When we compare that to when it talks about the ability of Canada to act in terms of Canadian law we see the following:
Government Orders
The parties to this agreement shall ensure that all necessary measures are taken in order to give effect to its provisions, including their observance, except as otherwise provided in this agreement by state, provincial and local governments.
We should note that the exception reads "as otherwise provided in this agreement". It does not say except as otherwise provided in the laws of Canada or any of the provinces. It appears that any exceptions to this act are contained in the act itself. Canadian law may not be as clearly subordinated to the FDA as implied in the Campbell article, but nowhere in this act is it stated that in the case of conflict previously enacted Canadian law prevails.
It seems to be very clear from the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement that there is one set of laws for the United States and another set for Canada. Our concern is that this would also apply to the NAFTA and further weaken Canadian sovereignty.
The other motion before us is one to guarantee that Canada will be allowed to process its natural resources before export. The concern is that some 47 per cent of Canadian exports to the United States consist of raw material. At some stage we are going to get smart as a country and we are going to demand that we process these raw materials before we export them. Lo and behold, quite a few countries, even so-called Third World countries, are now beginning to demand that value added be placed on their natural resources.
Many countries that used to export hard lumber no longer allow the export of logs. They demand that value added be placed on wood products. Hopefully and conceivably when we have a more progressive government in place, a government that acts in the interests of Canadians and Canadian workers, we will also begin to enact similar laws. We want to make certain the NAFTA would allow us to do that. Unfortunately the existing agreement casts grave doubt on our ability to have some control over our natural resources.
In another motion before us we want to ensure that in any dispute settlement mechanism more than just government organizations are able to appear and to make presentations. Therefore the motion in the name of my colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca would ensure that citizens either individually or in groups would be

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
able to appear before any dispute settlement body established pursuant to the agreement.
We are interested in the democratization of the process. This is important. There is much in this agreement that we feel is not in the interests of the Canadian public, of the American public or of the Mexican public. It is not in the interests of working men and women on our continent. It is more a constitution that is being written to help the transnational and multinational corporations.
The multinationals will benefit from it, not the Mexican workers, the American workers or the Canadian workers. It is not those people who believe that through our collective efforts as a society we can put into place environmental laws, social laws and structures and labour legislation to ensure a fair distribution of wealth. It is not to help any of these progressive causes that we have this agreement. It is to ensure the multinational and the transnational corporations have access to the resources wherever and whenever they want and to cheap labour. That is the purpose behind this agreement.
It is a sad day for democracy when a government low in the polls is trying in its dying days to push through an agreement that will have tremendous negative effects on Canadians without having the decency to wait until an election is held, without waiting to see what the American legislation will be, without waiting to see what parallel accords will accompany the agreement. They are forcing Parliament to accept something the Canadian public is against, and we have no clear idea what we are agreeing to.
We have seen the effects of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement in our province of Saskatchewan. We have seen the abolition of the two-price system of wheat which has had devastating results for farmers. We have seen the attack on the wheat board. Now the Minister of Agriculture has expressed his desire to remove barley from the wheat board; another attack on orderly marketing, on the institutions we have built to protect our farmers.
They are all endangered by the free trade agreements negotiated by this government. This government is not committed to the welfare of Canadian farmers or Canadian workers. It is not committed to the well-being of our country environmentally and our social programs and policies. It is only concerned with the well-being of
the transnational corporations and the multinational corporations. It has betrayed Canada. Canada has been weakened because of the policies of this government. As a nation we stand crippled. The only desire of all Canadians is to have an election soon to turf this bunch out of office.

Mr. Speaker, good morning. I will be serving breakfast later, bacon and eggs and toast.
The basic question we ought to be asking this morning is why the government is not listening. There is nothing in these amendments that should frighten the government. There is nothing in these amendments that will not respond to a number of concerns that have been voiced by Canadians throughout the country.
For example let us look at the first amendment. There should be nothing brought forward-essentially that is what it says-that would be in conflict with Canadian law. In other words, if is in conflict with Canadian law, it will not go into effect. What is wrong with that?
Surely in our own country Canadian law should prevail. That seems quite reasonable to me. Why is the government not listening? Why is the government not reading? I suspect it is not unlike-you will remember that Mr. Speaker because you have an excellent memory-Bill C-93 when the government was given ample opportunity to withdraw. Despite all the evidence it decided not to. I guess it was not listening there either.
Let us look at the second amendment that says the processing of raw materials or raw resources before exporting should not be prevented. What in the world is wrong with that? Increasingly we are looking for value added in order to increase the number of good, long term jobs for Canadians. That is a reasonable amendment and so are the others we have discussed. But here again the government is not listening. Why is the government not listening? I shall try to answer that question shortly.
The third amendment says nothing shall prevent Canadian citizens individually or in groups from appearing before any dispute settling body. What is wrong with that? Surely fundamental justice demands that if someone wants to appeal a particular question then he or she, individually or collectively, should be able to appear to present a case. Why is the government not listening?
May 25, 1993

The fourth amendment says that control of our water must be maintained. Surely that is quite quite reasonable. Why is the government not listening?

I cannot understand why the government refuses to listen. Some of the amendments before us are completely reasonable. This is true not only of this series of amendments, but of the others we have discussed as well. I completely fail to understand why the government refuses to consider each of the amendments that addresses the needs expressed by Canadian workers.

Why is the government rushing through this? There is an election coming. It wants to get this through. It wants to create a bit of space hoping that Canadians will have forgotten that it rammed this through. Or is it the second hypothesis that the Prime Minister wants to be able to go down in the history books as the one who brought in the Canada-U.S. trade agreement and the NAFTA agreement?
I would rather not go down in the history books and have that quotation beside my name. I certainly would prefer not to have that and so would you, Mr. Speaker.
If the government is so certain this is such a good idea, why does it not go out and ask people. I have. Last week I went to my riding. It is a very representative riding. It is the geographic centre of Canada. I asked my constituents how they like the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and if they think we ought to proceed with the North American free trade agreement. The answer was an overwhelming no. I did not hear one person say yes. Ask my constituents if they believe the Canada-U.S. trade agreement has created jobs for them.
Ask my constituents if they think NAFTA will create jobs for them. Ask them if the government will level with Canadians. When it says jobs are being created will it talk about the kinds of jobs, the kinds of remunerations and the kinds of benefits?
Will the government talk about the other side of the coin? How many jobs have been destroyed and what kinds of jobs? Of course some jobs have been created

I think my colleague has finally come to life and I appreciate that. I want him to listen very carefully to the following. We in the Liberal Party of Canada have made a number of requests. We have said what a wonderful opportunity this would be to correct the flaws in the Canada-U.S. trade agreement if the government would only listen. Why not define subsidies? Why not define anti-dumping? Why not do it now? Why not have appropriate agreements with respect to labour and environmental standards? Why wait?
Why not have adjustment programs? My colleagues will be very interested in this because the Prime Minister and his government, of which they are a part, had promised the best training programs in the world so companies and workers could adjust to the Canada-U.S. trade impact.
What happened? Nothing.

Nothing. Nothing at all. We are still waiting. Really, there is absolutely nothing.

It is really unfortunate it did not take advantage of this situation to come to grips with the dispute settlement. There is nothing in here that will make it less costly.
The government lost a golden opportunity to make sure we had the same deal the Mexicans negotiated over their energy needs.

It did not understand anything, they did not hear anything and they did not see anything. It is too bad. This is why it is not making any headway in the polls. This is why the Canadian people are going to tear it to pieces very soon. We will not have to wait long now. Why? Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether I can reach the oratorical levels of my good colleague from St. Boniface. I will try but after all, it is 5.25 a.m. I am not too sure how well I function so early in the day.
When I was driving to the House a few minutes ago I was wondering whether the Tories would get it. One
might ask, get what? I will answer my own question because I do not think they do get it. I do not think they understand the gravity of the situation. I do not think they understand the concerns of Canadians. We have a bill that is before us and Canadians are demanding not only that it be thoroughly debated, but that we also address all the questions arising from NAFTA.
Canadians are going through tough times, terrible times. They are not going to take an agreement of this kind lying down, especially in the wake of the FTA. They are not just going to take it according to the creed set down by the Progressive Conservative Party.
Canadians know that the Conservative Party is now totally intoxicated, drunk on its own ideology. It has been listening to itself for about nine years and its members have become true believers in everything they have said. They have lost all balance. Canadians are saying that we must get back to some sanity.
Look at the cluster of motions before us. Speakers before me have addressed these motions individually. What do the motions say? Motion No. 6 for example is designed to explicitly state that we Canadians have control over water. Nobody else, just us. The motion in effect is asking this government to put explicitly into NAFTA that we have the final say. Nobody else. We have the final say and all say explicitly in NAFTA.
What is wrong with that? What is it really designed to do? It is designed to give us control over our lives. It will strengthen our democracy. Is there anything wrong with that? I would not think there is anything wrong with it.
I guess according to the ideology of that party there is something wrong because according to this government it should be the marketplace that decides and that always makes the final decision. The marketplace has the final say. Not our public institutions, not our democracy, not Canadians, but the marketplace.
What has happened to Canadians? Are we not capable of making our own decisions any more? Do we just take whatever the marketplace serves us? Have we come to the point that we cannot make decisions on our own?
I believe in market economics, not unfettered market economics. I believe in the marketplace. I would like to give the marketplace as much manoeuvrability and power as possible. However things can go wrong in the marketplace and it can make mistakes.
May 25, 1993

When the marketplace is not functioning properly we, on behalf of Canadians, have the responsibility to step in and see what we can do. We do not walk on water and we do not always make the best decisions, but we cannot just stand back and accept anything that is served up by the market.
There was a column written the other day in the Toronto Star by Carol Goar. She was citing a recent UN report. Let me just quote a couple of passages from that UN report.
Listen to this one: "Markets should serve people rather than people serving markets". Anything wrong with that? I do not see anything wrong with that. Yet this government says: "No, you will not have any more say. We are not here to draw up any laws concerning international trade or international business. The market will decide". Of course when it says that the market will decide really what it is saying is that the multinationals and the transnationals with their headquarters in New York, London, Paris and Tokyo will decide. Certainly it is not going to be the servants of the people.
What else does this UN report say? It says: "Markets are not automatically or inevitably people friendly. For all their efficiency at matching buyers and sellers they could also be associated with increasing inequality and poverty as well as large-scale unemployment". Anything wrong with that? I think that is common sense. Some people say that common sense is not so common. Well whatever you want to call it, that makes a lot of sense.
I have one more quote from the UN report because it is relevant to this cluster of motions. This cluster of motions in effect says: Give us more control over our lives through the NAFTA. The UN report says: "Market friendly policies of the 1980s should be replaced with policies to make markets more people friendly". Again, what in the world is wrong with that? Nothing.
Canadians are saying to us in Parliament that we should get a grip on ourselves, get a grip on what is happening in this country. Sure there is globalization. There are challenges out there that we have not experienced before. We know it is more competitive.
Competitiveness and globalization. Those words should ring loudly with the Conservatives on the other
Government Orders
side of the House. That is their new mantra, their new chant. They cannot walk five feet without uttering the word globalization or the word competitiveness. We know that.
We know that there are new dimensions to the global economy, but do we sit back and do nothing or do we try to get a grip on the situation? That is what Canadians are saying. They are saying they do not like the way things are going and they do not like the way the Tories are handling things.
We can do something. We just do not have to say that we are impotent, that the markets are deciding, or that if you just play smart, or if you just be smart everything will be okay. I wish it were as simple as that but it is not.
Good things just do not happen. I think I am old enough now not to believe in too many miracles, especially when it comes to the economy. Good things have happened because first of all there were good ideas and good hard-working people took those ideas and implemented them into real practical things.
Look at the history of Canada. Does anyone really think that our founding fathers-that is more of an American term is it not-our Fathers of Confederation said one day: "Canada needs a national railway, but we do not have to do anything, right? The marketplace will decide that and the marketplace will just give us the CPR". I am looking at my good friend from Toronto and he is nodding his head in the affirmative. Well, that just did not happen. The politicians of the day decided they had to take the bull by the horns. They had to get a grip on things and they made it happen.
Do you think the St. Lawrence seaway just happened? Did the marketplace just serve up the St. Lawrence seaway? I do not think so. Canadian and American politicians got together and decided that this was needed and then they would have it.
Now we have this so-called NAFTA and before that the FTA. We have the global economy. The global economy has been given to us by the world marketplace and it has given us many challenges and many problems. Ask the unemployed. Do we say: "Do not worry. The marketplace will just take care of that". Or, do we do something?

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
I submit that we do something. This cluster of motions before us is trying to do this. They are trying to get a grip on things. Motion No. 6 has to do with water. Motion No. 4 has to do with getting a grip on our natural resources. Motion No. 2 states that Canadian law is to prevail in any conflict. Is there anything wrong with that?
We in the Liberal Party have been talking about an anti-dumping code and a subsidies code. Why do we advocate those two things, among others, to strengthen and improve the NAFTA? It is because the way things are set now, we are judged by American law. When we go into their marketplace, we are subject to American law and American trade remedies.
To me that does not make any sense. What we should have is a common law. If we are going to have a North American free trade area, we had better have some common rules, rules the Americans must observe and rules Canadians must also observe and so on.
Let me just say we support this cluster of motions. They would strengthen our control over our own lives.

Mr. Speaker,
I would like to point out that it is now 5:37 in the morning of what is actually Wednesday although if you look at the calendar, it is Tuesday. Hopefully, as the time progresses, Wednesday will cease to exist.
The way this second group of amendments has been put together puts them in conflict as far as the law is concerned. They make reference to raw materials in Motion No. 4. Motion No. 5 talks about the initiating of disputes in the agreement. Motion No. 6 makes reference to anything that is not in the agreement as being a possibility to open itself up for interpretations other than we might ordinarily think.
I would like to make mention to some of things which have been said earlier, particularly on the government side. One of the previous speakers mentioned that since the free trade agreement came into effect, and they were using that as the basis for how wonderful things would be under the North American free trade agreement, there had been an increase of approximately 15 per cent in trade between Canada and the United States in Canada's favour.
The fact of the matter is that if you add the inflation which has occurred since the free trade agreement was put into effect with the United States and if you also add the lower value of the Canadian dollar, what you end up with is something very closely approximating 15 per cent. Whenever the government refers to the increases under the free trade agreement, it always refers to it in terms of dollars and not in terms of the actual trade itself, which has been minimal and in some cases has been on the negative side.
In other words we have had a heck of a lot more increase in trade coming into Canada from the United States than vice versa. If you look strictly at the dollar value of Canadian exports, you would believe otherwise. The government does its best to try and convince us that that is the case.
Referring to the second amendment in this group, we have to use the North American free trade agreement as the example. The North American free trade agreement makes specific reference to the fact that the agreement shall not be in conflict with American law. Motion No. 2, proposed so wisely and presciently by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca, says that if we go by the free trade agreement then United States law is going to be predominant. All we are saying is that there ought to be a provision in the bill that nothing in the free trade agreement shall override Canadian law.
The free trade agreement does not make reference to Canadian law but it sure does as far as American law is concerned. I know that sounds repetitive but it is a point which absolutely has to be made. It is ironic that there is specific reference that the agreements in the free trade agreement will not override American law. We can only assume that in reference to the North American free trade agreement the same conditions will prevail.
We had assurances from the government side that it is not necessary to make specific reference to Canadian law and the supremacy of it as far as Canadians are concerned because the dispute mechanism is there. There is something within our Constitution that obviates the necessity for having that kind of wording.
May 25, 1993

The fact of the matter is that if we are going to have protection as Canadians we have to have those references in there because the Americans pay no attention to what is in agreements anyway. We have the case of Canadian agriculture being absolutely devastated by the actions of the United States government and its export enhancement program. This program was instituted by the Americans in direct violation of the free trade agreement. The free trade agreement says that the two parties to the agreement will recognize the usual common traditional markets of the other.
I suspect what it really may have done was wake the Americans up to the fact that Canadians in their exports, particularly of wheat, had some pretty lucrative, good, solid and economically advantageous agreements with other countries and summarily proceeded to delve into those markets. Without listing them, there are numerous countries where the United States through its export enhancement program and in violation of the free trade agreement have stolen Canadian wheat markets.
The reference in Motion No. 4 is to the ability of Canadians to have value-added processing to raw materials. The free trade agreement again is a good example of how cautious Canada has to be whenever it is getting into an agreement with our neighbours to the south because of course the free trade agreement extends it one more country.
We have the example of fish where the dispute panel ruled against Canada and we lost the ability to say that fish caught by Canadians in Canadian waters ought to be processed in Canada. It is to the everlasting disgrace of the government opposite that it was party to an agreement where in the final analysis this kind of processing was able to be carried out south of the border by other than those who caught the fish, or I would suggest in the broader sense of our natural resources, of those who did the mining of the material or the growing of it.
Motion No. 5 refers to who may initiate disputes under the free trade agreement. Originally the motion which the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca put forward wanted it to be possible for individuals, ordinary Canadians, to be able to initiate these kinds of disputes.
Of course the North American free trade agreement limits it to its signatories, in other words, the governments and in some cases companies. This adds a whole new dimension to the international situation as far as Canada and the United States is concerned. In the long
Government Orders
term it is not going to be governments, even of Canada I would suggest, or on a smaller level the governments of some of the provinces that are able to initiate actions under this. It will be solely the purview of the multinational corporations which, having felt their rights to have been violated, will have the ability to initiate dispute mechanisms.
In the long run this will result in the rules of NAFTA becoming the governing mechanism by which international trade disputes and the settlement mechanisms between Canada and the United States and Mexico will be settled. If this agreement goes on and on, which was promised by the free traders-freebooters would probably be a better description-because we anticipate that the agreement will-
