speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: What did Trudeau do?

I will get into this NDP nonsense in a minute. The member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan is a colleague of mine in the transport committee. We usually work very well together but when we are in here it is a whole different ball game.
If the Prime Minister sticks to his spring election plans then Canadians will no longer have a chance to have a say on the trade deal. I dare say this government wants my constituents to forget about a few things between now and then, and that is why we have so much debate on this trade deal.
Forget about what kind of things? At 11.4 per cent unemployment today is almost as bad as it was in September 1984. It was 11.6 per cent in 1984. In the fiscal year just ended the federal deficit was $35.5 billion, a shade below the $38.5 billion record set in 1984-85. The
public debt meanwhile has more than doubled in those eight years.
The Bank of Canada just this month said that: "There was little net change in cost competitiveness on an economy-wide basis". That was from 1980 to 1992. The bank said: "The manufacturing sector, in contrast, has experienced a substantial deterioration in competitiveness in recent years reflecting the fact that productivity growth in the Canadian manufacturing sector has lagged behind its U.S. counterpart".
As for the prosperity of this nation, Statistics Canada reported during the week of May 10, this month, that the real after-tax income of the average Canadian family in 1991 was no higher than in 1976.
Isn't that a record to be proud of? However we will debate free trade because that is what is on the minds of Canadians today, that is according to this government and the member for Simcoe Centre.
She became disgusted when my colleague from St. Boniface started talking about talking to his constituents, as I have in my riding, as my colleague has in Broadview-Greenwood and as we all have. Our constituents do not want this deal. She got in a huff.
She rose in her seat.

Off she went into the lobby. It is not just the opposition that is saying this.
It is fun to look back in the papers. One year ago today, on May 11, 1992, The Toronto Star said that only 1 in 25 Canadians polled, 4 per cent, said that the agreement, NAFTA, should continue in its present form. That was the government's position.
What about the NDP's position of scrapping it? Slightly more than a quarter of adult citizens, 27 per cent, preferred that the agreement be terminated. What was the support for maintaining the deal but making the changes necessary to it? A solid majority of the public, 61 per cent, said it should be maintained.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: That is the Liberal position.

Of course there should be changes made to it. Also, 7 per cent had no opinion at all. They have a right to have no opinion. I respect that.
May 25, 1993

I addressed steel eight hours ago when I was up and this time I want to address textiles. Textiles are a concern in my riding. There is the KoBe group which employs many hundreds of individuals.
And in Quebec.

Of course in Quebec and especially in Montreal.
What does Jack Kivenko, president of the Canadian Apparel Manufacturers Institute, have to say about NAFTA?
He says that the industry is keen on increasing its market access in the United States and the apparel industry believes that free trade is in its interests. However the proposed NAFTA creates "hurdles" which do not create "a level playing field with open competition". Mr. Kivenko says: "For our sector the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement was about liberalizing trade in some products some of the time".
NAFTA, because it has substantially tightened the rules governing preferential trade between countries, will mean liberalized trade in fewer products, fewer times, but provide openings in the Canadian market for Mexican-assembled U.S.-branded apparel. As a result of this Kivenko gave this assessment of the proposed NAFTA: "Left to us the North American free trade agreement would not be implemented in its current form. In our view, it threatens Canadian businesses, Canadian jobs and Canadian investments".
Let us move over to what the Canadian director of the Amalgamated Clothing and Textile Workers Union, John L. Alleruzzo, had to say. He said the proposed NAFTA contains three important changes to the FTA, the free trade agreement, which will accelerate the negative impact the FTA has already had on the Canadian textile and clothing industries.
First, concerning the transformation test, the FTA required that apparel producers demonstrate that they sourced fabric from either Canada or the U.S. in order to qualify for free trade rates. If they did not meet FTA content requirements they had to make use of tariff rate quotas, TRQs. Large multinational textile producers were able to deal with these provisions through relocation to the U.S., but smaller apparel producers were not.
Government Orders
Canadian manufacturers of men's fine wool clothing which imported wool from third countries were the exception. He said that one specific area of the apparel industry that was able to be successful in using the TRQs was the men's fine wool clothing sector. Although it was able to considerably increase the export of men's wool suits to the U.S. and increase its market share it still had only a minuscule share of the total market.
I could go on about the problems we have in the textile sector. I will come back a little later and read a few more instances where we have problems with NAFTA in the textile apparel industry. It is important and I think we will have the opportunity a little later on this morning to again address this issue because there will be more amendments forthcoming.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, good morning to you. It is three minutes to six on this Wednesday morning.
By the parliamentary calendar this is technically still Tuesday. However we will not bore Canadians with the technical details of why we insist that this is still Tuesday. The long and the short of it is that we have been up all night on this debate on the North American free trade agreement.
We are talking about a deal that is some 1,500 pages long. We are talking about a bill that is close to 200 pages of text and the government wants this whole thing passed unamended.
I am not one of those who is against negotiating a trilateral trade agreement between Canada, the U.S. and Mexico and I do not believe that it is the position of our party that we should not have been at that negotiating table. Our critic has been quite clear that given that we are part of a Canada-U.S. free trade deal, and have been for almost five years, whether we like it or not we would be bound by some of the decisions taken in these negotiations and therefore should be at the table to ensure that we get the best deal for Canada. However we did not get the best deal for Canada. This agreement has not been negotiated well.
Why do I say that? I say that because another party to the agreement is already negotiating amendments to the agreement which has not passed. I know Tories across the way will say that is not the NAFTA they are negotiating but parallel accords which are quite separate. One would have to be very naive to believe that.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
The Americans have said they will not sign the deal unless the parallel accords are passed to their satisfaction. Therefore they become de facto part of the same deal, whether we like it or not.
What kind of a negotiating strategy do we have here in Canada? How does passing this deal now when the Americans refuse to pass it strengthen our hand in the parallel accord discussions? It obviously does not.
The Tories think it does.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
The government obviously thinks this is just swell. I do not agree because there are plenty of things in the agreement which could be improved.
I will give an example. I was recently approached by a firm in my riding that sells steel structures. They are called steel weighed buildings and are prefabricated modular buildings that are put together to make arenas, hangars and so on.	.
This company has just been made aware of a bid in the United States, and I will read some excerpts from this invitation for bids. It states: "Invitation for bids for pre-engineered metal buildings at Fort Lewis and Yakima firing centre''. This is from the U.S army corps of engineers.
First of all, it says that this procurement is 100 percent set aside for small business. That is what the Americans are doing. That is a great idea, but one wonders. If any of us proposed to do that in the House then the government across the way would probably say that it would contravene the FTA.
Let us see what this said. Let me read clause 1.29 of this particular tender. It says: "The buy American act, section 41, provides that the government give preference to domestic end products". Is that not interesting? What if we tried to do that?
It states: "Components as used in this clause means those articles, materials and supplies incorporated directly into the end product. Domestic end product as used in this clause means: 1) an unmanufactured end product mined or produced in the United States, or 2) an end product manufactured in the United States if the cost of its components mined, produced, or manufactured in the United States exceeds 50 per cent of the cost of all its components. Components of foreign origin of the same class or kind as the product referred to in subparagraph (b)(2) of this clause shall be treated as domestic. Scrap generated, collected, or prepared for processing in the United States is considered domestic. On acquisition of above $25,000 in value, components of Canadian origin are to be treated as domestic only if they are $25,000 in value or more". That is for a component.
If one is building one of these structures using panels and putting them together not one of them would be $25,000. One could build a structure worth millions with parts that are worth at the most a few thousand dollars each. They are constructing this huge hangar for the U.S. corps of engineers using the buy American clause to get around the free trade agreement.
Right now we are negotiating NAFTA. The government says we are completing it. We are negotiating parallel accords. How come we are not getting this fixed in the parallel accords? The government says that agreement is fine as far as it is concerned. This company in my riding, and it also has an office in Aylmer, Ontario, which I believe is in southwestern Ontario, sure does not think this deal is fine. It thinks it needs to be repaired, but this government does not think so. It does not think that we need to negotiate the parallel accords in such a way as to improve those things which are otherwise deficient presently.
I disagree, and as I say, I am not one of those who is against signing a trade deal with Mexico. I am not against that per se and I am not against the fact that those deals should be signed if they are to the best advantage of Canada. I cannot swallow the argument that says that we should have never negotiated, we should not have been at the table, we should not have been there from the beginning, we should not have signed anything and so on and so forth. That is not going to change the reality that is happening around the world right now. It is not going to change the fact that the European Economic Community exists. It is not going to change the fact that the East Asian countries are forming as a trading bloc. Those are realities that are there. I do not like them but they are there.
May 25, 1993

We have the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. I did not vote for it because I thought it was poorly structured. All of the flaws in it were stated quite well at the time by the member for Vancouver Quadra and they have been proven to be true. If anything, they have been proven to be worse than anything he had predicted. That agreement obviously needs to be repaired.
It was a bad deal.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
The New Democratic member says that it was a bad deal. Yes, there were serious flaws in it. There were a few winners and many losers. Unfortunately, we have already lost many of the jobs. Couple that with the disastrous provincial government that we have in Ontario that chased so many jobs out of my riding and elsewhere south of the border. It has been a tremendous disadvantage for all of us.
I will come back later on other amendments. I want to talk about the textile industry because it affects my riding as well. There are a few winners in the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. The apparel manufacturing industry was one of those small winners, if I can call it that, but now it is going to end up losing the gains that it made in NAFTA. I want to get back later and speak about that issue. Unless what is negotiated in NAFTA is corrected it is going to be disadvantageous for my constituents as well.
How time flies. I guess I have already used up my time but I will be back to speak about this at a later opportunity.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to welcome you back to the chair this morning. In your absence we have done what a lot of executives I think would love to have the opportunity to do. So far we have created a 30-hour day. We are working on 31 and maybe we will go up to 36 if not more as we debate the amendments to the North American free trade agreement enacting legislation.
I want to deal with two of the amendments that are in this grouping because they are amendments that have a direct relationship to the area of the country that I represent which is northwestern Ontario.
The first one, Motion No. 2, is an attempt by my colleague, the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca who is the trade critic for my caucus, to ensure that within a dispute Canadian law shall be supreme. As I understand it, in the way the legislation is written it is not
Government Orders
the case. We want to ensure that Canadian law is supreme because we have found the hard way that under the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement it is written in such a way that if there is a dispute between Canada and the United States and it goes to the dispute settlement mechanism panel, all they can do is to determine whether American law has been applied appropriately. It is not whether the American law is appropriate, but just if it has been applied in the right way.
Let me relate that to my area because one of the major issues that has affected the economy of northwestern Ontario has been the softwood lumber dispute which is now still in the dispute settlement mechanism. We are waiting for yet another shoe to drop as the 90 days wind through the process in the commerce department of the United States government.
.3010
However, all through the battle we have argued and the Americans have argued that under this agreement American law prevails. In fairness let us mention the reverse too. If there is a dispute initiated by the Americans suggesting that we are doing something that is in violation of the free trade agreement the dispute settlement mechanism will determine if Canadian law applies only in Canada and not whether the law is fair.
If it was to be a proper trade agreement then one would have a mechanism that would ensure that the appropriateness of the legislation or the subsidy would be determined in that context.
In the North American free trade agreement, which is what we are debating, I want to draw attention to a comment made by the former U.S. Attorney General, Elliot Richardson. This comes from an article in The Toronto Star of February 21, 1991. Richardson noted that though the proposed law would violate the agreement, the implementing legislation states that U.S. law shall override the FTA in case of conflict. Canadian law on the other hand is subordinate to the agreement.
Let me elaborate a little bit on that. The act that was passed by the U.S. government-and I use it in the broad sense-the United States-Canada Free Trade Implementation Act of 1988, title 1, section 102, relationship of the agreement to United States law, page 1853, states: "(a) United States law is to prevail in conflict. No provisions of the agreement nor the application of any such provision to any person or circumstances which is in conflict with any law of the United States shall have effect".

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
This language is quite forthright. Canadian law however is another story. If one compares the U.S. wording as I have just described it to the weaker language provided in our Canadian counterpart then one will note the difference. The act to implement the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States of America, volume 2, schedule part A, article 103, extent of obligation on page 2 states: "The parties to this agreement shall ensure that all necessary measures are taken in order to give effect to its provisions including their observance except as otherwise provided in this agreement by state, provincial, and local governments".
Note that the exception reads only "as otherwise provided in this agreement". It does not say "except as otherwise provided in the laws of Canada or any province". It appears that any exceptions to this act are contained in the act itself. Canadian law may not be as clearly subordinate to the FTA as implied in this particular package but nowhere in the act is it stated that in the case of conflict previously enacted Canadian law prevails. I would argue that in the terms of the North American free trade implementing legislation that that is even worse.
We have seen the devastation of the softwood lumber issue in northern Ontario. We have had a number of sawmills wiped off the face of the earth. We have had a number that struggled all through that period of time and have only found themselves rejuvenated in large part because the NDP government of Ontario that my Liberal colleagues like to bash so much came in and worked with the companies, unions and communities and developed a package that provided for their survivability and their ongoing economic viability.
I would challenge any member of this House to come with me to Atikokan and visit the workers in Sapawe and ask them who came to their aid. The Liberals did not do it when they were in government in Ontario. The Government of Canada, the Conservative government, did not come to their aid. We got nothing from them other than a few letters that said that it was looking at it. In the meantime the Ontario government acted and protected those jobs and in fact the sawmills in northwestern Ontario are expanding their operations as we speak because of the assistance applied to them by the Ontario government.
I want to deal with the second issue. Motion No. 6 standing in the name of my colleague from Esquimau- Juan de Fuca deals with the question of water. We have had a number of debates about water in the House over the last eight, nine or ten hours as we have debated through the night. However I want to put it into historical context again from the area of northwestern Ontario that I represent.
One of my earliest exposures to the question of interbasin water transfers was by a group called Damn the Dams. In the late 1950s or early 1960s the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers was doing survey work throughout northwestern Ontario and looking for ways in which to divert the fresh water of northern Ontario south of the border. That campaign was led by a very remarkable lady, Millie Barrett, who has now passed on. She fought along with community groups throughout the northwest to chase the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers back across the border.
We do have some diversions in place. We have the Algoki-Longlac diversion which diverts water into Lake Superior. I cannot remember the correct name, but there is a canal or a channel in Chicago that diverts some water from the Great Lakes into the Mississippi system. It is highly regulated. It cannot be used for anything other than the sanitation purposes for which it was provided. However there is a real danger with the water thirsty southern United States, whether it be for agricultural purposes or for maritime commerce purposes. Those ol us who sat on the transport committee and dealt with a Seaway subcommittee report know the very real threat that the Mississippi water system has for the movement of grain, the movement of bulk products south of the border as opposed to east and west.
It is extremely important. In spite of what the government says we need to put in place enabling legislation with very clear wording that there shall be no interbasin transfers of water under the NAFTA.

Madam Speaker, I would like to continue on the point made by my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell earlier this evening. He brought to the attention of the House and Canadians something I believe will emerge as a real deal breaker on the free trade agreement. He talked about his constituent, Steelway Building Systems, that
May 25, 1993

sent him this information. It had to do with an invitation for bids for pre-engineered metal buildings.
It is interesting that on the cover of the bid the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has this bold face statement: "This procurement is 100 per cent set aside for small business". I think that is a good idea. I wish all our bids at all levels of government, whether federal, provincial or municipal, had a clearly defined program where procurement would be 100 per cent set aside for small business.
Then we get into the body of the tender. The Army Corps of Engineers refers to the buy America act and states: "The buy America act provides that the government give preference to domestic end products".
On the face of it we would say that because of the free trade agreement and a national treatment clause Canadian small businesses would have the same treatment as U.S. companies. Therefore what is the big deal?
We then get into the further description of the bid. It reads that on components if the acquisition value is above 25 per cent then the Canadian company is treated as a domestic. Each individual component must be above $25,000 but under $25,000 the company would not be eligible to bid on these contracts.
This is a perfect example of how the Americans are getting away with the free trade agreement advantages. They are really showing that it is a disadvantage for Canadian small businesses. This is the type of thing that causes us in the Liberal Party to say time out to the free trade agreement as well as NAFTA. Roll the car back.
The current trade agreement is filled with many flaws and so many issues that need to be cleared up and here is one that affects small business. The government has stated repeatedly that small business is where we have the greatest hope for new job creation. Here is a perfect example of where the free trade agreement is not really going to work for small business.
Certainly when it comes to the buy America policy, how many businesses are building products with component parts having a value in excess of $25,000 a compo-
Govemment Orders
nent? An individual component part must have a value in excess of $25,000. That is the only way one can become eligible under the buy America preference plan. It rules out a whole sector of our economy in relation to the free trade agreement that we were hoping would be the greatest source of our revival for new jobs.
How can the government not be concerned about an issue like this? How can it not be concerned about similar problems in this hastily negotiated NAFTA?
Earlier in this House today I raised another point in relation to NAFTA in the area of the environment and harmful production processes. There are definitely environmental wrongdoings. A process may be wrong but because it is separate from the actual product, the product can have a free flow. It can be exported or imported.
In other words, a product can be made in Mexico with an environmental process that is definitely harmful but because the actual product itself is not environmentally harmful it can be exported. That is wrong. That means in any business when we talk about being competitive we talk about the cost of doing business not just in relation to labour.
I am not even going to make something of the fact that we have child labour and wages at $1.50 or $2 an hour. When a plant is put up where the land costs and infrastructure costs are practically nil-I am talking about Mexico right now-and there are no worries about the environmental process being deficient, where is the level playing field?
Businesses here have to live with municipal environmental standards or provincial environmental standards at the process level. If we have plants in our ridings where the process is wrong, we shut them down. We do not care if the product itself is environmentally friendly. We are not even going to let a business make that product unless the plant and its process are correct. When that process is correct we will allow that product to be made and exported anywhere in the world.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
Under the NAFTA the process can be environmentally deficient as long as the actual product is environmentally friendly. The product can be exported and we have to take it in, even if the whole environmental process is deficient.
That is a serious flaw in NAFTA. I cannot imagine a member of parliament in the Conservative Party who could go into any high school or grade school or talk to any of their kids and say to just write off the process.
What about acid rain?
Just write off the process. The member from Cambridge says: "What about weather?"
Are we going to close INCO?
Are we going to close INCO? No.
As well as the acid rain from Sudbury?

No, no. Hold it. That is a perfect example of why we have to take time out here. If the member wants to refer to INCO, let me tell him about INCO.
Six years ago INCO came up with a technology that it spent about a half a billion dollars on, which helped clean up that plant. It now exports that technology. In fact, that technology is making more on exports than the actual operating company. That is the point I am trying to make.
We have a chance in this country because of our commitment to the environment to export our environmental technology and make sure the Mexicans and others have our standards. Why are we lowering ourselves to their standards?
Even the Americans, even A1 Gore and President Clinton are saying time out. This is not working. This deal is not committed to an environmental principle to save the planet. Here we are in the middle of the night because the government is afraid to debate this and we are jamming it through. It is wrong.

Madam Speaker, it pleases me to have this opportunity at this hour of the morning to get up and indicate my feelings about these particular motions relative to the North American free trade agreement.
I will start by speaking on Motion No. 2 which states:
That Bill C-115 be amended by adding immediately after line 45,
at page 3, the following new clause:
"3.1 Canadian Laws to Prevail in Conflict. No provision of the Agreement, nor the application of any such provision to any person or circumstances, which is in conflict with any law of the United States shall have effect."
In other words all we are asking is that our law have the same weight in this agreement as does U.S. law. By putting this particular clause in, the Americans made it possible for them to absolutely control the structure. Any U.S. law has effect. It says so in the U.S. implementation act of 1988. We are suggesting that maybe we, the Canadian people, the Canadian government should have the same kind of power over this particular act.
In Motions Nos. 4 and 5 we are also asking to have the ability to process our products before we ship them. That
is,	we want to keep those products here long enough to do something with them. The present act does not allow us to do that.
Even if we passed a law saying that we will not ship anything out of Canada which is not processed, we could not do that under this act because we do not have the kind of legislative structure which would allow us to do
it.	The U.S. could do it. It is in the act at the moment and the Conservative government accepted that.
We have accepted very little of what the Conservative government put in these acts in the sense that they basically sold out our right to develop our economy. We as a party believe that trade is very important to Canada, but trade under circumstances which give us the power to develop and the ability to develop our economy within the structure that we believe should be in place.
With Motion No. 2 we wish to put into the act the fact that Canadian laws are to prevail in conflict. Anytime we get into a disagreement with the United States we apply the laws of Canada just as they now apply their own laws when they get into conflict.
One of the big things that has affected us in the agricultural industry has been the export enhancement policy of the United States. The Americans have put millions of dollars from their treasury into the sale of grains particularly, but other products as well.
What has affected the farmers most in Canada has been the export enhancement program which spends millions of dollars on selling the grain. Because of the way it is set up, this particular enhancement does not necessarily go directly to the farmer. We cannot call it a farm or an agricultural subsidy directly. What it does do is make sure that a company in the United States buys the grain from the farmer at a particular price and sells it
May 25, 1993

to another country, say Algeria. Then the farmers get some subsidization at the price that they get but the company that sells the grain then can add as much as the total price of the grain initially.
The lowest they have sold grain as far as I know, and it may have gone lower, was a couple of years ago. Under the export enhancement program United States companies sold to Norway a number of tonnes of wheat for $52 a tonne. Nobody in the United States or Canada could possibly raise wheat at $52 a tonne. What the Norwegians paid was $52 a tonne, but what the company got after paying the farmer was probably another $50 a tonne.
Therefore the companies made their money anyway. It did not matter to the corporation that was selling the grain into the Norwegian market that this price was lower than the possible production of the grain. It did not matter to the U.S. corporation or the U.S. that in the process they were undercutting the EEC market which I guess was its intention in the first place. It was also affecting the Norwegian market in such a way that it was almost worthless to try to grow wheat. Surprisingly, Norway grows a considerable amount of cereal grains.
The farmer finds himself competing against an almost limitless U.S. treasury. There is no way that the Canadian farmer or the Canadian government can fight the almost unlimited funds available to the U.S. treasury. Not only are the funds seemingly unlimited, but it does not bother the Americans at all to go deeply into debt.
The United States has had deficit situations for many years and it continues to do so. A good portion of that deficit has been its expenditures on export enhancement. Therefore the farmers are affected directly by legislation which the United States has in place.
We can shout as much as we want about this export enhancement being unfair and we have. We have shouted about it. We have told them that it is unfair, but the U.S. application of the free trade agreement is that United States law is to prevail in any conflict. The United States can point to this and say that its law says it can provide export enhancement.
Government Orders
This export enhancement has led to the devastation of the cereal grain industry in Canada. It has not just led to the fact that we are having difficulty penetrating certain markets now. It has not led to the fact that in some areas of the world we are unable to celebrate at all because we cannot match the low prices that the export enhancement brings.
I would challenge any farmer to produce wheat at $120 a tonne because that is very low, but the fellow who sells it for the United States gets another $50 enhancement. He is sure to make a profit so it does not matter whether he sells it at a much lower price. He could sell it at $50 a tonne and still make some money. How has that affected the farmer directly? It has been devastating. As I have pointed out, it has affected the price of wheat which means the operation of the farm is in jeopardy.
Also, in my community probably 30 or 40 per cent of the farmers have lost their land. They are now out of farming entirely. Not myself particularly but many of the other farmers are picking up the slack. In my own case, I had a farmer who was working my land tell me the other day: "I am sorry. I can no longer afford to farm your land. You will have to farm it yourself". He was helping me out but it was costing him too much.
This is the kind of change we need to put in place. We need to be sure that we give our own country an opportunity to develop its economy even as we trade with different parts of the world.

Madam Speaker, I must say that I am delighted to be here with so many of my colleagues to participate in this important debate.
May I say that I think the Speaker has done a tremendous job of maintaining a rather excellent decorum in this place despite the great heat that has been generated because of the importance of this debate.
I walked in a few minutes ago having just watched on television the tremendous speech by the member for Broadview-Greenwood, pouring out his heart and his passion for Canada. I wondered what could possibly bring the government to force this kind of debate on Canadians at this eleventh hour.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
Outside on Parliament Hill I watched a flock of pigeons trotting across the road. I thought to myself that those pigeons had more sense of self-determination, more sense of worth, more ability to make a decision than members opposite who blindly follow this path of pushing this bill upon the Parliament of Canada at the eleventh hour as some kind of senseless monument to a leader who is departing in a few days. They are trying to force this bill on Parliament at the last second, authorizing the North American free trade agreement in advance of side deals even being negotiated. They are asking us to pass judgment on the North American free trade agreement before we even know what is going to be in it.
Parliamentarians and government members opposite have completely divested themselves in the dying days of this administration of any sense of responsibility in undertaking their duties as members of Parliament. Even a pigeon knows it is time to fly the coop when it has been fouled. Not so members opposite.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Not so with the bird-brains across the way.

Not so, as my colleague says, with the bird-brains across the way.
If it were not so serious it would perhaps be humorous, but there is nothing humorous in what is going on. Canadians have to know that the only reason members have been here all night long and this most distinguished Deputy Speaker has occupied the Chair all night long is that parliamentarians have flocked to this place.
I hate to use the word. I hate to borrow the example from south of the border but this is the Canadian Alamo. A handful of parliamentarians are standing and mounting the barricades in the face of this onslaught against responsible democracy.
How many Canadians recognize and realize what process is under way here today? How many Canadians understand that 295 members of Parliament are being asked to cast judgment on a trade arrangement that is not yet negotiated?
How many Canadians understand that in the United States Congress the legitimate elected representatives of the people of the United States are not seized with this
issue because the Americans have not yet finished negotiating?
How many people understand that what we are doing in this place now and the only reason we are here is to try to bring a sense of sanity to the megalomania that drives the decisions opposite?
Why are we here? Why are we considering a trade deal that is not yet negotiated? In Ottawa last week trade negotiators to the three countries failed to provide, as President Clinton says he wants, a new definition for the environmental code and a labour code. Why a week later are we here in Canada seeking to rush a trade deal through Parliament that was the subject of a failed negotiating exercise last week? Why?
There is only one reason. It is not a negotiating tactic. That makes no sense. We are not being asked to cast judgment on a finished document. That is not the case. Why? This exercise is more boarish than the hunting expedition the Prime Minister took in Russia a few weeks ago.
This is an attempt by a Prime Minister driven by his own visions of grandeur and his own delusions of greatness to finish his agenda in advance of his departure from the office of Prime Minister, which is coming none too soon for the people of Canada.
How outrageous it is. How without precedent is it in the annals of Canadian parliamentary history for sober, serious, responsible, dedicated and interested parliamentarians to be asked to consider something as substantial and important to the future of the country as a comprehensive trade deal with our largest trading partner and with a smaller, but becoming more important, trade partner, Mexico, in advance of having a finished deal on the table.
Is there one lonely Canadian out there who, against all of his or her better instincts and the experience of the last eight or nine years, clings on with shattered fingernails against the slick mausoleum of reality; who believes this government has changed; who believes the leadership campaign across the way represents renewal; who believes that some sense of conscience or responsibility has been restored to the party opposite, the Progressive
May 25, 1993

Conservative Party of Canada? That is an oxymoron if there ever was one.
If there is one lonely last Canadian standing on the bill of Cape St. George, facing the Atlantic Ocean, seeing the storm brewing and believing there has really been change, this bucket of cold water, this so-called exercise in democracy that has been slapped across the face of Canadians will bring that last lonely, foolish Canadian- if there is one-to his or her senses. There are no enemies of Canada. There are no ordinary Canadians in their T-shirts, beer in hand, as described by certain people opposite, notably the minister of defence.
There are no sons of Bs, there are only sons of Ps and daughters of Ps, of pioneers who built this country, founded upon the principle of democracy. There are no Canadians who can be purchased at $50,000 a pop, as slick, manipulative advertising consultants. There are only Canadians who recognize that their institution-not ours as we are temporary custodians at best-their Parliament has been hijacked. It has been made subject to a foolish, last, twisted, misguided, egotistical grasp by a departing Prime Minister who feels power slipping away. It is a vain exercise on the part of that individual. It is a corrosive exercise in the context of Canadian democracy.
If this government has any sense whatsoever it will withdraw this bill. It will accord not the members on the opposition benches, not the Liberals or the New Democrats, but Canadians the basic respect for their intelligence.
Madam Speaker, would you buy a car without seeing it? I know you would not. Would you sign up for insurance without reading the fine print? Would you sign a mortgage without knowing what the details were in the mortgage? You would do none of those things. Madam Speaker. I know that if you were not constrained by the steely cage and the total impartiality of that chair you would be on your feet rebelling as instinct would tell you to do to save this democracy.
My time is up and so is the time of this government. It will happen as soon as it has the gall and the courage to
Government Orders
ask the people of Canada to cast judgment on this shameful act and call an election. The sooner the better.

Madam Speaker, I rise to debate some of the amendments that are proposed at this stage of the free trade agreement debate.
Bill C-115 intends to implement the North American free trade agreement. There is no way to stop the agreement at this stage. What we are doing here is simply trying to make amendments which at this stage deal with the interpretation of the agreement.
We are trying to make a bad deal more acceptable at this stage. Later we can debate it at third and final reading and try to defeat the whole package. Right now we are simply trying to make a bad deal more acceptable.
There are four motions in the grouping that we are dealing with here, Motions Nos. 2, 4, 5 and 6.1 will spend a few moments going through the reasons why we think there should be some amendments made.
The first one proposes to amend the proposed act so that Canadian laws may prevail where there is conflict. This simply says:
No provision of the Agreement, nor the application of any such
provision to any person or circumstances, which is in conflict with any
law of Canada shall have effect".
Those are fairly strong words. Why is it there? It is there simply because similar wording is there on the American side. It states quite clearly that no clause in the agreement shall have effect over the American law.
In other words this three-nation agreement cannot supersede American law. That is the nub of the whole problem I have had with the idea of international trade agreements with the Americans that the government has been pushing for the last five or six years.
The government misjudged the effect of a smaller economy trying to get equal treatment with an economy 10 or 11 times larger. Politicians might make that error since they have very little business experience in the front benches of the Conservative government. However being politicians they should definitely not have missed that the American Constitution is quite a different document from the one we are used to operating with. Our Canadian Constitution is based on practice in the United Kingdom which uses a much different foundation

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
for the establishment of laws than the United States Congress.
By its constitution, the Congress of the United States can, may and is required in cases to have power over the President in the signing of international agreements. It does not matter what the President and his or her administration might decide to sign. In the final analysis at the time of the signing or any time in the future, the U.S. Congress has the right by the Constitution of the United States of America to overturn that.
It does not matter what we sign with them. It is only as good as the current Congress decides it should be.
While I can forgive the leaders of the government for having been so naive as to have missed the consequences of the economics of a closer union with the United States I cannot forgive them for being so stupid as to have missed that vital difference in power that the U.S. Constitution gives the U.S. Congress.
That is because there is no way in the future that this country will have an equal trading arrangement with the United States of America simply because Congress can override the agreement at any time the Congress so desires.
We have had many instances of this with the implementation of the Canada-U.S. agreement. I think that experience is pertinent because the North American free trade agreement uses the same foundations to extend the agreement into Mexico and to include three countries in the agreement.
We have seen the constant and continuing disputes over softwood lumber. It was not initiated by any reason of unfair practice on the Canadian side. It was probably initiated because the Canadian dollar fell and we became as a result more competitive in the United States. The problems arose because producers of softwood lumber in the United States put political pressure on their congressmen and initiated the countervail actions that are now history. Eventually we work our way through them.
I might remind us that before this agreement we used to work our way through the agreements. We would work our way through any international disputes on the
myriad of commodities that had no duties between ourselves and the United States and we managed.
We are still managing, but this agreement has not made it a whole lot easier. It is not going to get any easier with the extension to include the country of Mexico because the U.S. Constitution stays the same as it has always been. We will always be at a disadvantage in dealing internationally with a country that has the power that it has given itself or taken by members of their Congress to override the international agreements that the President might sign.
This particular amendment one might call an equitable clause. It simply says that where there is a dispute then Canadian law shall apply. It is the same as American law that now applies any time there is a dispute. Motion No. 4 says:
Nothing in this Act or the Agreement shall be interpreted so as to prohibit a Party to the Agreement from requiring another Party to the Agreement to process raw materials or raw resources before exporting such materials or resources.
Again, our experience in the last four and a half years with the Canada-U.S. agreement has shown that the U.S. Congress has been able to force Canada, one of the signing parties of that agreement, to make decisions that are not necessarily in our best interests. There is one that talks about raw products whether it is raw logs, raw fish or raw anything. We have been required on a number of occasions to ship raw product into the United States in order to "comply with the agreement".
The one that I recall most notably was the raw fish dispute that occurred on the west coast. Canada recognized that we were having some difficulty maintaining fish stocks, particularly salmon stocks. In order to count the catch and to regulate the catch so that we would know whether we were in fact overfishing or keeping the fishing levels at a level where the stock could regenerate itself, we had required that all catches in Canadian waters had to be landed in Canada to be weighed. Because they were already landed to be weighed and measured they were usually processed here.
After taking that law or that practice to the international disputes settling mechanism the United States insisted upon and won the right to take raw fish out of Canada and process it in the United States.
May 25, 1993

Not only did we lose the sovereign right to manage our own resources, but we watched as fish processing jobs went south of the border to Oregon and Washington.
There are two more motions as well but I see you are giving me the time signal, Madam Speaker. I understand that my time is up. I would urge members to support all four of these motions. They were put forward as a means of demonstrating that Canada could have negotiated a more equitable agreement. We do not think that the whole process of the agreement in the first place was a very smart move, but if we are into it then we could at least at this stage make it a more equitable and more fair agreement. These four motions I recommend highly to the government members and to the rest of the House because I think they would go some way to achieving that.

Madam Speaker, it is seven o'clock a.m. Eastern Daylight Time. This debate has gone all night. I have to ask myself why it is that this government has forced Parliament into sitting all night. Why is it that through the dead of night this government has forced the debate on this? Why is it that the government has not allowed the people of Canada to scrutinize this agreement in the hard, cold light of day?
Is it because it is afraid of what is in that agreement? Is it because the people of Canada do not want the agreement and the government is trying to sneak it through like a pack of bandits in the dead of night? It is because the total sovereignty of this nation is at stake within the North American free trade agreement?
I would suggest that it is probably all of those things. It has not allowed full debate at second reading. It closed off debate through closure after fewer than six hours. Did it allow the committee to proceed across Canada to talk to the people of Canada and and find what they thought about the North American free trade agreement? Was there an explanation of what was in this agreement?
No, it did not do this. It allowed a few people to come in, some of its friends and associates, to talk a little bit about the North American free trade agreement. It did not allow any open debate across Canada. It did not even allow the provision of the agreement in the libraries across the country. We in our party supplied the libraries
Government Orders
in our areas with copies of the North American free trade agreement so that the people could see what is in it. This government would not do it.
This agreement is about the loss of sovereignty of Canadians and the loss of many of the things that we as Canadians have held near and dear. First it was the free trade agreement and all that went with it. There was the erasure of the border between Canada and the United States. I would suggest that this now furthers the erosion of the sovereignty of Canada.
If we look at some of the motions that my friend and colleague for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca has put forward then we will see at least some attempt to salvage some of what Canadians have been telling us. I am pleased that the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca has stayed here all night. He has been up on Parliament Hill and has been here in the House for the last many hours awaiting his chance to put forward further amendments and motions on this matter.
One of the amendments that the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca wants is to ensure that Canadian laws prevail in any conflict. When I talk about the loss of sovereignty I refer specifically to that. What is it when we get in a conflict? Are we to be guided by the provisions of United States laws or can we be guided by our own? This amendment ensures that Canadian laws prevail in a conflict. "No provision of this agreement nor the application of any such provision to any person or circumstances, which is in conflict with any law of Canada shall have effect."
It shows that we can turn to the laws of Canada. That is in some doubt in the present presentation under section 3 of the NAFTA implementation agreement. What do we turn to in the event of a conflict? We have heard speaker after speaker tonight talk about that very problem in this agreement. That is not all that troubles us.
Motion No. 6, which the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca proposed, attempts to protect our water within the agreement. We have heard it time and time again from the members of the government that water is not an issue, that it is not included in the agreement. Yet it would be so easy to simply put in a provision, as there is with softwood lumber, as there is with processed fish from the east coast and Quebec, saying specifically that

Government Orders
the export of water is not included in the agreement between Canada and the United States and Mexico.
The amendment that is proposed states as follows in subsection (2):
Notwithstanding subsection (1), nothing in this Act or the
Agreement applies to any water transported by a pipeline or diverted
by reason of diversion of a river.
We know there are all sorts of diversionary plans. In British Columbia, for instance, one plan is to divert the North Thompson into the Columbia River basin, take the water down and export it by pipeline from the south end of the Columbia River into the dry belt of California and Mexico.
The NAWAPA, the North American Water and Power Alliance, has proposed to flood the whole Rocky Mountain trench, diverting all the rivers into that and exporting the water.
It goes on and on, the diversion in the Columbia River Treaty and the question of the sovereignty of British Columbia and Canada with respect to water. Within that agreement, signed in 1964, we lost the right to ensure that we can govern our own water resources.
In that agreement we set out that we must provide flood control essentially into perpetuity. As long as those three dams on the Columbia River that were in the agreement-the Duncan, the Keenleyside and the Mica dams-are standing, we must provide 8.5 million acre feet of flood control for the Americans. I say that is not good enough. We have to specifically exclude that.
Motion No. 4 is one I am quite interested in with respect to the processing of raw materials and raw resources for export. We have to provide jobs for future generations and we must do it by ensuring that we have value added production. We have to ensure that the Americans and the Mexicans are not allowed to process our raw materials, that we are not simply the miners and the hewers of wood, the drawers of water. We must not export the raw materials down into Mexico where there is cheap labour for the furtherance of jobs in those areas.
We have to look at the value added production of those areas and we have to ensure that jobs are looked after for our future generations.
With that in mind, I read into the record clause 3.1:
Nothing in this Act or the Agreement shall be interpreted so as to prohibit a Party to the Agreement from requiring another Party to the Agreement to process raw materials or raw resources before exporting such materials and resources.
At this time I would like to propose an amendment to Motion No. 4 as follows:
That Motion No. 4, as it appears under Notices of Motions pursuant to Standing Order 76(2) dated May 25,1993, be amended by deleting after the word "requiring" the words "another party to the agreement" and inserting in their place the words "commercial entities within its sovereign territory".

Madam Speaker, I want to speak directly to the amendment to my motion by giving a bit of history of its importance.
Some months ago the members for Okanagan-Simil-kameen-Merritt, Prince George-Bulkley Valley, Kamloops and Okanagan-Shuswap, four members from the interior of the province of British Columbia, visited Washington, D.C., relative to gathering information vis-a-vis the American intentions on the softwood lumber dispute.
Just before the provincial election in British Columbia the federal government had arbitrarily removed itself from the agreement it had established with the United States of America that had imposed a 15 per cent tariff on softwood lumber. The timing of that to some of us was directly related to the connection between the government of the day in Ottawa and the government of the day then in British Columbia, the Social Credit government, in an attempt to bolster its re-election chances.
The import of the removal of that unnecessary and ill-founded surcharge on Canadian softwood lumber was politically motivated at the time and left the Americans with the position of immediately slapping back that 6 per cent which actually was what it was reduced to.
My colleagues who I mentioned went to the United States to raise this matter in conversation with and for the information of the American officials. They were told at that time the Americans needed the tariff to protect their softwood lumber even though technically it was a violation of the protection we should have had allegedly from this government on the free trade agree-

ment. However, with more than a wink and a nudge my colleagues were told that should the Government of British Columbia lift its ban on the export of whole logs it would be received as a welcome sign that the Government of British Columbia was prepared to make a deal. Therefore there would no longer be a barrier as far as the Americans could see in putting up the 6 per cent against softwood lumber.
This was all contrary to the free trade agreement, leverage known as bullying and with no protection left even under the free trade agreement for the Government of British Columbia and ultimately the people of this country to protect resources and to use them in value added and secondary or tertiary processes as the government of the day or as industry, as the particular amendment points out, may want to do in terms of maximizing its capital investment. Maximizing their capital investment would employ more Canadians. It was a goal shared rashly by most economists in this country, that every step of value added in terms of secondary and tertiary development coming out of capital investment, whether it is private or public, benefits the well-being of this nation.
What we are asking for in this amendment is the simple permission for the Canadian people through their provincial governments to establish self-determination vis-a-vis maximizing the use of resources.
My good friend, the member for Okanagan-Similka-meen-Merritt, has made a valid point in amending our amendment. By doing so he focused on a serious problem both in a general sense and a particular sense that there is no policy by this government as exposed in the agreement it has signed to ensure there are more jobs in Canada for Canadians out of Canadian resources.
The government has signed a deal that does not permit us to be masters in our own house, maitres chez nous, in determining how we want to develop our resources in terms of secondary and tertiary investment and secondary and tertiary job creation out of that investment.
Government Orders
Did the government do this consciously? If it did, it stands to be condemned. Did the government sign this without knowing what it was signing? That would even be worse. It is a fact that frequently for the last year in Question Period I have stood in this Chamber to ask for sector-by-sector studies by the government on the North American free trade agreement relative to the use of resources both in terms of capital investment and in terms of labour potential.
Not once in the House has any member seen a single sector-by-sector study that should have been done by the government before it signed the agreement. Not only is this Chamber being asked to ram through a bill before the drafts are even completed for the U.S. Congress, but this Chamber and the Canadian people are being asked to blindly endorse a deal. Not a single bit of evidence in terms of sector-by-sector studies vis-a-vis the impact of the application of secondary and tertiary labour has been available to the House.
Where are the studies on oil, gas and energy? Where are the studies on labour? Where are the studies on the forest industry? Where are the studies on fisheries? None have been presented. Excellent points have been made by the members of the opposition and of the government. Not a single government backbencher has an amendment.
All those points were not been made around the fact that the bill is being rammed through but that there has been no information provided. I asked department after department as they appeared before the committee to give us the sectoral studies. If they were done they have been kept secret. If they have not been done then the government is being condemned for not doing them.
How could this government and a minister who has not been here for a single minute of this debate ask-

Oh, oh.

speechtext: Just a moment, please. It would be wise for both sides of the House to avoid referring to the presence or the absence of members or ministers during debate.

Madam Speaker, naturally tempers get flared after this long in the House. If I have offended the rules of the House I withdraw. However, I will say that since the debate started there still has not been presented to the House one sector-by-sector study. Do they exist? I ask the government this simple question: Do those studies exist? They do not.
With everything I have been involved in during this debate I believe the government has actually gone into the signing of this agreement without doing sectoral studies. I ask the government to prove me wrong, to prove to the Canadian people that every sector covered by this amendment in terms of the right for value added was thoroughly examined before it signed the deal.
I do not believe it has been done. There has been not one shred of evidence that with all the billions of dollars necessarily spent by a government in maintaining department after department relative to sectors of the resources a single penny was spent on doing sectoral studies.
How many thousands of jobs are slipping away because of the lack of that research? How many thousands of jobs and how many small businesses are at risk because that value added work was not done? How many Canadians are now out there looking at their sons and daughters who cannot find work and do not know that the attempt to maximize the job potential of those resources was not even initiated by studies by this government? How many people waiting in line at a food bank who are not members of government staff and are expecting to have jobs know where to train for the opportunity to even rationally look in a sector that is potentially developing because of this agreement?
How can the government say that it is initiating training programs to accommodate this agreement when it does not know on which areas to focus in those training programs because the sector studies were not done?
I appreciate that my 10 minutes are up. However an important point has been made here tonight by this very limited debate. It has exposed layer by layer the stupidity and incompetence or culpability of this government in
ramming this bill through. There is no explanation. Let the Canadian people understand how blind, how pitifully weak and how this government has totally sold us out in this kind of legislation.

Madam Speaker, I begin by complimenting the member for Esquimau-Juan de Fuca on the point he has made about the analysis. However I want to say to him at the same time I disagree with his comments that I heard on the radio a few minutes ago. He did not really feel there was much benefit to this debate.
At the time I made that statement I did not think so.

He indicated that it would not accomplish much. I disagree. We may not be accomplishing much in terms of causing the government to listen today or tomorrow, but I believe the point he just made is an important one for all Canadians to be aware of. When we go to the people for accountability 12 weeks from now I believe the government will be out of business partly as a result of our determination in the last 24 hours to bring it to the attention of Canadians. There may be only a few right now but there are some substantive flaws in this particular agreement.
I want to build on the point that the hon. member just made. I cannot believe for a second that all of these corporations that are moving and setting up in Mexico, whether it be Northern Telecom, General Motors, the Magna, or the Volkswagen, that these transnational or multinational corporations are not doing research and that they are not putting forward proper business plans which they take back to their boards for approval.
There is absolutely no way that General Motors would be investing hundreds of millions of dollars in a country which is not exactly stable in terms of its over-all business practice. It would not be doing this unless there was some cost benefit analysis. It is just not common business practice to go and make these investments without having the approval of the board of directors. It is that fundamental.
I support what the member from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca is saying. We are the nation's boardroom and we are asking the government to show us the sector by sector analysis of the cost benefit to Canada and Canadians. We want to see the analysis that the government must have.
May 25, 1993

A decision cannot be made that is going to affect the entire fiscal framework of a nation without having some kind of analysis. It is like doing a budget without crunching the numbers in finance. It is like making a commitment on social policy without knowing what it is going to cost. It is just not done.
The government should bring those sectoral analyses forward. What is the cost benefit analysis in terms of the automotive industry of this country? What are the benefits? What are the costs? We have to know that.
In my community we just lost the first complete assembly plant in Canada's history, the Scarborough van plant. The amendment before us and the subamendment to Motion No. 4 says nothing in this act or agreement shall be interpreted so as to prohibit a party to the agreement from requiring commercial entities within its sovereign territory to process raw materials or raw resources before exporting such materials or resources.
This is a very important amendment because the history of Canada in many ways has been to try to build a nation where we process our resources within this nation. In the past we have been disproportionately dependent on raw resources. Eighty per cent of our wheat and coarse grains shipped internationally are unprocessed. It is top quality, but not made into biscuits or other food that is edible, but shipped in the raw. Or it may be lumber that is shipped in the round log, or in coarse lumber.
This proposed amendment really spells out that we should maintain the ability of Canada to process its raw resources. Those of us who come from resource sectors of the country, whether it is in western Canada or northern Ontario or Atlantic or northern Quebec or some of the other parts of the country, are very conscious of this because all kinds of blocks have been put in our way.
For instance, in my constituency we have the uranium mines at Elliot Lake. That whole industry collapsed in 1959 when the United States Atomic Energy Commission cancelled the contracts for further purchase of uranium from Elliot Lake. We had some 13 producing uranium mines there which had expanded dramatically during the last half of the 1950s. Those contracts were snuffed out in 1959.
It is interesting that during that period of the 1950s the United States was demanding more and more uranium. As soon as those contracts to take our uranium were cancelled in 1959, laws were brought in the United States whereby they would not take any Canadian uranium because the demand for the nuclear weapons program was fulfilled. They were looking after their own electrical generating plants by preventing any Canadian uranium.
We are in this motion before the House trying to ensure that Canadians have the opportunity to process whatever resources they have in this country, and are not
subjected to pressure under this agreement to prevent that. There is the obvious example in British Columbia of round logs being sold to the United States rather than being made into lumber, materials, desks, furniture or whatever.
I believe the example which is going to be coming to the fore in the next decade is the whole question of the production of ethanol on the prairies. I think it gives the greatest opportunity for diversification that I can think of in the prairie region. We know the western sedimentary basin has been a tremendous resource in terms of natural gas. There are still great reserves there.
When we move over to crude oil, we will find that by the middle of this decade some 500,000 barrels a day of light sweet crude will have to be imported into this country. That represents almost one-third of our petroleum demand.
As we move toward a more environmentally sustainable economy and environment, we should be moving toward the use of ethanol. In fact, in many parts of the United States the old petroleum industry is being supplanted with some 5 per cent or 10 per cent of ethanol being used in automotive fuels. That is not only possible if you are in Canada, it is desirable. If we are spending billions of dollars importing 500,000 barrels a day of crude oil from offshore, then we certainly should be moving to supplant some 10 per cent of our automotive petroleum needs through the use of ethanol. It provides for great diversification of the prairie economy.
Last year about this time I had a chance to visit a plant in Lanigan, Saskatchewan, some 70 miles east of Saskatoon. That plant utilizes one million bushels of feed wheat. It produces 10 million litres of ethanol a year. It has on feed something like 18,000 head of cattle. That is going to be expanded to some 40,000 head of cattle.
This is the kind of diversification and further processing of our raw resources that we need, in this case our wheat, barley, and other grains to do really two or three things. First of all, to diversify that economy, get the value-added, provide a more environmentally acceptable fuel for our gas and for our automotive fuel supplies, and utilize that production that is available.

The North American free trade agreement expands this so that now the food market in particular can probably be serviced as a processed product from the United States into Mexico and into Canada. All we are doing is cementing the ability of these multinational agribusiness companies to cement their hold on the marketplace.
One of the telling signs in all of this is that one of the largest multinational agribusiness corporations operating in Canada now, Cargill Inc., has already moved to establish a plant in Mexico in order to be able to utilize some of the raw product out of Canada and the United States to be processed in Mexico at much reduced prices and then sold back into our marketplace.
We are going to be reduced to a consumer society with no funds with which to purchase those consumable goods. Agribusiness and the multinational corporations by pursuing this strategy may find that eventually they have bought themselves right out of a market. That is some time down the road and we as Canadian producers and workers are going to be the ones who will pay the price in the meantime.

The subamendment simply reads: "Nothing in this act or the agreements shall be interpreted so as to prohibit a party to the agreement from requiring commercial entities within its sovereign territory to process raw materials or raw resources before exporting such materials or resources".
Essentially what we are saying is that Canada should be able to require that some product be supported for processing and manufacturing within Canada and that we not be penalized if in fact we try to do that.
We take a look at the North American free trade agreement on another aspect and this becomes more important. That is when we realize that the North American free trade agreement actually prohibits a buy Canadian type of a program in this country. When we cannot even get into a program that is going to promote Canadian products within Canadian territory, how are we ever going to protect fledgling industries in rural communities where investments are not great from developing, particularly industries that have a lot to do with the resources?
Over the last year I have done a fair bit of study on the economy of Saskatchewan. I would like to put on the record some of the things I found out about the Saskatchewan economy. It will be seen how important value added processing is going to be to the future of communities like those within my constituency boundaries, the smaller communities where we have to take agricultural products and own them for a little longer in the process in order to achieve greater returns at the farm gate.
Agriculture makes up about 14 per cent of the over-all economic activity in the province of Saskatchewan. In terms of that 14 per cent of activities for agriculture, this is the highest of any province in Canada. Prince Edward Island is second in terms of its agriculture production. Agriculture is the single biggest contributor of any economic activity in the province of Saskatchewan.
Of the farm cash receipts to date, 50 per cent comes from wheat, 18 per cent from cattle, 11 per cent from canola and 6 per cent from the other groups, the barleys, the peas and oats. The industry has diversified over the years. In 1951 we were seeding 23.7 million acres and in 1991, we were seeding 33.3 million acres.
Wheat has gone from 64 per cent of the crops sown to 52 per cent of the crops sown today. Specialty crops and canola for example really is the area which has benefited the most from diversification on the prairies. Canola went from virtually no production a few years ago to 10 per cent of the acres sown in the province now.
The processing is obviously something that is very much desired.
So why do the polls support NAFTA?

They do not. The polls certainly do not. That is a good example of how the government does not even know what the agriculture producers in western Canada are saying.
It is interesting to look at the ratio of farm gate sales to food manufacturing and processing sales in Saskatchewan and other provinces. It should be known that Saskatchewan, where agriculture is the single largest economic activity, is also the province with the lowest ratio of farm gate sales to food manufacturers and processors in all of Canada. In Saskatchewan we get 30 cents of processed product for every dollar of farm gate sales. It just shows how dependent we are on farm gate sales.
The Atlantic provinces get $4.45 for every dollar that comes from farm gate sales. That is $4.45 in processed goods for every dollar in farm gate sales. B.C. gets $2.76 on every dollar. Quebec gets $3 on every dollar. As I mentioned, in Saskatchewan we get just 30 cents of processed product for every dollar in farm gate sales.
It can be seen that Saskatchewan lags far behind the other provinces in processing. It is very important that we find ways to protect the growth of the processing value added industries in Canada if our province is going to survive. That means this amendment must be supported by this House.
