Since the free trade agreement there has been the chilling effect of continued U.S. trade actions of countervail and the like.
There have been the delays, the costs and the lack of binding decisions in the dispute settlement mechanism that was supposed to be one of the great positive features of the Canada-U.S. deal. All this is making Canadian businesses decide they should just as well set up in the United States where they can serve both the American market and the Canadian market without facing the threat or the risk of U.S. trade harassment.
In addition to their broken promises regarding what the Iree trade deal would do to end trade harassment and provide secure access for exports to the United States the Conservatives broke another promise. They did not carry out their pledge to have the best adjustment programs in the world to help Canadian workers whose jobs would be eliminated because of the Canada-United States deal.
Madam Speaker, why do I tell you this? Why do I tell the House this? It is because the very same bunch, the very same Conservative gang that brought us the Canada-U.S. free trade deal, has now brought us a new trade deal, the NAFTA. The same Conservative gang that
botched and bungled the negotiations for the Canada-U.S. deal and brought us that flawed arrangement has now negotiated another deal.
They say it is good for Canada and in fact it is better than the U.S.-Canada deal. They say it corrects all its errors and omissions. Why should Canadians believe them now? How can we believe them now when we can clearly see their failures when it comes to the Canada-U.S. deal.
Canadians can see how they failed to carry out their promises to end U.S. trade harassment, to create totally secure access for Canadian trade to that country, to create hundreds of thousands of more jobs through the deal and to provide marvellous new adjustment programs for our workers.
None of this has come true. How can Canadians believe the Conservatives now when they make the same kinds of promises all over again for the NAFTA? Why should Canadians allow themselves to be fooled, to be deceived for a second time by the Conservatives into accepting their NAFTA deal.
NAFTA does not correct the flaws of the free trade deal in that there is still no subsidies code. We are still open to U.S. trade harassment. Its anti-dumping and countervail laws are still there. What was supposed to be the marvel of the free trade deal, the dispute settlement mechanism, even under the new NAFTA would still be too long, too cumbersome, too costly, and decisions at the end of the process would still not be final and binding in every case.
There are new and additional problems now that Mexico is to be added under the NAFTA. There is nothing to prevent unfair competition for Canadian plants and workers arising from the extremely low wages of Mexican workers. It does nothing to prevent unfair competition from plants in Mexico due to their lack of labour, health, safety and environmental standards similar to our own or the lack of any real enforcement of any such standards in that country.
This will mean the companies operating in Mexico can have an unfair cost advantage over companies in Canada that have to pay Canadian wages and live up to our health, safety and environmental standards. Also under the NAFTA Canada would not have the same degree of sovereignty over its natural resources that Mexico would have over Mexican natural resources.
May 25, 1993

The flawed Canada-U.S. free trade deal would be rolled over. It would be included in the NAFTA. Liberals say we have to negotiate a better deal for Canada which responds to the kinds of concerns I mentioned. If this cannot be done Liberals say the deal whether it is the present U.S.-Canada deal or the NAFTA would be abrogated.
It makes sense first to try to negotiate a better deal for Canada because of the opportunities created by the installation of the new Clinton Democratic administration in the United States. It sees many of the same problems we do in the NAFTA deal. It says it will not present its legislation to implement NAFTA to the U.S. Congress unless there are first signed what it calls side agreements on major concerns it has about the NAFTA. These include labour and environmental standards. The Clinton administration says the NAFTA implementing legislation will go to Congress only in a package with the side agreements it agrees to.
These agreements have not been negotiated. They are far from being negotiated. Only last week it was announced that Canada, Mexico and the United States were at an impasse in negotiating these agreements. Yet this crippled and dying Conservative government insists on using its majority to force this massive NAFTA, all 4,500 pages of it, through the House after only three days of debate this week and after only a few inadequate days of committee hearings. Why? For what purpose?
The Americans have not passed the legislation. Mexico has not passed the legislation so we are not losing or missing any trade opportunities. Leaders of the Congress have told President Clinton publicly that if the legislation were presented to the Congress of the United States now clearly it would be defeated. It may not come up for a vote until next year, if at all, and well after the original proposed date of implementation.
What is the rush for Canada? We do not miss anything worth while if we wait. We will not lose anything if this government gives Canadians a full opportunity which we have not had to debate the deal, to urge changes and improvements, and to say if we want it at all even if there are changes.
Why will the Conservatives not let Canadians take the time needed to debate this deal? What has it to hide?
Government Orders
Why does it fear the common sense and good judgment of Canadians? It must be because the Conservatives know they have not made a good deal. They know the deal will not stand up to the scrutiny of full parliamentary debate.
I call on this Conservative government to come to its senses, let this happen and not force a vote this week. I call upon it to put the interests of Canada and Canadians ahead of the desires of the Prime Minister to add yet another tarnished page to the soiled record of himself and this government. I call upon this government not to proceed. I call upon this House to defeat this legislation.

Madam Speaker, in coming to assess and judge the proposal before us in the House and the amendments in front of us, the government has had only one major argument in its defence that we hear day in and day out: the free trade agreements it has negotiated and is negotiating have been good for Canada's trade performance.
How often do we hear the minister of trade ask how we can oppose the free trade agreements or NAFTA when we have had such demonstrated success in developing a bountiful expanding trade performance for Canada? The minister of trade does not know of what he speaks. Canada's trade performance has not improved as a result of the free trade agreement. In fact it has worsened.
I want to put on the record this morning what I consider to be the true facts. They are not generated by some paid by government think tank or by some Tory public relations firms but by Statistics Canada, an agency of the government known and recognized for its own honesty and integrity.
Let us come to one fundamental and clear case. The trade surplus in the four years before the free trade agreement was signed has fallen by 26.9 per cent since the free trade agreement. We have declined in our total global trade by over 25 per cent after the free trade as before the free trade agreement.
The argument put forward by the government is that somehow we should now renegotiate the NAFTA to further compound that mistake. It is important to show in these figures that not only has our trade with the United States begun to decline but most significantly our trade with every other part of the world has dropped drastically since the signing of the free trade agreement.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
If we look at the figures in the first quarter of 1993 the global trade surplus shrank by $886 million. Our trade surplus with the United States fell by $116 million and then dropped by $520 million from February to March 1993.
It is incredible that the minister of trade has the audacity to stand in the House day after day to defend a trade agreement when the figures of his own agency demonstrate it has been an unmitigated disaster. What is even more significant is that we are losing the opportunities by this narrow focus on our trade with the United States to open up and expand around the world. When my colleague from Newfoundland and I visited Japan in early January we were told in clear terms that the NAFTA was seen by the Japanese as discriminatoiy against them in a number of areas-banking, financial services, automobiles, textiles-and that it was clearly contrary to fundamental international trade rules of not trying to divert trade to one country.
What is the fastest growing economic region of the world? China, Japan, Malaysia, Thailand, the area where economic growth in the Pacific Rim is going up 10, 12 or 15 per cent. We are signing a trade agreement that in effect sets up barriers to that area of the Pacific Rim. It precludes Canadian traders and exporters from having maximum opportunity. If you are on the other side of the fence being erected by NAFTA, what are you going to say? Why should we trade with Canadians when they are signing an agreement that keeps us out?
In my own province of Manitoba, a province highly dependent upon international trade, the centre of the grain export market for Canada, look at the figures, the hard numbers, not the figments of imagination by the minister of trade, not the fantasy of his public relations team, but the hard figures of Stats Canada. Manitoba's surplus with all other principal trading areas fell by $451 million between 1988 and 1992.
Since the signing of the free trade agreement, the province of Manitoba lost close to a half billion in trade as a result of this great agreement. Manitoba's trade deficit with the United States grew by $298 million. We lost trade with the United States in the very same period.
Manitoba's global trade surplus, the centre of the grain trade, became a deficit of $494 million from a surplus of $255 million four years earlier.
Is that the record on what one defends these magnificent trade agreements? Our trade around the world is in decline. Our merchandise trade, our equipment, computers, and others is in serious decline with the United States. Yet this is the only defence that is being offered by the minister of trade. He is saying that Canada is locking itself into a narrow trade arrangement and denying the opportunities and openness that Canada has traditionally sought out in its trade strategy. As my colleague from Etobicoke, our trade critic, points out, we are hampered even further by a dispute settlement mechanism that is inferior to the one we had under the international trade agreements, allowing more harassment.
I just want to point out that yesterday the leader of our party put forward a series of foreign policy proposals that a Liberal government has indicated it will follow when it becomes the government in two or three months.
One of the interesting proposals made by the leader is the idea of looking at the western hemisphere as a new area of opportunity for Canada, not defined by the NAFTA free market definition, but by saying that there is a whole series of issues dealing with how to integrate and develop our economic relationships in the entire hemisphere on a multilateral basis working through the international bank, working through multilateral trade agreements.
It is interesting that the World Bank, an agency that one has to pay some heed to, points out that the most important requirements in the western hemisphere are to continue investment and human capital, social infrastructure, education, social welfare, environment friendly production, none of which is permitted under the NAFTA because this is geared solely to a free market, laissez-faire ideology which in fact penalizes any form of government investment. Part of the problem we have had in Canada under the FTA is that we had our own ability to clearly invest in our economy hindered and hampered by the FTA. We now want to export that same kind of ideology to the rest of the hemisphere.
May 25, 1993

We are proposing a positive alternative by which Canada could work with the United States and Latin American countries to develop a multilateral, economic arrangement dealing with debt problems, with the foreign investment problems, with new trade arrangements, working out in relationship to these countries the kind of approach that would not rely upon trickle down economics but upon a positive, constructive approach. It is interesting that one of the most noted U.S. experts in this area, Andler Moss of the North South Centre at the University of Miami said: "Supply side economics simply fail to provide sufficient trickle down in either Los Angeles or Caracas". We might add Calgary as well. It simply does not work.
What we are putting on the record this morning is a clear repudiation of the only defence, the only argument, the only position that the government has tried to put forward to substantiate and support the NAFTA. They said FTA was such a great success we should now build upon it with a NAFTA. If you take that argument and look at the figures, the abject failure of the FTA to substantially improve Canada's trading position means that by following their own logic we have only one recourse. That is to reject this agreement which our party intends to do.

Madam Speaker, I am glad to have a further chance in this marathon debate to speak against the NAFTA bill which was rammed through Parliament in five days of debate at second reading. A huge long bill which was rammed through the committee in a few days without hearings across the country is now given three days for debate on the amendments and third reading.
I wish to speak now on amendment No. 4. Amendment No. 4, moved by my friend and colleague the member for Esquimau-Juan de Fuca says: "Nothing in this act or the agreement shall be interpreted so as to prohibit a party to the agreement from requiring commercial entities within its sovereign territory to process raw materials or raw resource before exporting such materials or resources".
The point is if Canada is to develop our secondary industries we must have the power to direct our natural
Government Orders
resources so that they can be used by Canadians in Canada to create value added, whether it is for the Canadian domestic market or whether it is for export.
The amendment in this is in the words "commercial entities within its sovereign territory". In other words, it is not enough to ask for an amendment that would require a foreign government such as the United States or Mexico to do this processing. The ones who are in fact conducting the business, the ones who are in fact seeking our cheap raw materials at the lowest price and our labour at the lowest price are not the governments of those countries, but the multinational corporations which control those governments.
Therefore, we have this subamendment to the amendment with the effect of saying that no corporation, no commercial entity can export our raw materials or our natural resource unless they do the value added work in Canada with Canadian labour. That should be required by any government which has any respect for the needs of the Canadian people.
It is fairly obvious in the case of the various minerals that we have that we need to be able to process more of them within Canada. During the last world war and during the Vietnam war Canada did some of that. Much more was done simply to ship it to the United States to build their industries. Now that we are not involved in any war, even indirectly, we should be giving attention to building our long term peace-time industries with those minerals and also with Canadian water. We need a rule that will protect Canadian water as well from being exported and then being subjected to the rule that once we have started exporting we cannot stop it, which is the rule of the free trade agreement.
We also need that rule to protect our oil which we need for many purposes in Canada. Madam Speaker, would you ask the Liberal caucus to conduct its meeting outside, please?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. When members are disturbed by comments being made or by conversations that are being held in the House it is my duty to ask members to hold their caucus behind the curtains, please.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders

Thank you, Madam Speaker.
I want to speak a little bit about a situation in southern Ontario. It is not a matter of minerals or oil but it is a matter of our agricultural produce. We have plenty of land capable of producing fruits and vegetables in southern Ontario. In the past there were a lot more small local processing stations, processing plants throughout southern Ontario producing preserves, producing jams, producing all kinds of products from our fruits.
What has happened, especially since the free trade agreement was signed, is that mammoth multinationals like Campbell's have been closing their plants in Canada and either ceasing to buy the Canadian product or buying it up only to ship it to the United States to process in their much larger plants there and sell back to Canada.
As a result we are becoming dependent on a foreign country for our food. When I grew up in this country I thought I was growing up in an agricultural country which also had manufacturing and commerce. It never occurred to me that we might ever approach the point where Canadian land would not feed Canadian people, where Canadian people would not be able to control the production of food and the processing of food in our own country. But in fact that is the prospect we are now facing with the NAFTA accord. We will be prevented from restoring the food processing industries in Canada by being told that any aid that the government gives is an unfair subsidy.
We have to protect the right, not so much of governments but sometimes with the help of governments, of people in any small town or any rural community elfectively to generate their own further employment by producing a cannery or a bottling plant or a jam factory, whatever you have, produce it and sell it locally without being swamped by cheap exports from the United States or Mexico. The United States blatantly violates the general principles of GATT with its export enhancement program. They can undersell any competitor in Canada and drive it out of business if we do not use our only defence against it which is the sovereign Government of Canada.
The same applies to Ontario's forest products industries. I worked for 18 years in one small branch of it, the production of corrugated paper boxes. I now learn that plants are being shut down in Canada because the boxes can be shipped in from the United States to serve the Canadian market. Some of those boxes are made with pulp produced in Canada, formerly used in Canada to make the boxes, now sent to the United States by the multinationals down there which control that part of the Canadian source and that part of the Canadian market.
Unemployment in cities as well as in the small rural towns is growing on account of the effective rule of the multinational corporations. It is killing local communities. It is causing people to move desperately into our larger cities, especially the three great metropolises, but not only those, and to empty and break up the fabric of rural communities in the countryside.
We need a chance to enable people in those places not only to grow food but to process it locally. That is why we need this subamendment. Without this amendment, NAFTA will continue to wipe out the food processing industry. It will block the possibility of creating new ones because of the multinationals flooding our market.
The general goal of the free trade agreement and the general goal of the North American free trade agreement, the so-called economic constitution for North America, is clearly to give the biggest companies the freest access to the cheapest materials and low wages or for some people, no wages.
The Tory government slogan of promoting this agreement about four or five years ago was: "Do not explain the agreement to the public; just sell it".
Also, the intention of the Tories was to do no studies ol the impact or to withhold any impact studies so that Canadians would not know the results to be expected. Their decision was to prohibit hearings across the country, except in a few places. They missed the two largest metropolises in Canada which with the regions around them represent about a quarter of the Canadian people. There were absolutely no hearings there.
May 25, 1993

It is therefore necessary that the people understand what is being done by this government to the people who entrusted it with this responsibility.

Madam Speaker, I could not help but notice your casual glance to the government benches across the way, just to check to see if one government member would utter a single solitary scrap of support for this deal that we have been debating all night and through this morning. Not a single one. Oh, the member for Cambridge has been a stalwart. He has been sitting in his chair and listening hard. He has not been saying much, just yelling little comments, but not saying much.
Maybe there is a minister in the House, maybe he is out there in the lobby somewhere. But it is very discouraging to talk to an empty House. Where are all these government members who are supporting this deal? It is supposed to be "the deal" for Canada, the deal for Canada that is going to push us into the global economic trading market. Where are they? I do not understand.
We in this party decided that we are going to work hard in order to try to demonstrate to Canadians why it is that the Liberal Party, Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, has to demonstrate to this government on behalf of our constituents just how lousy this deal is, on the heels of course of the FTA. It has been repeated time and time again by my colleagues and sometimes by the NDP.
Now, that is another thing. Not only have we got the government benches all empty, but also the NDP. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca came in here this morning, having stirred up the beehive last night. He got us all going on this debate, and rightly so because we ought to be debating this thing, but then goes to bed. Not a bad deal. And we sit around trying to debate this whole thing. Then he gets up, at around five or six this morning and wonders: "How the hell it is going?" He turns the television on and holy smoke, the debate is still going on. Then he goes on CBC and says: "Well, you know, we made our point in this debate. Maybe we should not have been carrying it on".
Why did the NDP not think about that? Now the NDP starts talking. Let us talk about the NDP for a second. How about the leader of the NDP? Let us begin right at the top. She has stated three positions on NAFTA. Position one: She will immediately cancel NAFTA.
Government Orders
Position two: She will immediately cancel both deals, FTA and NAFTA. Position three: In an interview she gave to The Financial Post I quote: "If elected we would sit down with the Americans and say how can we make this thing work?"
Do I hear the NDP leader saying renegotiation if necessary, but not necessarily abrogation? Where do I find myself today? My colleagues and I this morning are privileged to be standing on our feet here in the highest court of the land. This is the third time for me in the last 12 hours to express on behalf of my constituents the fears that the Canada-U.S.-Mexico deal will exacerbate the problems, the disastrous effects of the free trade agreement.
It will make us more dependent on our U.S. neighbours and will devastate an already gutted manufacturing sector in this country. Wake up, Mr. Prime Minister. Look at all the heads bounce, in our party anyway. We have been here all day and all night while the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca has been catching his beauty sleep. God knows he needs a lot of beauty sleep.
We are being betrayed. That is what my constituents are saying. The NDP caucus is in tatters, having run out of things to say. Perhaps it is out of fear of contradicting each other. What do the New Democrats do? They train their political guns on the Official Opposition. That makes a lot of sense but that is their tactic.
When you are as low in the polls as they are, that is what you have to do. We beg our constituents at home to hearken back and remember the debate of 1988. The last election campaign, my first election campaign, saw the NDP and its leader, Ed Broadbent, forget to mention the free trade agreement. He forgot to mention the free trade agreement in the opening speech of the 1988 election campaign. Thanks to the Liberal Party, the FTA became the major issue.
Here he is.

Good morning to the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. He looks pretty fresh. I would be fresh too if I had stirred up the hornet's nest and then went off for about eight hours' sleep and came back for the closing remarks and probably some questions in Question Period.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
Then and only then do the NDP wake up. What do they do? They train their political guns on the Liberals. Remember the last 10 days of the 1988 campaign and all those vicious attacks on the leader of the Liberal Party of the day. Do you know what happened?
He got paid for it.
We all paid for that.
Ed Broadbent got his payola.

Yes, he got his payola. Probably double dipping. One of the problems we have is that we are trying to get away from that nonsense of collecting a pension after serving some time and working for the government and collecting a pay cheque. Is that not what the member of the NDP is doing? That is something we are on record as being against.
What happened as a result of all this argument of course is that it cost us seats. It cost the Liberals seats. It cost the NDP seats. Of course the Tories were reelected. Here we go again as if there was not a lesson to be learned in the 1988 campaign.
The NDP caucus split all over the map. Their leader was on the skids. There were confusing messages coming from the New Democrats on matters of finance and trade. Again what do they do? They train their guns on the Official Opposition. It does not make a heck of a lot of sense. It is not working and it is confusing the heck out of their leader.
I am getting carried away. I wanted to come back as I promised in my last intervention to the matter of textiles and apparel goods. That is important to my riding because of the Coppley group which is a major employer. Hundreds of people work for that suit maker.
I already mentioned the testimony to the subcommittee by the Minister for International Trade to explain that the federal government would have preferred a more open trading regime in textiles and apparel but it could not be achieved. "This area of negotiations is not wholly satisfactory. The U.S. and Mexico agreed to a rule of origin which was not satisfactory as far as Canadian companies were concerned". Why are we signing this thing? That is another reason we ought to sit back should we not?
Hang around Stan. I will be in Hamilton during the election.

There goes the hon. member for Cambridge again prepared to interrupt me from across the floor. But not once in the last three hours that I have seen him has he got on his feet and defended the deal.
Then I mentioned the Canadian director of the Amalgamated Clothing and Textile Workers Union's remarks, and I will ask my constituents to go back and read that.
Another intervention I wanted to make was that NAFTA now requires a third stage of transformation whereby producers qualify for free trade rates if they produce their products in North America using North American fabric which is made from North American yams or fibres. These rules will make it increasingly difficult for Canadian producers to qualify for free trade rates. The second important exchange is restrictions on tariffs rate quotas.
I also wanted to make mention of the remarks made by Mr. Alleruzzo, the Canadian director of the Amalgamated Clothing and Textile Workers Union who said that he was concerned about the extent to which increased competition would lead to greater use of home workers by the Canadian apparel manufacturers.
"Many apparel manufacturers are increasingly making use of home workers to lower their costs. When resorting to ship their production to workers at home, the cost for manufacturers decreases substantially as they exploit the workers by paying less and giving no benefits. The workers at home see long hours, little pay and no benefits. At the end, many do not qualify for unemployment insurance or pensions because they were never registered in the first place."
There is so much evidence. I am glad that we are getting the opportunity to bring it forward to our constituents, to the Canadian public, to the 74 per cent of Canadians out there who say that we have a deal.
The NDP wants to scrap it. That is crazy and irresponsible. The responsible thing to do is to not rush this deal. God knows the Americans are not. Do not sign a blank cheque. Do not buy the house without looking at the details of the mortgage. Let us just sit back, have a look at this sensibly, sign a proper document, make the adjustments that have to be made to make it a good deal for Canada, which this deal is not.
May 25, 1993

Madam Speaker,
I join my colleagues this morning in this debate which has gone on now for many hours. A lot has been said about the deal. A lot has been said in favour and a lot has been said in opposition and some in between.
I listened attentively to all of the speakers throughout the night until early morning. I went away for a while and came back. The trend and the message which is getting out to our constituents is: Why do we have to shove this deal through today? Why does this have to take place in such a fast track manner?
We have heard from our neighbours south of the border, the U.S. Congress. They as yet are not prepared to see this thing go through. There is an argument within the Democratic caucus as to whether the side deals are the way to go or whether to open this agreement up and renegotiate it totally. I believe as has been said here many times today and last night that this is what has to be done.
We have also to look at what is happening to the labour standards and the environmental standards and all of these things. One time as we negotiated with other countries throughout the world the idea was that we would try to bring the standards of other countries up to our standards.
.(3355)
I believe we cannot stop this. We have to continue this. This is something that has been in Canada's favour over the years. There was a time when Canada's negotiators were looked up to and the people knew that when they went out and negotiated, they were negotiating in the best interests of this country. The negotiating skill displayed by this government does not live up to former standards.
We went through the same type of debates in 1988 at Christmas time. The government said we have to get that famous Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement ratified and shoved through this House. It did it in the same manner, closure, push the deal on, sign it and give away our freedom. Everybody you talk to in your constituencies wonders what this deal is going to do in comparison to what the Canada-U.S. deal already did to this country.
Government Orders
We have seen thousands and thousands of jobs flee this country across the border. I heard a Democratic congressmen from Minnesota on TV this morning saying that one of the big problems with this agreement, when you negotiate free trade agreements with other countries, the idea is that these people can buy the products that are being produced. The situation with the Mexican end of it is that they are not making enough money to buy these products so they are going to be manufacturing goods and shipping them back into our country.
When I talk to people in my constituency and I look at the fast tracking of NAFTA, wondering why this has to be done when the United States, the big partner in this deal is saying it is not sure it is going to put this thing through. Why are we bowing down to the people who we have already made commitments to that we will get this thing through by January of next year.
As the previous speaker from Hamilton just said, I believe that we have to make sure this is a good deal for Canada. We have to renegotiate the Canada-U.S. deal. We have to make sure this is a good agreement for Canada.
I ask my colleagues who are supporting this deal wholeheartedly: What can we say to our constituents when they ask what is this going to do for me? How is this going to affect the unemployment rate in each area that we represent? One and a half million people are unemployed today. Another two million are on welfare. We are looking at large numbers of people with no jobs. What is this going to do for them? I do not have an answer for them. I do not think that anybody else in this great hall has either.
We have said that we want to see this deal made in the best interest of this country, that the manufacturers, the small businesses and the workers are going to know at the end of the day that when this thing is negotiated, everybody is going to benefit from it.
As I said we went through this in 1988. There were the same stories going across that this was going to be nothing but great benefit to this country. This has not happened. You know that, I know that and everybody in this House knows that. We look at the manufacturing heartland of our country. It has been destroyed totally.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
I say to the government that before we sign on the dotted line, let us make sure and be honest and true that this is indeed the best deal for this country.

Mr. Speaker, I was going to comment on the remarks of the member for Hamilton West who, if his party has no policy on something decides that he should attack the other, but he seems to have disappeared, so there is no value in making those kinds of remarks.
One of the main concerns of many people in this party and many people across Canada regarding this legislation is that it gives up the levers of power relative to the economy of Canada. Those levers of power are necessary for Canada to re-establish the growth of its economy and the building of its economy.
This subamendment tries on behalf of Canada to repossess some of those levers of power. Many of the clauses and agreements accepted in the free trade agreement have weakened Canada's ability to make use of the natural advantages which Canada has.
What the free trade agreements have done is weaken the position so we cannot use those natural advantages to develop our own economy and make sure that we have a stable and secure structure which will continue year after year.
I refer of course to a number of clauses, one of them being the natural treatment clause which requires governments and corporations to give U.S. companies the same treatment as if they were local. This clause lost us the ability to give preferential treatment to Canadians companies. That is the kind of negotiation that has been going on in the free trade agreement which has weakened Canada's economy. It made it less able, more difficult for Canada to establish a solid base for its economy and make sure that companies can compete in our own market as well as in other markets of the world.
Worse still is the free trade agreement's requirement to sell our energy to the United States at the same price as we sell it to a Canadian company. In other words we cannot use our cheaper gas, petroleum projects, cheaper hydro to convince companies around the world to come to Canada because we can give them a little benefit of our natural advantage in energy production. If we could offer them hydro or gas at cost, they would come to Canada.
The Quebec government has been doing this and is trying to do it still. It found itself being pinpointed by the U.S. because it had offered a Norwegian company a better deal on hydroelectric power than it was selling that power to the United States. Quebec was forced to back off that particular agreement.
This clause forces Canada not to sell energy at cost, but to charge the same as it charges in the United States. What we charge in the United States is what the market will bear in most cases. It does not help us to build a stable and effective economy at home.
The Mexicans were smarter. In the NAFTA they said: "We will not have you affecting our energy production. Our hydro and our gas and oil will be controlled by us. We will sell it at whatever price we hit and we will sell it to anybody we want to". They have taken advantage of their natural advantage in oil and gas and hydro.
In the free trade agreement we have given up these natural advantages. This subamendment, in fact this whole amendment, would at least let us try and regain some of the advantages we lost on the free trade agreement by making this bad deal of NAFTA at least a better deal.
We are discussing amendments which would try and make a bad deal a better deal if it does pass. Hopefully we can stop it from passing but with a government majority, under our present system of government, if the government decides it is going to pass it is likely to do so if the government can keep us around long enough.
By this amendment and the subamendment we will allow Canadian governments to require, if they wish, that our resources be processed before they are exported. Again this is an effort on the part of this party to put into the NAFTA the kind of levers of power which would allow us to make sure our economy can be improved and stabilized by those advantages which we do have.
Levers of power are important and most countries use them quite well. Sometimes they are levers of power just by the size of the purchase. For instance Japan buys a considerable amount of our canola. It demands all of it to be unprocessed. The seed is shipped to Japan. It would not be very profitable for us to ship that canola there as oil because then the processing would happen here in Canada.
May 25, 1993

However the U.S. tries not to buy our oil. They want the canola whole. This is a use of the levers of power. Marginally these would not be affected by NAFTA but that is the kind of power which we should be grasping here in Canada to make sure that our economy is solid and able to grow.
The point I make here is that we can only develop our economy if we have the power to require processing of our resources. That is what this subamendment does. Things like the production of grain, minerals and energy are natural advantages which could make our economy more vibrant, help it to grow and make it more stable. If we do this kind of processing at home then we have the effects of that growth and that vibrancy.
This amendment and subamendment would allow us to make sure if we decided we want to do it to be able to do it. Processing our resources, manufacturing and fabricating projects for ourselves and for the export market makes sense and is supported by all of the economists, even those who support the NAFTA deal.
They all say that what we need to do is more processing at home. That is the basis under which they say our economy can grow. All this subamendment does is say put that into this act so that we have the power to require, if possible, anyone within our jurisdiction, within the sovereign state or the sovereign provinces as it happens, to require any product shipped out of that area to be processed if that is desirable.
Why then is the government making this kind of stupid mistake in giving away an advantage and then not making it part of the law of Canada? Why is it taking an almost anti-Canadian position as far as development, as far as processing, fabrication and manufacturing is concerned, forcing companies to go where it is cheaper to buy, to build and not asking them to take at least a pro Canadian position.
The subamendment has special effects on agriculture. We could and should be self-sufficient in food. We are losing that ability of self-sufficiency quickly because we are not making use of the possibilities of processing our products at home. The philosophy of free trade carried to its final level will force all kinds of production out of

Canada into areas where they might have a slight advantage in other ways.

Mr. Speaker,
I am pleased to speak on this subamendment to Bill C-115. This amendment is based on common sense. Common sense is the approach of the Liberal Party when it comes to this whole discussion of our trading relationships with the United States and Mexico.
The Conservative government wants to barrel ahead with NAFTA just for the sake of having a deal. The Conservative philosophy is that any deal is a good deal. New Democrats are as bad as the Conservatives. The NDP will oppose any trade agreement just for the sake of opposing it.
The Liberal Party, on the other hand, looks at Canada's trading problems and opportunities with realism and honesty. We know that Canada is a trading nation. We know that fair trading relationships are important for Canada's future. We know that it is possible to sign good agreements and it is possible to sign bad agreements. That is the straightforward and rational approach we are taking to this debate.
That rational approach leads us to question the wisdom of this legislation implementing NAFTA. I believe that most people in my riding of Hamilton Mountain have the same fair-minded approach and therefore the same deeply felt concerns about this legislation.
The citizens of Hamilton Mountain are asking: What is the Conservative government's rush? Why do the Conservatives want Parliament to pass a bill implementing NAFTA when no such legislation has even been introduced in the United States Congress?
Why should Canada push ahead with the agreement when the negotiations are still going on? What bargaining room will Canada have if we pass the deal first and negotiate later?
More important, voters in Hamilton are asking why the government insists on passing the trade agreement with Mexico and the United States when the agreement fails to meet any real Canadian objectives, and fails to correct the errors of the previous free trade agreement.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
The United States is continuing to push for new arrangements that will suit American objectives. Why is the Canadian government not pushing for new arrangements that will suit our country's objectives?
For the people of Hamilton Mountain these are not academic questions. These are questions that affect their ability to earn a living, put food on the table for their families and ensure a bright future for their children.
Hamiltonians know better than anyone else in Canada that we suffer when the government signs bad trade deals. Hamiltonians know better than anyone else that unfair trade rules can cost jobs.
Hamiltonians know we need trade rules that will allow Canadian businesses to compete fairly and without harassment from other countries. Hamiltonians certainly know better than to trust the promises made about trade agreements by the Conservative government.
During the last election the Conservatives promised that the free trade deal with the United States would do wonders for Hamilton's economy. The sad fact is that 19,000 more Hamiltonians are jobless than were jobless at the time of the last election. Hamilton's businesses and workers have been hammered time and again by unfair American trade actions, despite all the promises made in the last election by the Conservative Party.
We do not blame the Americans for that. They are just being hard-nosed business people. We blame the Conservative government for not actively pursuing the means to close the loopholes that allow our American neighbours to take those actions in the first place.
The government does have another choice than to try to just ram NAFTA through Parliament. The government could take the opportunity presented by ongoing negotiations to fight for a proper definition of subsidies, to fight for new anti-dumping rules, and to fight for an agreement on countervail regulations and trade remedy laws. Hamiltonians cannot understand why the Conservatives are not seizing the moment to do just that.
A proper definition of subsidies would ensure that Canadians could take steps to help our weaker regions, strengthen our social programs, build up new entrepreneurs or cut taxes without worrying that the United
States or Mexico might claim that these measures represent unfair subsidies to Canadian businesses. With a proper definition of subsidies Canada, the United States and Mexico would all be playing by the same rules and we would all know the rules. Without a proper definition this trade deal is hardly worth the paper on which it is printed.
We all know that even with new definitions of subsidies it would still be possible for someone to break the rules. In that case the country which suffers must be able to cry foul.
People in my riding of Hamilton Mountain understand that and they favour that. What they do not understand is why under current arrangements the United States can cry foul and then impose such an incredible temporary penalty on Canadians without proving any damage to American firms.
Our steel companies in Hamilton are frequently wrongly accused by their American competitors of selling steel below the actual cost of production in order to capture customers. The American steel companies, backed up by their government, use anti-dumping laws to charge our Hamilton companies with unfair competition.
After a few years of complicated hearings Canadian companies are found to have done absolutely nothing wrong. Unfortunately under current American trade remedy laws our Canadian companies have paid a heavy price for their innocence. They are forced to raise the prices during the time of hearings and to post a bond. The bottom line is that Canadian businesses lose customers and money and Canadian steelworkers lose jobs while waiting for a final determination of the case.
There is a very simple comparison. It is as though all the American teams in the NHL playoffs were allowed to charge the Maple Leafs and Canadiens with a penalty any time they felt like it. Players from Canadian teams would be sent off the ice to the penalty box until later in the game when the referee finally decided there was no infraction after all. Meanwhile the American teams would have been on an unjustified power play.
May 25, 1993

Those kinds of rules do not make any sense in a hockey game. They make even less sense when jobs are at stake, when businesses are at stake and when the future of our Canadian economy is at stake. That is why it is shocking to have the Conservative government try to put such rules in place through the North American free trade agreement.
Simple plain common sense would tell the Conservatives not to try to rush NAFTA through Parliament but instead to continue to negotiate with Mexico and the United States for rules which are fair to everybody. Simple plain common sense would tell the Conservatives not to rush through a deal which fails to correct the weaknesses of their previous deal. Simple plain common sense would tell the Conservatives to learn from past mistakes and take the time to get a good deal, not just any deal.
There is too much at stake for my riding to act in haste. There is too much at stake for the future of our country.

I was in the House about 1.30 this morning when the Minister for International Trade actually had the nerve to say when asked very specific questions about how the trade deal was not working for steel: "Well, where is Hamilton anyway?"

I was examining the job losses and outlining the fact that in my riding alone 10,000 people have lost their jobs in the steel industry directly. I did not have an opportunity in the 10 minutes allotted to outline the fact that

I want to talk about some specific steel facts that I would like to put on the record. I heard the Minister for International Trade last week say: "Kentucky can get them cheaper power rates". This is a given. He said: "Kentucky has more productive person power". That is false. He said: "Kentucky has all these things to offer that Hamilton does not". My colleagues and I went to the source. We went to the z line and saw the greatest new investment in jobs for Canadians. In fact, the Canadian steel producers are facing unfair subsidies from the United States.
If the minister took the time to do his homework he could pick up a copy of a study, not done by the Liberals but by Ernst and Young. For the record I would like to table some of the information about the grants, loans, subsidies and direct payments that are going out to U.S. steel producers that are costing Canadian jobs.
These are strictly federal. They do not take into account state or local subsidies by the Americans, the
great free traders: grants, $236 million; concessionary financing, $300 million; tax concessions, $7.7 billion; assumption of obligations by the federal government, $3.7 billion; regulatory concessions, $2.5 billion; subsidized services, $500 million; procurement, the figure has not been dated but it is a potentially large one; upstream assistance, $2 billion; downstream assistance, $2 billion; and trade protection assistance, $8 billion.

There is not a government member on that side of the House because they do not want to hear the real news. The real news is that this agreement has been working to the benefit of the Americans and the second stage of the NAFTA will give us more of the same.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the applause from the Liberal members. I know they are anticipating my speech and I appreciate the standing ovation they just gave. It is suitable and fitting because the amendment that is being proposed to the motion in front of us has the effect of giving countries, and in this case Canada, the right to control commercial entities within our sovereign territory.
That is a vital part of any trade agreement or any international agreement, particularly in this so-called new environment when we have globalization, the new world order and so on. It is time we began to question what the new world order and globalization involve. We have been closing our eyes to what is really meant by globalization. The parties in the House have not always stated clearly what they see as globalization in the current context.
What is it that we are preparing for? To whose benefit? Are we creating an upgraded global economy for people within our own sovereign territories? Are we doing it for the business entities within our own territories? Just who is going to benefit from this kind of globalization?
Government Orders
I note that there have not been many statements on what we are aiming for, what are our goals. The NDP use of globalization has always been for the benefit of people. Yet the international agreements we have been seeing signed on our behalf by our sovereign elected governments whether Conservative or Liberal in the past have tended to free up and unshackle corporations and corporate entities.
It is veiy strange because we have not had a reassessment in the past several decades of the role of the corporation. Those who have looked at the economic history of the corporation will know that for several hundred years a new entity was being developed. Corporations in this country were so special in the early days that it took an act of Parliament and the approval of the Senate before a corporation could get the privileges we grant to that kind of business entity. They are special privileges, privileges with a capital P.
They allow for a competitive edge over the ordinary private entrepreneur because first of all the corporation never dies. A corporate entity lives forever and as a result has a great many benefits. It does not have to restructure every generation. It simply goes on and on. It does not have to worry about finally paying deferred taxes because the head of the family business unit has died. The corporation goes on and on. It virtually never pays the deferred taxes that our tax system permits. As well the corporate sector is granted in this country and virtually every other country around the globe a special privilege on the amount of taxation it pays.
I have heard arguments in this House from members on the Conservative side-we are not sure where the Liberals stand on it-that corporations should pay zero taxes and it is the shareholders who ought to be paying the tax. I could perhaps see the logic of that if it were made illegal for corporations to maintain and build up funds to be there for the use of the corporation on its own account and to do its own expansion. However that is not the way it works. If the expansion of the corporation were dependent upon the input of more money, more capital investment from the shareholders, perhaps we could justify that kind of system.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
In reality what we have is corporate entities competing against private individuals running their own small businesses. The rules of the game are not fair. Yet in the name of the new world order and the new kind of globalization we are still struggling with to understand, some of us of simple mind can see already that the new order of globalization is an attempt to take away any sovereign control over those very entities, those very corporations our national governments established.
The new rules, including the rules that are being proposed under the current NAFTA before this House today and the Canada-U.S. trade agreement that went through here four and a half years ago, let the corporation run unhampered and unshackled by any rules set by national governments.
The only impediment to trade between the United States and us, as I pointed out earlier this morning, as a result of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement are those impediments which exist because of the U.S. constitution that gives the Congress the right to change rules established internationally by presidential decree and presidential signature. No matter what we sign with the United States the Congress can always overrule it. That is the source of most of the trade irritants that have existed between us.
Whether the Liberals form the next government or the New Democrats form the next government, the reality is that the constitution of the United States will prevent the leader of the current opposition from making it a better agreement because he is not going to be able to convince Congress to change its constitution and transfer its rights into an international agreement. It is dreaming in Technicolor to think we are going to be able to sign a better agreement or negotiate something better. We are simply going to have to live with the giant beside which we were put by fate and by birth and figure out ways of getting around it.
The kind of institutions this country's people have tried to establish to be able to better compete globally include those that are best known to me as a farmer and from a farming community in western Canada. The globalized institutions that permit us to operate in a global economy as producers in western Canada are institutions such as the Canadian Wheat Board and the Canadian Grains Commission. They permit us to go into other countries to provide them with guarantees as to the quality and the type of the product we are selling, thanks to the Canadian Grains Commission standards,
and provide them with guarantees as to price and delivery, thanks to the guarantees presented and available through the Canadian Wheat Board, guarantees that very few other countries can offer.
They are only getting better. They are absolutely necessary if we as Canadian producers and farmers in this country are going to compete globally. They are institutions which give us an edge in a global economy. Now is not the time to take away the power of those institutions. We need those tools if we are going to be players in the global economy. I wish that government members would understand that and start defending the position of the government because I think it is indefensible. I understand why very few of them have bothered to speak on the North American free trade agreement because it is an indefensible agreement.
And they haven't read it either. [Translation]
