Mr. Speaker, that was a remarkable speech by the Leader of the Opposition. We have heard as we heard from a number of our colleagues over the course of the past 24 hours that the government is proceeding in a wholly irresponsible way.
I want to say something about two other aspects of the debate on NAFTA. Before doing so I want to underline once again that the procedure this government follows is wholly reprehensible. The fact is that we are severely
limiting our negotiating possibilities as Canada proceeds through the discussion of the side agreements on the environment and on the labour standards.
This government has placed Canada in a situation where its hands are tied. It will be the one country of the three which has endorsed the agreement. The other two are negotiating from positions of strength leaving Canada in a weak position at the bargaining table.
Let me also add that the government's decision to proceed now is wholly incomprehensible when one considers not only where the United States is on the side agreements but where the United States is on introducing its own implementing legislation. We do not know when that will be. The government does not know when that will be. The people of Canada do not know when that will be. It is quite conceivable that there will be further change and further amendment to the circumstances of the NAFTA, yet we will have gone ahead and implemented the legislation to make a reality of the NAFTA.
I want to turn to two subjects that we have not spent a whole lot of time on but are fundamental to any understanding of NAFTA, indeed any understanding of what Canada's trade policies should be.
One subject is obviously that whole area called adjustment assistance, a name that has a rather bureaucratic ring about it but covers a reality for a great many Canadians. This government has introduced freer trade without introducing the measures that can make Canadians beneficiaries of freer trade rather than the victims of freer trade.
Let me suggest that the government in introducing its legislation on NAFTA has consistently referred for example to the de Grandpre report on adjustment assistance. If you take the trouble to read that report of five years ago it contains a range of proposals, new programs and new activities that would have helped Canadians adjust to and benefit from freer global trade.
I speak not just of the continental approach that this government has taken but rather a truly multilateral approach. Education and skills training. Obviously this government has not proceeded in a dynamic and national fashion to make a reality of a training culture in Canada.
May 25, 1993

We have seen its failure consistently to develop good understanding between organized labour and business in such a way as to ensure that freer trade is implemented in a method that gives the possibilities to Canadians to benefit and not to be victimized.
In research and development, in science and technology, in the whole area of technological innovation this government has consistently failed to match its commitment to freer trade with the programs at home in science and technology that would have helped Canadians to be yet more globally competitive.
One of the major issues that this government consistently has failed to address over the past five years is the issue of interprovincial trade barriers. How can we hope in Canada to compete effectively globally when we cannot even create a freer trade environment in our own country? We have barriers across our country to the free movement of people, goods, services and capital which militate against the rise of effective Canadian companies that can compete globally.
The government has taken a dab at that issue in recent months but throughout its time in office it never did address in any effective manner the whole issue of the barriers that the Canadian governments of the past have allowed to be erected across our country.
However there is no area where there has been a greater failure than in the area of small business. We have had all sorts of discussion and comment in this House about a jobless recovery. It is true to a degree that as larger corporations accept the challenge of global competition, they are scaling down on their work force and looking for a greater degree of productivity in that sense.
At the same time the jobs will find creation. They will be created in the small and medium-sized companies. What has this government done in the way of helping small business? It has put up interest rates to unprecedented levels. I speak of real interest rates and not the nominal interest rates this government always refers to. It has put up real interest rates. It has only tinkered with the Small Businesses Loans Act in recent months. It has not effectively addressed the ways in which the national government can play a major innovative role in assisting small business to fulfil its employment goals and its entrepreneurial tasks in our society.
Government Orders
Let me turn to a second major area of failure of this government. It has made a commitment to continental freer trade but it has neglected the opportunities around the world. It has eschewed the multilateral approach in favour of a continental approach. It has played a minor role in the Uruguay round of the GATT It has not played the dynamic role that one would have expected Canada to play, given its history of innovation and commitment in the GAIT since 1948.
Beyond the GATT and the Uruguay round which will have a far more pervasive effect in Canada than continental free trade or hemispheric free trade that this government has pursued beyond the Uruguay round of the GATT remains a whole range of issues that should have and could still have been taken with the Pacific Rim countries and Europe of 1992, the new single market Europe.
What has this government done to match its commitment to continental free trade or hemispheric free trade with real initiative in Asia and Europe? Some years ago it launched a Pacific rim initiative. We have heard nothing more about that. It came to nothing. The lack of commitment to developing new trade relations with Europe is so obvious it needs no particular emphasis from me.
Beyond that it has failed to provide the structure in our own country to give export orientation to our corporations and small businesses. There are all sorts of opportunities it could have taken in co-operation with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce which has come forward with a number of innovative ideas. It could have supported the export association in its proposals. It supported none of that.
It has turned its back on Asia. It has turned its back on Europe and concentrated entirely on its preoccupation with the continent and now the hemisphere.
Let me draw attention to an initiative the United States ironically has taken in recent weeks. It has gone to the ASEAN countries of Singapore and Malaysia, among others, and asked if they could work out freer trade relations, closer trade relations between NAFTA and the ASEAN countries.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
Leave it to the United States to take such an initiative. Why is Canada not out there talking to the ASEAN countries about new trade relations? Why is it not a Canadian initiative to seek out those opportunities which are so important to Canadians and certainly important to western Canadians who are fully conscious of the opportunities that are rapidly opening across the Pacific.
It is that sort of dynamic trade policy that we in the Liberal Party and the official opposition are committed to. When we form the government we will be taking initiatives on a multilateral basis across the globe that will make a real reality of Canadian opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the motion before us on this extremely important piece of legislation. I am proud that members of the New Democratic Party have forced a further debate on this legislation. We want to have the opportunity to pose those questions and raise the issues that Canadians have not had the opportunity to raise. This government has made sure Canadians do not have a voice. It has decreased the time for debate and indeed has not televised public hearings as we have asked.
I think what we are debating here today is extremely important because it is not just a debate about trade. It is a debate about how Canada will go into the 21st century. The Conservative government would see us go into the 21st century as the 51st state and we are here to say that is the main intention of NAFTA. We do not accept that as the future of Canada.
There are many things about the procedure of this legislation that are really open to question. One of those questions is why this legislation is being rushed through the House of Commons at this time. There is no logical reason. There is no necessity. We know this has not come before Congress and in fact Congress will not review this legislation until all negotiations are completed. Yet the government persists in ramming this legislation through the House of Commons now. Why? I think there can only be one reason and that is this government has some hidden agenda.
We remember that the Canada-U.S. trade deal was predicated and developed on the basis that we would have about a 75-cent dollar. We have not had that since the Canada-U.S. trade deal was signed. A lot of questions were raised about whether this government had agreed to keep the dollar high, although not specifically in the Canada-U.S. trade deal but it did stay high. A former minister of that government raised the question that perhaps there was an agreement by the government to keep the dollar at a high level.
I am asking today in raising this question with the government and the people of Canada, what is the hidden agenda of this government? Why is it trying to ram the legislation through? Has it made some deals? Has it made some commitments? Who has it made the commitments to?
Canadians have a right to know if this government has made some promises or commitments to the government of the United States or the international business community that they are not sharing with Canadians. I challenge the government side to come clean with Canadians and tell us why it is ramming through this legislation. There certainly is no other reason that one can draw the conclusion from.
There are many things in this legislation that we believe will be very detrimental to the future of Canada. There are issues of sovereignty. How ironic it is that on the one hand we are negotiating and in some cases concluding self-government agreements with Canada's First Nations and on the other hand we are giving away the sovereignty of Canada through the NAFTA agreement.
What is this government's intention? That is the real question. It will say it is to increase jobs in Canada and make Canada more productive but in fact we have lost jobs. We continue to lose jobs and the rate of unemployment continues to go up.
I would tell the government to get out of Ottawa. Sit down at the kitchen table with the 3,000 workers from that Scarborough plant and their families who were just laid off because the plant moved to the United States. Talk to them about what effect bad trade deals have had on their lives.
There are other implications that are of equal concern because this is not just a commercial deal. We are entering into a trade agreement with Mexico that has, as my predecessor has very often pointed out, an extremely bad record in terms of human rights.
May 25, 1993

We in this country are free to speak out, to have debates all night and that is something we should be proud of. Canadians of any political party can speak their minds, say what they have to say in this public forum and have it recorded. That is not the case in Mexico. In Mexico, whether one is a journalist or a politician one is not always free to speak one's mind.
I must say this is a very concerning aspect. I think everyone agrees we are entering into much more than a commercial agreement with a country that has been shown by the United Nations to have not complied with United Nations' standards on human rights. There are documented cases of torture and death. In this new world, this new community as we move into the 21st century, what are the relationships that we see between countries and among countries? Surely there are certain principles and standards that we wish to see developed such as human rights, democracy, the freedom to participate, the ability to have a job and the ability to have basic social standards.
We know that in NAFTA there is no provision, as there is in the European Community's agreement, for social rights and a social charter to protect workers and health standards and indeed to work with those regions that might lose jobs because of the NAFTA deal.
The debate on this of legislation is extremely important because it will set a direction for the future of Canada. It is a direction which I profoundly believe will be absolutely disastrous for this country. This is not an agreement that can be renegotiated as some would say. This is not an agreement that can be fixed up by some kind of side agreement. There are no band-aids to fix this agreement. It is bad for Canada, it is bad for the workers of Mexico and it will not offer this country a prosperous future.
I suppose if there is any one question I hear most often posed as I go around the country it is the uncertainty people feel about their own future and especially the future of their children. Will there be jobs for them when they grow up? I have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, many people feel there might not be a future. Trade deals like this set that direction, take away hope from
Government Orders
Canadians and increase the insecurity that so many Canadians feel.
The other question is not just that one can be opposed to this but what is the option, what is the alternative? Some people will say: "Well there is no alternative. We are powerless. It is a global world. We just have to accept what happens to us". But we are not powerless. I want to say that as Canadians we do not have to accept bad trade arrangements. If we do not have the NAFTA the GATT rules will apply. We will be able to enter into sectoral agreements. We will be able to expand our trade beyond the borders of North America into Asia and the rapidly growing markets.
The alternative is that if we accept these kinds of agreements, which mean lower wages, are we in Canada going to go to the standard of Mexico at $3 or $4 a day? Who is going to buy the products? Anybody can understand that this is absolutely ludicrous and will not work.
This debate is not just a wake up call for the government. It tells Canadians: "Stand up now. Call your member of Parliament and say no to NAFTA because that means saying yes to Canada and our future".

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the New Democratic Party is looking very refreshed this morning as is the leader of the Liberal Party. I thought he was in excellent form no doubt buoyed by the results in Nova Scotia yesterday. I would like to tell him that we have an old saying: "As goes Nova Scotia, so not necessarily goes the nation".
Nothing more poignantly illustrates the position of the New Democratic Party in this whole debate on the issue of NAFTA than the subamendment before the House right now. I intend to speak to this subamendment because I think it clearly and unequivocally illustrates the problem that the New Democratic Party has, not only in the area of trade but indeed in many other areas of policy as well.
The motion which this subamendment proposes to amend is an illustration of the unrealistic of the approach the New Democratic Party is taking. The New

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
Democratic Party proposes to raise great walls around this nation to protect us from the horrors beyond and
keep out the evil traitors from abroad. It may be its intent and part of its party policy as well that Canada should withdraw from the GATT. Maybe it does not think we should be a part of the international trading community. The reason why the main motion is unacceptable is the unequivocal fact that it violates the GATT with respect to trade restricting practices.
As a sovereign nation Canada of course can decide it is not going to be a part of this. We can make whatever rules we want but if we are going to make rules that are in contravention of the international trading community then obviously we cannot expect to be a part of that international trading community.
The impact of the subamendment, were it to be implemented, would be to give governments the right to go to corporations or companies such as fish companies and tell them they cannot export raw fish. We would not want to see that happen.
On the other hand, like it or lump it, one of the realities of the world-and the government, unlike the opposition, is bound by reality-is that the GATT is very important to Canada and we have to be a part of the GATT. That is why, even if we might like to impose restrictions such as the one proposed in the amendment and the subamendment, it would not work. It would be unacceptable under the GATT as we found out in the B.C. salmon and herring case not so long ago.
It is interesting to note however that this does not necessarily work to the disadvantage of Canada, as could be implied by my friends opposite. If we look at the outcome of herring four years later in British Columbia-my hon. friends from British Columbia in the House will know-we have had more raw fish coming from the United States into Canada in British Columbia than the other way around.
The same thing is happening right now in my own province of Nova Scotia where we are very frustrated to see raw fish being exported from Nova Scotia to New England. It is really quite annoying. On the other hand, if we were to put on an imposition and say they cannot do that any more, what would happen to the fish that is
coming from the United States into Nova Scotia right now, particularly pollock and cod from Alaska?
If we want to play in the big leagues and be a part of the international trading community then unfortunately we have to be bound by its rules. That is why I think the New Democratic Party will have a permanent spot in the comer of the House and will never even move up to the centre part let alone to this side.
Canadians, when push comes to shove, judge the realities that are before them. Canadians judge who they can safely entrust their country to in terms of future directions. When they look at those kinds of policies that ignore international legal reality, of course they say: "Well we cannot go with these fellows, even though what they want to do sounds kind of warm and fuzzy". However, the reality is that if we put these fellows in power and give them an opportunity to try to implement their ideas, we have seen what happens in a province like Ontario.
The hardest thing to find in the province of Ontario I understand is somebody who voted for the NDP in the provincial election. It is pretty hard to find those people I am told. Obviously some people did but they do not want to admit it any more. That is the reality of the situation.
I listened with great interest to my good friend the Leader of the Opposition who obviously had his wheaties this morning, as they say. It struck me that he was in pretty good form. I have not seen him in such good form. Perhaps he was buoyed by what happened in my province yesterday. I want to take this opportunity to publicly congratulate Mr. Savage on his victory and to congratulate all those who were elected in the Nova Scotia election.
I want to say to the five new members of the legislature elected from South Shore, three of whom are new MLAs who I want to congratulate particularly on their election, politics is politics. Four of those people are Liberals and we all have to do our political thing but when it comes to serving the public I say to them as I have said to those who were there during the last four and a half years that I have been a member, I look forward to working with you on behalf of the people of South Shore. When we have to do our political thing we do our political thing, but we are all here to serve the people we represent first, regardless of our particular political stripe.
May 25, 1993

I listened to the Leader of the Opposition and the one question that he did not answer in my mind was where the Liberal Party stands on this business of NAFTA. I was listening to the debate and he congratulated his members for carrying the debate last night.
I must say there were a few Liberals here last night who did an excellent job. The member for Hamilton East was here most of the night as well as the member for Haldimand-Norfolk, the member for Kenora-Rainy River and of course the hon. member for Etobicoke North. There was a little rump of Liberals but I notice an awful lot of them look pretty well rested today just as there are a few New Democrats in the House who are pretty well rested because there was only a handful of them here last night. I must say there were only a handful of us over here as well, but we did have a good debate. When people talk about the lack of opportunity to debate this thing I find it amazing but I think there will be other speakers who will speak to that point.
There is a question that Canadians really should be putting to the leader of the Liberal Party. When the leader of the Liberal Party and the New Democrats stand and ask why we are rushing this legislation through the House, I want to remind them of something. 'Hie practical reality is that this House is going to rise some time in the near future. It could well be Parliament does not sit for a while. It could be Parliament does not sit until after an election.
What happens if the Americans and the Mexicans implement NAFTA and Canada is stuck not having dealt with the situation?
Should we set our legislative agenda by the Americans? Should we let the Americans call the shots in our legislative agenda? The position over here is very simply no, we should not. We set it by our own agenda.
That is why if my hon. friends opposite will take the time to read the bill they will notice the last article, 247.1 want to read it into the record:
Government Orders
247. (1) Subject to this Act, this Act or any provision thereof, or any provision of any Act as enacted by this Act, shall come into force on a day or days to be fixed by order of the Governor in Council.
(2) No order shall be made under subsection (1) unless the Governor in Council is satisfied that the Government of the United Mexican States and the Government of the United States of America have taken satisfactory steps to implement the Agreement.
In other words this is enabling legislation. It does not take effect until it is proclaimed. Therefore we get the framework in place because it is in the interest of Canada.
Should there be an election before it is implemented we know if the New Democrats are elected to power that will be the end of it. It will never be proclaimed. We know that if the Progressive Conservative Party is reelected as I fully anticipate it will be, when the American and the Mexicans have done their thing it will be proclaimed.
We do not know what the Liberals are going to do. Of course, we will never find out because we know the Liberals are not going to be elected in the fall. We know that Canadians will come to the team of men and women who have stood for Canada and have taken the tough decisions.
They have shown true leadership and will return, with a third successive majority, the Progressive Conservative Party on dynamic new leadership, whatever it may be. I invite my hon. friends opposite to stay tuned. I look forward to their comments in the debate.

Mr. Speaker, my how the empire is crumbling on the other side.
This debate on NAFTA is as much about trade as it is about how this government has chosen to govern this country and Canadians. The Leader of the Opposition said a few moments ago when he concentrated his remarks on the process that it shows an abuse for legitimate authority to have it discharged in this way.
The president and the American trade representative have said as clearly as they can that this agreement will not be going to Congress. Moreover, the American administration is pushing for the so-called side deals to

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
correct the flaws and without those side deals there is basically no deal.
Rather than responding to that in the best interests of our nation by trying to keep our negotiation cards for Canada and protect number one, this government instead pushes the House of Commons, Canadians and our country into ratifying a deal that is very far from being complete.
The minister of defence suggests there is an era of new politics, the politics of inclusion that will listen to all the voices in the debate within the Canadian family. Those words are hollow. They are a pale piece of rhetoric when they fly against the reality of what this government and this administration is about to do.
Rather than taking the time to negotiate properly and cement an agreement that speaks to and for Canada this government is basically making us a hostage in the face of the two other partners which have not had their debates. They have not ratified their deals and are not prepared to ratify them until it is time to cross the t, dot the i and put the signature on that piece of legislation.
The leader talked this morning about the triple crown. He said this is more an agenda of the Prime Ministers to complete the triple crown. He defined the triple crown as the free trade agreement of 1988, the GST and now NAFTA. It is more a crown of thorns for the country.
It is not because this party is against trade and not because Canadians do not understand the importance that trade provides to our national economy but the government has placed the emphasis too much on the words free trade when instead it should be emphasized as fair trade.
Trade should be conducted by a set of rules and regulations that provide a level playing field for Canadians as well as Americans and Mexicans. If it is done on the basis of fair trade we do not have anything to fear in this country. Our businesses do not feel insecure when
they have to compete with Mexicans, Americans or any other business from any part of this world.
When a trade deal is flawed and there is a bad negotiating strategy it gives rise to insecurity and fear. The Tories are basically asking Canadians to trust them. They are taking a "trust us, we know what we are doing" attitude once again.
Canadians are not as stupid or gullible as this government would like to portray them. Those very same Canadians are living day in and day out the ramifications of the first round of negotiations, the free trade agreement.
They remember the Tories saying in 1988 in this House and during the campaign that if we did not grab the FTA we would miss the economic whirlwinds that would be ours. If we did not get into the free trade agreement the Americans would take their business south. If the employees did not support the big multinational corporations their jobs would be lost.
Where are those promises today? Where are those promises in my own city of metropolitan Toronto that during the recession lost half of all the jobs that the country lost? There were over 225,000 jobs lost in the metropolitan Toronto area alone. Most of those lost jobs and opportunities were in the manufacturing sector.
Do you not think the free trade agreement exacerbated that economic recession? Do you not think the free trade agreement has aggravated the loss of manufacturing jobs in Toronto, North York, Etobicoke and other parts of our manufacturing centres? Do you think Canadians believe that the free trade agreement did not aggravate the job situation, the number of plant closings, the direction of dollars and profits in research and development to the American head companies situated in American cities and towns?
What about the adjustment programs? The Prime Minister in this House and during the campaign actually had the temerity to suggest if the free trade agreement was blessed by Canadians he would have the best transition programs in the western hemisphere. Imagine.
Where are those workers today who have been displaced by the free trade agreement? Where is their adjustment assistance? Where are the adjustment programs? Where is the adjustment training to help Cana-
May 25, 1993

Government Orders
dians through this point of transition into a so-called newer economy? They are on the roadside. On top of it this the government gets tough with the UI recipients. The hon. member for Don Valley North gets tough with the food bank recipients. The government gets tough with the refugees. That is who it gets tough with.
Where are the promises today? It does not matter that the Americans are still dealing for their sake or the Mexicans. The government comes to Canadians and to this House saying: "Trust us. We know what is good for you". The message from Canadians in any public survey about NAFTA is thanks but no thanks. They are living the practicality of a badly negotiated deal already.
They are not saying it in theory. They are not saying it in the abstract. TTie breadwinners who are still looking for that job are living it and they are unfortunate testimonies to a flawed negotiated free trade agreement.
Even Statistics Canada-not Liberal Party research- says that in January to February of this year we lost in our trading relationship with the United States $393 million in trade deficits on top of those that were already provided in the past number of years. The government's own statistics do not live up to the rhetoric that it is espousing during this debate.
In conclusion, we are not suggesting that anybody is against trade for goodness' sake. People know that our country depends on trade, but we require fair and honest trade and a level playing field trade practice.
We need a government to look after number one and number one happens to be this country. If it can learn anything through this debate, it is to simply hold on. There is no mad rush to sign, seal and deliver a deal simply because the Tories want to use this on the Friday night of their convention to paint the Prime Minister in some kind of godlike light.
Take a look at the country. Feel the pain. Talk to the businesses and those who are going down. Talk to the employees who are searching for work. Be smart and take a page out of the American play book because they are looking after number one as they should and we are saying that the Canadian government should do la meme chose.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to register my opposition to the bill to implement the North American free trade agreement.

In terms of trade, NAFTA represents a tremendous opportunity lost for Canada. Today, however, I would like to limit my remarks to its environmental aspects.

NAFTA has failed miserably to reconcile economic and trade objectives with environmental concerns. What should have been a model for future free trade agreements has become a lost opportunity. If we want better trade agreements, they will have to promote environmental protection as well as the trade objectives contained in these agreements.
When it condemned this development almost a year ago, the Liberal Party clearly identified what we considered to be key environmental concerns that had to be an integral part of NAFTA.
Our four basic conditions were as follows:

The conditions we have posed for the successful integration of environmental and trade matters are as follows. There should be: first, clear principles for the harmonization of environmental standards between all countries in the agreement; second, a clear commitment that the objective of this harmonization should be to establish the highest level of environmental protection; third, the incorporation of environmental considerations openly and publicly in the dispute settlement resolution process; and fourth, the establishment of an environmental threshold for new country accession to the agreement. Unfortunately the legal text of the NAFTA has failed this test on every count.
The environmental provisions now contained in the NAFTA are simply inadequate and incomplete. The promotion of a multi-party environmental protection agenda is more than a simple matter of altruism. It is a matter of the economic self-interest of this country.
In the words of Hilary French from the Worldwatch Institute: "Trade is neither inherently good nor bad, but how it is conducted in the future is now a matter of deep concern and unprecedented opportunity. It can spread wealth and knowledge or it can accelerate the destructive trends that are now underway. To those who have come to recognize that the list of living systems and materials that make up the earth's environment, constitute the global economy's main inventory of economic assets, there is no question what that choice must be".

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
For this government to push ahead now without us knowing the contents of the environmental side agreement, without fair and reasoned debate within the country, it is very clear that this government once again has made the wrong choice.
There are now wide expectations that environmental issues will feature prominently in future GATT negotiations. All parties concerned with the environment and trade must begin to grapple with the innovations needed to merge these two fields. It is a merger which is so required and so paramount in contemporary policy but unfortunately operates all too often in two solitudes.
The negotiation of the environmental accord to NAFTA offers an unparalleled opportunity to achieve this reconciliation. It is now obvious that nothing less than a strong agreement on the environment will win approval for the NAFTA, the U.S. Congress and its President. This situation offers Canada a challenge which is virtually unheard of and we must now respond with a strong agenda of our own.
Where is the Conservative government's agenda on these side agreements? What are its priorities? Who has it consulted to formulate its bottom line?
The truth is, as in everything else this government does, that its entire environmental accord has been driven by the American agenda and Canada's position has simply been a knee-jerk reaction to another country's pressure.
We on this side of the House believe that Canada should stand firm behind principles that are designed to further the interests of this country, behind our own priorities and behind our own national objectives.

In this respect, we believe that a North American agreement on the environment should first of all create a North American environmental commission with the power and responsibility to promote environmental cooperation among the signatories to the agreement and to investigate trade and environmental issues related to NAFTA. Second, we must adopt a common set of basic principles to deal with environmental problems. Third, we must clarify potential interpretations of the present wording of NAFTA. Fourth, we must aim for the highest
possible common standards for environmental protection. And fifth, we must provide for greater environmental expertise, in other words, openness and dispute settlement mechanisms that include environmental concerns.

These proposals and those made by other interested parties have been on the table for discussion for some time now. Unfortunately neither this House nor the relevant House committees have had the opportunity to debate many of these issues.
It is morally reprehensible that this government has so stymied debate in the country. It is morally reprehensible that this government is now seeking to go ahead before Canadians know what the final environmental side agreement will be.
The serious examination of instruments to integrate environment and trade objectives in international agreements has only just begun. The implication of various options are only now being explored. In fact the environmental accord now under negotiation appears likely to have significant implications for Canada's trade and its environmental regimes.
This underlines our dismay that the NAFTA legislation is being brought before the House now before negotiations on the environmental accord have even been concluded.
Options for this accord deserve a thorough and a reasoned debate and the development of a pro-Canadian agenda. The haste of the Tories to push NAFTA through Parliament has foreclosed this prospect. It is disgraceful for those on the other side of the House to label those who oppose NAFTA as enemies of trade. For many of us the prospect of a freer, fairer and environmentally sound trade agreement is a very worthy goal.
However those of us who look down the road as we Liberals do see a great deal more that should have been covered in this debate and in this agreement.
The Liberal outline for a North American environmental accord offers a modern approach to environment and trade. This is one that can usher in a new era in our trading relationships by forming links between the environment and trade.
May 25, 1993



Measured against Brundtland and our major commitments at the Rio summit, NAFTA stands as an initial, disappointing attempt to merge environmental and trade concerns in a single agreement.
Once again, this failure demonstrates the ever widening gap between the government's free trade rhetoric and its meagre achievements.
This bill does not meet any of the objectives identified by the Liberal Party and environmentalists as a prerequisite for Canada's signature on an international trade agreement of this kind, any more than it prepares us for competing on the global market of the 21st century, which is our main objection to this bill.

Mr. Speaker, we have actually been witnessing quite a remarkable debate in this Parliament. In fact this debate is the longest continuous debate in the life of this Parliament. It began yesterday afternoon as a result of a motion by one of my colleagues in the NDP. The hours were extended. The debate has gone on all night and will continue as long as we have breath or the government does not use its majority to cut off the debate.
During the course of this debate we have heard speeches, intelligent and otherwise, on the issues in front the House. We have covered a wide range of the issues that are raised by the legislation here before us. This is legislation which would implement the North American free trade agreement.
The legislation before the House is of profound importance to Canada. Among other elements in the legislation are provisions which effectively turn over to a secret or private group appointed by the three governments which will have the power to override the Parliament of Canada or any of the legislatures should they have the temerity to try to adopt legislation which would be deemed by this group to offend against NAFTA.
Given that power it becomes therefore doubly important that the people of Canada and this Parliament understand what has been given away in this agreement. We have all become familiar over the last four and a half years with the giveaways in the free trade agreement the devastating effect on manufacturing jobs and on other jobs across Canada.
Government Orders
The NAFTA legislation continues that process and makes it worse. It ties the hands of provincial and federal Parliaments to protect the regions of this country, to protect existing jobs and to develop social, economic and environmental policies which reflect the values of the people of this country.
It is true that of course we live in a world in which the barriers are slowly coming down. Part of that is of course our own fault as a country. We have joined over the last 40 years, despite the opposition I may say from this corner of the House, step by step in enacting an economic agenda driven primarily by corporate America which has turned the assets of this country over to private multinational, transnational corporations. As we have given virtual open access to the ownership of our assets this bill, and its predecessor the free trade legislation, reduces even further our capacity to protect our values as a country.
One of the historic challenges of Canadian governments is the challenge facing any government of a country that lives next to a substantially larger country. We look at Finland, Norway and Canada as different examples of smaller countries next to giants. From the beginning of the history of this country, almost 126 years ago, one of the key objectives was to develop sensitive, effective policies so that we could have in this country some measure of independence and some capacity in this country to develop institutions and values different from our neighbour to the south.
None of this was in any disrespect to our neighbour to the south. The peoples of that country have a democratic government. They choose the way they want to do business. However, if we wish to choose the way we want to do business then we have to act with courage and skill. Step by step over the last 20 years we have seen successive governments, Liberal and Conservative, fail in that fundamental historic test of Canadian governments. It is the test of preserving our capacity to develop our own country in the way we wish to do so.
The vision that most Canadians have of Canada is a country which shares its resources among its people on some basis of equity. We have not done terribly well at that but we have tried. We have a number of programs that have given effect to that value.

May 25, 1993
Government Orders
Over a period of time we have debated frequently in this House and around the country other ideas to improve the equity and justice and social justice that we see as important values across Canada. There were regional development policies so that areas like Cape Breton or Newfoundland are not forced to have 70 per cent unemployment. We across Canada have accepted the importance of trying to share the wealth in this country.
We have looked at social programs such as medicare and at new areas where we have not been able to advance such as national child care programs and programs to bring justice to our aboriginal people. These at least we debate in this Parliament and on the hustings. We thought we were at least making step by step progress.
However, over the last number of years we have seen not further progress in this regard, but the beginning of a significant erosion of these programs which have given voice to this value of social justice and equity in Canada. Accompanying it has been the erosion of our capacity internationally to make that kind of contribution.
Consider if this was a theoretical debate on economic policies or if the government could say at least: "Well, we may have lost a little bit here but at least we have gained on the economic side". Then at least Canadians would see a trade off.
However, the opposite has been the result of this government's policies. It was totally predictable because in trading away our capacity as a country to hold on to the social values and to try to provide us with a capacity to enact those and the environmental standards we would like to see in this wonderful country of ours, we have also traded away our capacity to protect and develop our economy.
The economic vision of the multinational corporations of corporate America is against the interests of Canadians and Canadian families across this country because as we begin to trade away the good manufacturing jobs they get replaced with less satisfactory jobs such as part-time jobs, occasional jobs, ancillary jobs, temporary
jobs and low paying jobs without benefits or pensions or without the protection of unions.
Therefore we have seen not only the continuing high unemployment, but a higher level of underemployment. We are building that Reagan, Thatcher and Mulroney vision which is of two nations living within one: a rich nation of a few privileged people and a class of people who are increasingly living in poverty.
That has been the vision which has been enacted by this government. It is a vision which will take clear, precise alternatives. But the first fundamental change which will have to take place if we are going to redirect our country is the abrogation of the free trade agreement and the defeat of the North American free trade agreement. To those two policies we in this party are pledged. We will fight for that for the rest of this debate. We will fight through the rest of this Parliament for that and we will fight in the next election on that and on that basis we will win.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say on behalf of the government that we thank the table officers, the staff, the translators and everybody else involved in maintaining the operation of this institution while we went through the prolonged debate.
For the record, in terms of the debate yesterday afternoon when we commenced report stage my staff had passed on to the staff of both parties opposite a consent motion suggesting that we sit extended hours to allow people to get on the record. Shortly thereafter the New Democratic Party member moved Standing Order 26(1) to not see the normal hour of adjournment and of course we supported it.
Nevertheless I think it is a good idea that in fact there is the time for debate for people to get their views on the record on this very important issue.
The hon. member who just spoke made some comment about worrying about manufacturing jobs. I was surprised that he did not mention the fact that last Friday Statistics Canada reported that over the last year Canada's manufacturing output has outstripped that of any other industrialized nation. He should be applauding the fact that in manufacturing over the last year we have done better than any other nation.
May 25. 1993

He also should be applauding that under the free trade agreement, not only have our total exports increased, but the percentage of exports made up of manufacturers increased as well. Not only do we have a higher percentage of North American trade, the percentage made up by manufacturers' high valued goods is even higher. The tremendous success and proof that in fact we can trade and trade well and create jobs is there for everybody to see if they have eyes to see and a willingness to accept facts for what they are.
This particular treaty and legislation has been under discussion for some considerable time. The Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade had 27 meetings, 203 witnesses and 95 submissions. The subcommittee on international trade had 29 meetings, 124 witnesses, 95 submissions, 23 exhibits, four appendices and visited 9 cities.
The number of days in the House of Commons on which the NAFTA was mentioned at least once was 234 times. The number of times it was raised in Question Period was 300 and that does not count supplementaries.
The number of statements by members was 22. The number of petitions was 14. Second reading debate was 4.5 hours. Committee study was 17 hours and 31 minutes. Report stage as of 8.30 this morning was 19 hours.
To ensure that members of the House were knowledgeable, briefings were offered to the opposition. On March 19 there was a confidential NAFTA briefing in Room 307 of the West Block. On March 31 there was a special NAFTA briefing. On April 1 we had a briefing by John Weekes who is our chief negotiator, on exports. There was a briefing on May 12 and on May 21.
The interesting thing about these briefings offered to Parliament was that the Liberals attended each of them, but the New Democratic Party members attended none
Government Orders
of them. Not one of these briefings did they attend. They said that we were trying to sneak or jam something through. They were offered five briefings and they attended none of them. Does that say something about their sincerity, their wish to know the truth, their willingness to look at both sides of the argument and their willingness to accept the facts or are they simply locked into a philosophy imposed on them by Bob White et al?
Debate and getting one's views on the record is fine, but in fact if there is an obvious unwillingness even to listen to the other side-the New Democratic Party will not even go to briefings to hear what it is all about- then one has to question how long it should go on.
I think this has been a good opportunity for everybody to get their views on the record. I am glad it happened but I think it is time to bring it to an end. I move:
That this House do now adjourn.
